comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to retain the 60-day grace period to avoid severe hardship for their family.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposal to eliminate or restrict the 60-day grace period terrifies me, because layoffs are completely outside an individual employee's control.

When a company downsizes or a project loses funding, it happens in minutes. An employee receives a meeting invite at 9:00 AM, an email from HR at 9:15 AM, and their laptop access is cut off by 9:30 AM. That worker did nothing wrong. They performed well, acted with integrity, and followed every law. Under the current rule, that 60-day window is the only thing standing between an unexpected corporate layoff and total personal ruin.

Without those 60 days, what is a person supposed to do?

It takes weeks just to navigate the legal hiring process. Even when a new company wants to hire you immediately, federal rules require them to file a Labor Condition Application with the Department of Labor, which takes at least a week to process before an H-1B transfer petition can even be submitted. You cannot complete that on Day Zero.

You cannot dissolve an entire life in 24 hours. Even if someone decides to pack up and leave the country, an orderly departure takes time. You cannot break an apartment lease, sell your car, close utility and bank accounts, ship your household goods across an ocean, and buy plane tickets overnight without suffering devastating financial penalties.

The toll on children and families is devastating. My child goes to school here, plays on local sports teams, and knows no other home. The thought that an arbitrary corporate restructuring could instantly turn my family out of status—without even a few weeks to finish a school term or say goodbye to friends—causes sleepless nights for thousands of families like mine.

We came to this country through the legal front door. We spent years navigating paperwork, background checks, and stringent visa requirements. To punish legal immigrants for corporate decisions they had zero say in is deeply unfair.

The 60-day grace period is not a loophole or a luxury; it is a basic human safety net. It allows people who have contributed honestly to this country the dignity to either find another employer who needs their skills or pack up their lives and leave with dignity.

Please do not take this away. Keep the 60-day grace period in place.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period causes severe hardship during sudden layoffs and makes leaving the country impossible.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Shrikant J
comments.commentText:
I am writing to respectfully oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other nonimmigrant workers after employment ends.

Me and my wife have lived and worked in the United States on H-1B status for 14 years. I have paid taxes every year, followed every rule, and built my life here. My two children are U.S. citizens, and we own a home in PA. This country is the only home my children have ever known, and we have always considered it ours.

Like many long-term H-1B workers, I am waiting for a green card because of the per-country backlog, a delay created by the immigration system and not by anything I did. Sixty days is already a short window to find a new sponsor, have a new petition filed, sell or arrange for a home, withdraw children from school, and wind down a life. Reducing that window to nothing would force families like mine into impossible decisions during the most stressful moment of our lives.

I understand that DHS cites administrative burden as a reason for this change. But administrative convenience should not outweigh the real harm to workers and their U.S.-citizen children. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and keep the 60-day grace period. If DHS moves forward, I ask that it at minimum:

Consider the effect on U.S.-citizen children and on homeowners and taxpayers who have contributed to their communities for many years.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

The 60-day grace period provides a reasonable transition period for workers who unexpectedly lose their jobs due to layoffs, corporate restructuring, budget cuts, or other circumstances beyond their control. Eliminating this protection would create significant uncertainty for highly skilled professionals who have maintained lawful immigration status and contributed to the United States for years.

Many employment-based workers pay substantial taxes, purchase homes, support local businesses, and build their lives and families in the United States. They may also spend years pursuing employment-based permanent residence, requiring significant investments of time, money, and effort from both employees and sponsoring employers. Losing a job should not automatically jeopardize these investments when the worker has otherwise complied with immigration requirements.

The grace period allows affected workers a reasonable opportunity to find another qualifying position, pursue a lawful change of status, or make appropriate arrangements. Without it, workers could be forced to leave the country before they have a realistic opportunity to secure new employment, even when another U.S. employer needs their skills.

Eliminating the grace period could also harm American businesses. Employers invest considerable resources in recruitment, onboarding, training, and immigration sponsorship. Forcing experienced workers to leave immediately after an unexpected layoff wastes these investments and may require companies to repeat expensive recruitment and training processes. Retaining the grace period promotes workforce mobility, reduces avoidable vacancies, and helps employers retain access to qualified professionals.

The impact extends to entire families. Workers may have spouses with careers, children attending American schools, mortgages, healthcare needs, and other long-term financial commitments. An unexpected job loss could disrupt an entire household, even when the termination results from business decisions rather than employee performance. A limited transition period helps families manage these circumstances while pursuing lawful immigration options.

The United States is also competing globally to lead in artificial intelligence, advanced computing, cybersecurity, semiconductors, and other strategically important technologies. Skilled engineers, scientists, researchers, and technical professionals are essential to developing these technologies and maintaining America’s competitive advantage. U.S. companies depend on experienced talent to innovate, build critical infrastructure, and deliver next-generation products and services. Eliminating the grace period could unnecessarily push skilled professionals out of the American workforce, weakening innovation, increasing hiring challenges, and benefiting competing economies. Retaining this protection helps U.S. employers continue using the expertise of professionals already trained and contributing here.

The current grace period is limited; it does not provide indefinite status or eliminate immigration requirements. It offers a short, practical opportunity to transition between employment or pursue another lawful option. Maintaining it balances immigration compliance with the economic realities of employment transitions.

I respectfully urge DHS to retain the 60-day grace period. Doing so would protect workforce mobility, preserve employer investments, reduce unnecessary family hardship, support continued tax contributions, and strengthen America’s ability to attract and retain the skilled professionals needed for long-term economic growth and technological leadership.
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period harms workers, employers, and families by causing unnecessary disruption.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Michael Cardinal
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (91 FR 57807)

I am writing in strong opposition to this proposed rule as someone whose lawful status in the United States depends directly on it. I am in E-3 status in Georgia. I have lived in the United States for 4 years. I work in Pilot. We also have a home we bought here.

I want to address the administrative burden rationale directly, because the rule appears to produce the opposite of what DHS predicts. Today a worker whose job ends is covered by a grace period that requires no application and no adjudication. Under this proposal, remaining lawfully requires a filing: Form I-129 from a new employer, or Form I-539 from the worker to change to another status, and a separate Form I-539 from every dependent whose status falls with theirs. DHS's own figures describe roughly 65,752 affected workers a year and more than 208,000 dependents. Form I-539 receipts already exceed 400,000 annually, with published processing times averaging nine to twelve months and backlogs reaching eighteen at some service centers, and since the Edakunni settlement expired on January 18, 2025, USCIS is no longer obliged to adjudicate dependent applications alongside the principal's petition. Adding tens of thousands of filings a year to that queue is not a reduction in agency workload, and the proposal neither estimates the increase nor explains why it is outweighed.

DHS characterizes this as restoring a prior policy, but that framing skips the most important question: what has been built in the years since. Nearly a decade of workers, employers, landlords and schools have arranged their affairs around a predictable 60-day window. Those reliance interests are legally relevant, and the proposal neither identifies nor weighs them. DHS should address this before it goes any further.

Dependent status is derivative, so this proposal reaches far past the person who lost a job. On DHS's own account, more than 208,000 spouses and children hold status tied to one of these workers. Under this rule they would fall out of status the day after a layoff they had no part in. A spouse with lawful work authorization would lose the right to work overnight; children would be pulled out of school mid-term. Many of these households also include U.S.-citizen children. Imposing that on family members for someone else's business decision is disproportionate, and the proposal never explains why it is necessary.

The asymmetry in this proposal's analysis is hard to overlook. The benefit side is asserted in general terms, program integrity and reduced administrative burden, with no figures attached. The cost side involves tens of thousands of workers a year plus more than 200,000 dependents, and is handled qualitatively. An agency cannot conclude that benefits justify costs when it has not seriously estimated either. I ask DHS to do that work and put it out for comment before finalizing.

To put a concrete case behind that, here is my own situation:

I moved here in 2021 with my Wife and cats, we bought a house not wanting to waist money on renting. It would very hard to sell up and move home in zero days. Realistically, I would need act fairly spritely and move back to Australia anyway without an income here, so most would have this natural need as well, but need the 60 days to finalize everything that has been set up to live here. Surely that is fair!

I urge DHS not to finalize this rule and to retain the existing grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). The record as it stands does not support the change: the benefits are asserted rather than measured, the costs fall on tens of thousands of families a year, and less drastic alternatives have not been addressed. Thank you for taking this comment into account.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly writes in strong opposition to the rule and argues it increases administrative burden.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I oppose the proposed removal of the grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing provision.

Losing employment can occur unexpectedly because of layoffs, funding changes, or organizational restructuring. Workers who have complied with immigration requirements should have a reasonable opportunity to arrange new employment, seek another eligible status, or organize an orderly departure.

Recruitment and immigration paperwork take time. Even a qualified worker with an interested employer cannot reasonably complete interviews, receive an offer, and arrange the necessary filings immediately after employment ends. Eliminating this transition period could also harm U.S. employers by making it harder to recruit skilled workers already living here.

The consequences extend to families. An abrupt loss of status can disrupt a spouse’s circumstances, children’s schooling, housing commitments, and ongoing medical care. A limited transition period helps families manage these obligations responsibly.

Removing the grace period could also make workers more reluctant to report mistreatment or leave problematic employment, because losing a job would carry more immediate immigration consequences.

DHS should assess these costs to workers, families, and employers against its claimed administrative savings. It should also explain why the existing discretionary framework cannot adequately address concerns about misuse.

Please withdraw the proposed elimination and preserve at least the existing up-to-60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes removing the grace period and asks DHS to retain it.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and their families.

We are living in an era of rapid technological change, artificial intelligence, and widespread corporate restructuring. Major companies such as Microsoft and Oracle have announced layoffs and workforce reductions. Many hardworking employees are losing their jobs due to business decisions, restructuring, and economic conditions completely beyond their control.

When an H-1B worker loses a job, it is not just one employee who is affected. There is an entire family behind that employee — a spouse, children, and dependents whose lives and futures depend on that job.

Many H-1B families are law-abiding, hardworking taxpayers who have lived in the United States for years. They contribute to the American economy, pay federal and state taxes, purchase homes, support local businesses, and raise their children in American schools.

Losing a job is already an extremely stressful experience. Imagine a family suddenly facing unemployment, mortgage or rent payments, children's education expenses, health insurance concerns, and the uncertainty of their immigration status — all at the same time.

Removing the 60-day grace period would place an enormous emotional, financial, and psychological burden on these families. Children should not have to worry about suddenly leaving their schools, friends, and communities because a parent was unexpectedly laid off.

Finding a new employer willing to sponsor an H-1B transfer, completing interviews, and processing immigration paperwork takes time. Even the existing 60-day grace period can be challenging in today's job market. Eliminating it would make an already difficult situation much worse.

Many H-1B workers have also been waiting years for employment-based green cards while continuously following immigration laws and contributing to this country. They deserve reasonable consideration and stability.

The existing 60-day grace period is a modest and reasonable protection. It does not remove immigration requirements or give workers unlimited time to remain in the country. It simply allows families a short opportunity to recover from an unexpected job loss and make lawful arrangements.

A job loss should not automatically become an immigration crisis for an entire family, especially when the employee has done nothing wrong.

I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to reconsider this proposal and retain the existing 60-day grace period. Please consider the real human impact on hardworking, law-abiding, tax-paying families and their children.

Protecting families during unexpected unemployment is a matter of fairness, compassion, and common sense. Please preserve the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly states strong opposition to eliminating the grace period due to the burden it places on families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Amit Kumar
comments.commentText:
Re: Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-day Grace Period

I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and their dependents.

I have lived in the United States legally for more than 14 years on an H-1B visa. Like many Indian-born professionals, I am stuck in the employment-based green card backlog, waiting not because of anything I have done, but because of per-country limits. During these years I have worked hard day & nights, paid taxes, never violate any law and built a stable life here.

My family’s life is fully rooted in this country. I own a home and a car. My children are in school. My son came to the United States when he was one year old; he is on an H-4 visa as my dependent and will soon start college. My daughter was born here and is a U.S. citizen. For my children, the United States is home. They do not know any other.

If I lose my job through no fault of my own, this rule would leave my family with essentially no time to respond. It is not realistic to sell a house, sell a car, withdraw one child from school and another from college, and move a family across the world on a day’s notice. The 60-day grace period does not give us any special benefit. It simply gives families who followed every rule a fair and humane window to find a new employer, change status, or prepare to leave in an orderly way.

Removing it would hurt the very people who have done everything right: those who came legally, stayed legally, and have contributed to this country with years of hard work. It would also affect U.S. citizen children like my daughter, who would be uprooted with no warning.

I am not asking for more time than the current rule provides. I am asking DHS not to take away the 60 days that families like mine depend on. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and keep the 60-day grace period in place.

Respectfully,
Amit Kumar
comments.reason: Removing the grace period leaves families with no time to respond to sudden layoffs after years of lawful contributions.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by santhosh vangapelli
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose eliminating the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). DHS created it in the 2016 final rule "Retention of EB-1, EB-2, and EB-3 Immigrant Workers" to fix a real problem. Taking it away would hurt workers, U.S. employers and American competitiveness, and it would not benefit U.S. workers in any meaningful way.

1. H-1B is no longer a "temporary job" visa in practice.
Congress made H-1B a dual-intent classification. Most H-1B workers are on a path to permanent residence, and many already have approved I-140 petitions. Because of per-country limits, workers born in India can wait decades for a green card in EB-2 or EB-3. These workers are often senior engineers, researchers and technical leads. In AI and other frontier fields they are frequently senior individual contributors whose expertise is hard to replace. Their companies have built critical systems around them, and they have built their lives, homes and families in the United States. A rule that treats them as short-term visitors who can be removed overnight does not match the reality Congress and DHS created.

2. Layoffs are rarely the worker's fault and are often sudden.
In the technology industry, layoffs often happen with no notice and as part of company-wide restructuring, not because of individual performance. Under this proposal, a worker who did nothing wrong could be out of status the day after termination. That leaves no time to find a new employer, which then still needs a certified Labor Condition Application and a filed petition. Even the best-qualified candidates cannot get through a senior-level interview process and LCA certification in days.

3. The result would be a loss of talent, not jobs for U.S. workers.
Without the grace period, laid-off workers would leave the country in a rush or turn to costly and uncertain stopgaps, like B-2 change-of-status filings. U.S. employers who want to hire these workers would lose them to Canada, the UK and other countries actively recruiting the same talent. In AI especially, where the U.S. is competing globally for a small pool of experts, this rule would hand that advantage to other countries.

4. Families and U.S.-citizen children would be harmed.
Many H-1B workers have spouses in dependent status and U.S.-citizen children. An instant loss of status could force a family to leave homes, schools and medical care with essentially no notice, or to split up.

5. The grace period is already limited and discretionary.
The current rule allows "up to" 60 days, once per validity period, and never past the end of the authorized stay. DHS keeps full discretion to shorten it. DHS has not shown that the current limited grace period causes harm that would justify eliminating it entirely.

Personal perspective. My family is directly affected. My spouse works as a senior software engineer on H-1B with an approved I-140. Like many in the Indian green-card backlog, we have lived in the U.S. for years, own our lives here, and are raising a U.S.-citizen child. The grace period is the only thing that keeps a sudden layoff from forcing our family to leave the country within a day.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and keep the 60-day grace period. If DHS has specific concerns, it should address them narrowly rather than remove a basic protection for highly skilled workers who are central to U.S. innovation.
comments.reason: Eliminating the grace period harms workers, employers, and American competitiveness, ignoring dual-intent reality.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Removing the H-1B grace period would create systemic economic instability across multiple sectors of the U.S. economy. For financial institutions, the sudden departure of high earners could trigger a surge in mortgage, auto, and personal loan defaults, while forcing premature property sales that destabilize local real estate markets. This loss of residency would further ripple through local economies, as landlords, retailers, and service providers lose a consistent consumer base, reducing overall revenue for small businesses.

From an operational standpoint, American employers would face immediate productivity losses and project delays due to the abrupt exit of experienced talent. The resulting need for urgent replacement hiring would drive up recruitment costs and operational overhead. These disruptions extend to the domestic workforce, as U.S. citizen employees working on integrated projects would see their own workflows hampered and job security threatened by reduced business revenue and stalled initiatives.

The fiscal impact on the American government and taxpayers would be equally negative. By eliminating the window for H-1B workers to secure new employment, the U.S. would lose significant contributions in income and payroll taxes, alongside a drop in general consumer spending. Furthermore, the loss of expertise in critical fields like AI, cybersecurity, healthcare, and engineering directly undermines U.S. global competitiveness, potentially shifting innovation and intellectual capital to competing nations.

Beyond the macroeconomic data, the proposal threatens the stability of U.S. citizen children whose education and family lives would be upended. While the government might see a minor reduction in USCIS paperwork, these gains would be offset by increased costs related to enforcement, visa processing, and readmission. Ultimately, maintaining the 60-day grace period is a strategic economic necessity that protects American jobs, financial stability, and national innovation.
comments.reason: Removing the grace period creates systemic economic instability, loan defaults, and operational losses for U.S. firms.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Peter C
comments.commentText:
Prioritizing American Workers and Strengthening the U.S. Economy
1. Put American Workers First

The United States should prioritize American workers when companies make hiring decisions, especially when qualified U.S. citizens and permanent residents are available to fill positions. American workers contribute to the country's economic growth through their earnings, spending, tax payments, and participation in local communities.

2. Review Cross-Border Remote Employment Policies

The growing trend of U.S.-based companies hiring remote workers in Canada deserves a closer examination. Policymakers should evaluate how these arrangements affect American employment opportunities, wage levels, tax revenues, and domestic investment. When companies can perform the same work using remote employees outside the United States, there may be less demand for workers in American communities. A careful review of cross-border employment policies could help ensure that international hiring decisions do not unnecessarily weaken the domestic workforce.

3. Ensure Fair Tax Contributions

Companies and employees should comply with applicable tax laws, regardless of where the work is performed. Canadian residents working remotely for American companies do not automatically owe U.S. income tax on their wages; their tax obligations depend on factors such as where the work is performed and the applicable tax rules. However, U.S.-based employers may still have American tax obligations and contribute to the U.S. economy through business taxes, payroll, investment, and other activities.

4. Protect American Jobs and Wages

American workers should not lose employment opportunities simply because a company can hire someone abroad at a lower cost. When qualified domestic candidates are available, employers should seriously consider the long-term value of hiring locally, including workforce stability, domestic spending, and the development of American skills. Policies that encourage fair hiring practices and prevent the misuse of international labor arrangements can help protect wages, strengthen job security, and ensure that American workers remain competitive.

5. Keep More Economic Activity Within the United States

When companies hire American workers, those employees generally spend a substantial portion of their earnings on housing, groceries, transportation, healthcare, and other goods and services in the U.S. economy. This spending supports local businesses, creates demand for additional services, and helps sustain jobs in American communities. Although Canadian remote workers may also contribute indirectly to U.S. economic activity by helping American companies grow, policymakers should carefully assess how different hiring arrangements distribute economic benefits between the United States and other countries.

6. Establish Fair Rules for International Hiring

The objective should not necessarily be to eliminate Canadian remote workers from the American labor market, but to establish clear and fair rules that protect domestic employment without unnecessarily restricting businesses. The government could examine whether certain tax incentives, procurement rules, or employment policies should favor domestic hiring when American workers possess the necessary qualifications. Any such measures should be designed carefully to comply with existing laws and international agreements while ensuring that companies cannot exploit cross-border arrangements to undermine American wages or employment standards.

7. Support Every Worker Who Contributes to America

The central issue should be whether employment policies serve the long-term interests of the American economy and the people who depend on it. American citizens, permanent residents, and other workers who legally work in the United States contribute through their labor, taxes, consumer spending, and skills. The government should recognize these contributions and ensure that workers who support American businesses are treated fairly. At the same time, it should distinguish between workers who are legally employed abroad and arrangements that genuinely create unfair competition or avoid applicable obligations.

8. Make Domestic Employment a Strategic Priority

The United States should adopt a long-term strategy that encourages companies to invest in American talent, train domestic workers, and create sustainable employment opportunities. Rather than relying solely on short-term labor-cost savings, businesses should consider the broader economic benefits of developing a skilled domestic workforce. A balanced approach that combines competitive wages, workforce training, responsible hiring incentives, and effective enforcement of tax and labor laws can help ensure that American workers share in the country's economic success
comments.reason: "Prioritizing American Workers and Strengthening the U.S. Economy" The commenter argues for prioritizing domestic workers and restricting foreign labor advantages.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Seth Shaffer
comments.commentText:
Seth Shaffer
Villanova University

The Secretary of Homeland Security is granted the power to promulgate and enforce rules pertaining to visas under 8 U.S.C. § 1101, 8 U.S.C. § 1103(a)(3), and 6 U.S.C. § 112. The current rule, codified at 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(I)(2), grants some visa holders a sixty-day grace period that triggers upon the cessation of a visa holder’s employment. This regulation includes the provision that DHS may shorten the grace period at its discretion.

USCIS and DHS are well within their authority to enact this proposed change. However, there is little value in doing so. The proposed rule would eliminate DHS’s discretionary flexibility under the current statute. The current regulation allows DHS to shorten the grace period at will. Functionally, the only thing that this change achieves is a reduction in case-by-case considerations. At face value, flattening the grace period seems like it would reduce the administrative burdens on DHS where visa holders could potentially have multiple touch points with the agency while seeking other employment before the expiration of the grace period. However, all this regulation does is shift the administrative burden to other parts of USCIS.

The stated goal of this proposed rule and the functional outcomes are not aligned. The rule gives more weight to administrative efficiency than to the long-term costs associated with the rule change. Although not explicitly stated, this rule is intended to dissuade skilled visa holders from entering the United States. DHS tacitly acknowledges that this rule discourages visa holders from entering the United States in the future by dismissing a visa holder’s reliance interests and property interests as less important than minor administrative savings. The rule is discouraging for visa holders because over half of skilled visa holders bring their families with them to the United States. This rule makes the United States less desirable than other countries for skilled workers and may ultimately serve to further reduce America’s standing as a global economic power and leader of innovation at a time when rapid technological advancement may be the key determinant of economic success.
comments.reason: The rule merely shifts administrative burdens and lacks value while penalizing skilled visa holders.

comments.title: MM59 Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule, which would eliminate the 60-day grace period currently available to H-1B, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, and TN nonimmigrant workers following cessation of employment.

This rule would cause severe, immediate harm to lawfully present workers and their families through no fault of their own. A layoff or business restructuring — events entirely outside an employee's control — would instantly render workers and their dependents out of status, with no time to pursue a new employer petition, change of status, or orderly departure. The human cost is real: families who have purchased homes, paid taxes, and built lives in U.S. communities would face sudden unlawful presence and potential bars to future admission.

DHS itself acknowledges these reliance interests in the preamble yet proceeds anyway. That is arbitrary and capricious. The agency's rationale — that the grace period is "discretionary" and resource-intensive — does not justify eliminating a protection that has functioned effectively since 2017 and that serves the legitimate interests of both workers and U.S. employers who have invested in sponsoring them.

This rule would also damage U.S. competitiveness by making the nonimmigrant work visa system more punitive and unpredictable, deterring global talent from choosing the United States.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule and asks DHS to withdraw the elimination of the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I oppose eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period. Losing a job is often sudden and outside a worker's control. The current 60 days is a modest, limited window to find a new sponsor, apply to change status, or make an orderly departure — not a right to keep working. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Swetha MS

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write to oppose the elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers. The proposal is framed as a question about what happens to a worker after a layoff. It is also a question about what happens to the work that worker leaves behind — and for specialty-occupation workers in research and development, that work is often an invention in progress, a patent application mid-prosecution, or a multi-year project that cannot simply be handed to someone else.

H-1B workers are, by definition, employed in specialty occupations — and a large share of them work as engineers, scientists, and researchers whose output is measured in patents, prototypes, and publications. Innovation does not pause for a layoff. A patent application names its inventors; it cannot be reassigned to a different mind mid-prosecution without cost, delay, and sometimes loss of the invention itself. A research project built around one scientist's expertise — a materials process, a chip architecture, a drug candidate — stalls when that scientist must leave the country within days rather than having 60 days to transfer to another U.S. employer willing to sponsor the same work. The 60-day window is what lets the invention stay in the United States: it is the bridge between one employer and the next for work that is, in practice, portable only if the worker can stay.

Eliminate the window, and the pipeline breaks at its most vulnerable point. A laid-off inventor with no time to transfer does not wait; the worker departs, and the project either dies or follows the worker abroad. Foreign competitors do not need to recruit American innovation away — under a zero-grace rule, the United States hands it to them, one stranded invention at a time. The employer that sponsored the research loses its sunk investment in the same moment, and the next employer — which might have hired the worker and continued the project — never gets the chance. This is not the same as ordinary labor-market churn. A sales role can be refilled; a patent portfolio mid-prosecution and a research program built on one person's expertise cannot.

The proposal's stated rationale does not address this loss at all. It treats the grace period as dead time between jobs, when for R&D workers it is the period in which inventions, prototypes, and research programs survive a layoff intact. A rule that strands inventions and exports research talent to competing countries does not strengthen the American innovation system; it weakens it, project by project. The agency should retain the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes eliminating the grace period, stating it disrupts ongoing research and innovation projects.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing as an H-1B worker who has lived in the United States for several years, and I oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period because this proposal would push law-abiding people out of the lawful immigration system it claims to protect.

I have always done everything the system asked of me. I have maintained status, paid taxes, renewed on time, and kept my address current. The 60-day grace period is the reason that record of compliance is possible after a layoff. It is the bridge between one lawful job and the next lawful step — time to find a new sponsor, file a transfer, or arrange an orderly departure. It does not excuse anyone from the rules. It gives people a lawful way to follow them.

Remove that bridge, and ask what lawful option remains on the first day after a layoff. There is none. A worker cannot lawfully work, cannot instantly sell a car, break a lease, withdraw children from school, and board a plane in a single day. Faced with instant unlawful presence through no fault of their own, some people who would otherwise have resolved their status in weeks will instead disappear from the system: overstaying quietly, working off the books, or paying unscrupulous brokers who promise a sham arrangement. Desperation creates exactly the underground economy DHS says it wants to eliminate.

That outcome helps no one. Workers pushed underground cannot report wage theft or unsafe conditions, cannot pay taxes openly, and cannot be reached by the government. Employers who follow the rules lose, while exploitative operators gain leverage over people with no lawful alternative. Enforcement becomes harder, not easier, because cases that would have closed themselves in 60 days become investigations, absconders, and overstay statistics manufactured by the rule itself.

A grace period of up to 60 days is discretionary. DHS can already deny it to anyone who abuses it. Keeping that discretion preserves a lawful path for the compliant majority while retaining every enforcement tool against the few who misuse it. Eliminating it does the opposite: it punishes compliance and rewards evasion. I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to express strong opposition to the proposed rule titled "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period." Rescinding this vital regulatory buffer will cause extreme hardship for immigrant families, disrupt critical sectors of the U.S. economy, and misalign with the realities of the American labor market.

1. Severe Humanitarian Impact on Families and Children
Requiring immediate departure upon job termination is practically impossible for families established in the United States. Packing up a household, terminating residential leases or selling property, un-enrolling children from school mid-term, and settling financial obligations cannot occur overnight. Ending the 60-day grace period forces families—including U.S.-born children—into unnecessary distress and administrative chaos, stripping them of a humane timeline to wrap up their lives in good standing.

2. Disruption to Critical American Innovation and Industries
H-1B visa holders fill essential, highly specialized roles in fields like technology, medical research, clean energy, and engineering. These professionals are not easily replaceable, and their contributions drive innovation, spur job creation, and maintain America's competitive edge globally. Eliminating the grace period creates a climate of severe insecurity, discouraging top international talent from choosing to build their careers, launch ventures, and contribute to the U.S. workforce. 

3. Misunderstanding of H-1B Volume and Economic Function
The premise that H-1B workers replace American labor overlooks the factual reality of the U.S. labor market:
- Scale: H-1B workers represent a small fraction of the total U.S. workforce (less than 1% of total U.S. employment), concentrated primarily in areas facing persistent local talent shortages.
- Hiring Friction: USCIS processing times and corporate onboarding procedures take weeks, if not months. A 60-day buffer is the minimum reasonable window needed for a prospective U.S. employer to complete statutory labor condition applications (LCAs) and petition filings to transfer an existing worker's status.

Without a reasonable grace period, U.S. businesses lose the ability to quickly rehire qualified talent already present in the country, increasing recruitment costs and delaying critical projects.

Conclusion
The 60-day grace period established in 2017 provides a balanced, predictable framework for both U.S. employers and specialized nonimmigrant workers. Removing it offers negligible administrative benefit while causing severe harm to families and key U.S. industries. I urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition due to severe humanitarian impacts and economic disruptions.

comments.title: MM38 Comment Submitted by Anonymous

I respectfully oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers.

I have been in US from past 16 years and have built a home here giving birth to twins, seeing them grow while making friends. Currently I am on H4, however I have worked in H1B and have paid taxes, supported American businesses, and contributed to my local community. I respectfully ask DHS to consider the real-life consequences this proposal could have on law-abiding workers and their families.

Most importantly, an H-1B worker is often supporting an entire family. Consider a family with an H-1B worker, an H-4 spouse, children in American schools, a mortgage or lease, car payments, health insurance, childcare expenses, and years of community ties. If the worker is unexpectedly terminated, the consequences affect everyone. The spouse may lose employment authorization, children may have to leave their schools, and the family may suddenly face the possibility of selling a home, terminating a lease, selling vehicles, arranging international travel, and leaving the country.

The 60-day grace period is extremely important because finding another H-1B job is not instantaneous. A worker may need weeks to apply, interview, receive an offer, complete background checks, provide immigration documents, and have the new employer and immigration attorneys prepare and file the required petition. The employer also needs time for internal approvals and immigration processing. Sixty days is therefore a practical transition period, not an excessive benefit.

This can happen to a family that has done everything correctly.

Without the grace period, a worker could be forced to leave the United States shortly after termination, even when an American employer is prepared to hire that person. This creates unnecessary disruption for the worker, family, employer and economy. The worker may ultimately return to the United States for another job, meaning the immediate departure may accomplish little beyond creating substantial financial and emotional costs.

This issue is especially significant for many Indian H-1B professionals who have spent years legally working in the United States while facing lengthy employment-based green-card backlogs. A person can have an approved I-140, years of U.S. employment, a home, children, tax history and deep community ties while still depending on H-1B status.

I respectfully urge DHS to preserve the discretionary 60-day grace period. It protects families, provides employers with flexibility, supports continued tax and economic contributions, and gives compliant workers a reasonable opportunity to respond to circumstances beyond their control.

Please preserve this important protection for H-1B workers and their families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment on Proposed Rule, "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period"
Docket No.: USCIS-2026-0364 

To Whom It May Concern, 

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers, including H-1B visa holders. As a legal high-skilled professional contributing to the U.S. economy, I believe this proposed change will create severe financial hardship for lawful residents, disrupt American business operations, and introduce unnecessary administrative burdens for U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). 

First, the elimination of the 60-day grace period ignores the operational realities of the modern corporate recruiting and immigration process. In the current job market, the lifecycle of a high-skilled hire—spanning multiple rounds of interviews, background checks, the drafting of a Labor Condition Application (LCA), and the preparation of an H-1B transfer petition—reasonably takes between 4 to 8 weeks. Eliminating the grace period means that a worker laid off due to sudden corporate restructuring or macroeconomic downturns would immediately lose status on day one. This completely deprives American employers of the opportunity to retain exceptional talent already vetted and residing within the United States. 

Second, the proposed rule creates disproportionate and immediate hardships for legal nonimmigrants and their families. H-1B workers are active contributors to their local communities who hold long-term residential leases, vehicle financing, bank accounts, and enroll their children in U.S. schools. Expecting an individual to abruptly liquidate their entire life, break legal contracts, and arrange international travel within 24 hours of an unexpected layoff is logistically impossible and financially ruinous. 

Furthermore, the proposed rule inflicts severe, unjust, and lasting disruption on the families and dependent children (H-4 nonimmigrants) of these workers. For school-aged children, education and development are continuous processes deeply tied to stability. Uprooting children overnight from their classrooms and stripping them of their familiar environment causes profound psychological distress, often triggering acute stress responses and anxiety. These children are forced to abruptly sever ties with their educators, peers, and foundational social support networks without any opportunity for closure. 

Beyond standard schooling, these children are deeply integrated into local communities through after-school care, athletic training, and structured activities such as gymnastics, ice skating, and soccer leagues. In the U.S., enrollment in these youth programs and community center memberships requires seasonal or annual contractual commitments with strict non-refundable prepayments. Similarly, standard daycare contracts require a 30-day written notice for withdrawal. Forcing an immediate departure from the country on day one legally coerces law-abiding international families into sudden contract breaches, resulting in unrecoverable financial penalties. More importantly, it inflicts severe social and emotional trauma on children. Expecting families to instantly dissolve these deep legal, financial, and developmental ties is profoundly impractical and inhumane. 

Final, this rule will backfire administratively. Instead of encouraging immediate departure, the elimination of the grace period will compel thousands of laid-off professionals to simultaneously file Form I-539 to change their status to B-1/B-2 (visitor) on the very day of termination to avoid accumulating unlawful presence. This influx of urgent, defensive filings will severely exacerbate the existing USCIS case backlogs and drain the agency's adjudicative resources, contradicting the administration's stated goals of government efficiency. 

For these reasons, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed rule and preserve the existing 60-day grace period, which has successfully balanced national security, regulatory compliance, and economic competitiveness since 2017. 

Thank you for your time and for considering these critical insights during the public comment period. 

Respectfully submitted,
A Legal Nonimmigrant Professional
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the rule, arguing it ignores recruiting timelines and causes financial hardship for workers and families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Chen Ko
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS's proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers and their families. The removal of this critical buffer window fails to account for the complex, real-world realities of modern life, family integration, and asset management in the United States.

The abrupt elimination of this grace period creates severe, undue hardships in several critical areas:

Disruption of Children’s Education: For families with children enrolled in U.S. schools, an immediate or near-immediate departure requirement causes educational trauma. School years, academic credits, and curriculum tracks cannot be wrapped up overnight. Forcing children to abruptly leave mid-term or mid-year without a reasonable transition window harms their academic progress, social well-being, and mental health. A 60-day window provides a vital buffer to finish a semester or safely transfer school records.

Impossibility of Orderly Asset Liquidation and Financial Wind-down: Living and working in the U.S. involves deep financial integration—including breaking residential leases, selling homes or vehicles, canceling utilities, settling localized debts, closing bank accounts, and liquidating personal property. Doing this responsibly takes months. Forcing families to suddenly abandon or fire-sale hard-earned assets within a truncated timeframe results in severe, irreversible financial devastation and loss.

Denial of Basic Human Stability: High-skilled workers contribute significantly to the U.S. economy and infrastructure. Treating families as entirely disposable by denying them even a brief two-month window to process a sudden job loss, secure new legal pathways, or simply pack up years of settled life undermines basic fairness and humanitarian consideration.

The existing 60-day grace period was thoughtfully introduced to provide vital stability, job portability, and a humane transition window. Removing it will not achieve administrative efficiency; instead, it will punish law-abiding families, disrupt children's education, and force chaotic, distress-driven departures.

I urge USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the 60-day grace period to protect families from unreasonable disruption.

Sincerely,
Chen Ko
comments.reason: Expresses strong opposition due to educational disruptions for children and the impossibility of orderly asset liquidation.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**USCIS and DHS: Please Retain the 60-Day Grace Period for Employment-Based Visa Holders**

I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to reconsider the proposed rule **RIN 1615-AD22, “Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period.”** The proposal, published in the Federal Register on September 11, 2026, would eliminate the existing grace period for several employment-based nonimmigrant categories, including H-1B, L-1, O-1, TN and others. The current regulation, **8 CFR 214.1(l)(2),** provides up to 60 days, or until the authorized stay expires, whichever comes first. This is a limited safety net—not an entitlement to work without authorization. Removing it would impose a disproportionate burden on workers and families who lose employment through circumstances beyond their control.

**First, job loss is not always a reflection of an employee’s performance or willingness to work.** 
Layoffs can result from corporate restructuring, canceled projects, funding cuts, mergers, economic uncertainty or a client’s decision to terminate a contract. Highly skilled professionals who have contributed years of expertise to U.S. employers can suddenly find themselves without a job through no fault of their own. Unlike many U.S. workers, employment-based visa holders face an additional immigration deadline while searching for their next position. A 60-day window is already short when recruiters, interviews, background checks, offer negotiations, immigration attorneys and employer-sponsored petition filings must all align. Eliminating this window would make an already difficult situation unnecessarily precarious.

**Second, retaining the grace period supports American businesses, workforce continuity and economic competitiveness.** 
DHS itself acknowledged in its 2016 rulemaking that the grace period helps high-skilled workers pursue new employment and enables U.S. employers to facilitate employment transitions more easily. Eliminating it could cause experienced professionals to leave the country before another employer has sufficient time to recruit them and complete the required immigration process. This would not necessarily protect American jobs; it could instead increase recruitment costs, disrupt projects, lead to the loss of institutional knowledge and make it harder for employers to retain specialized talent. A policy intended to improve immigration administration should also consider these real-world consequences for American businesses and the economy.

**Third, the proposal risks imposing serious consequences on entire families for a temporary employment interruption.** 
Many visa holders have spouses and children who have built their lives in the United States, attended American schools, received medical care, paid taxes and contributed to their local communities. An unexpected layoff can put a family’s housing, health insurance, children’s education and financial stability at risk. Requiring immediate departure or a rapid change in immigration circumstances can create avoidable disruption, even when a worker has a realistic prospect of securing a new qualifying job. Immigration compliance and national interests are important, but a reasonable transition period is also consistent with fairness, predictability and responsible administration.

**Finally, DHS’s stated concerns about administrative burden and maintaining the connection between visa status and employment deserve consideration—but eliminating the grace period is not the only solution.** 
The existing regulation already limits the period to 60 days or the end of authorized stay, whichever comes first, and permits DHS to shorten or eliminate it as a matter of discretion. USCIS could improve efficiency through clearer documentation requirements, standardized adjudication guidance and targeted enforcement against genuine violations, while retaining the limited grace period for bona fide employment interruptions. I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to **withdraw the proposed elimination and preserve the 60-day grace period**. A system can uphold immigration laws, protect program integrity and still recognize that legitimate job transitions require a reasonable amount of time. Please choose a balanced approach that protects compliance without unnecessarily destabilizing workers, families and the U.S. employers who depend on their skills.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to retain the grace period, citing unfair burdens on laid-off workers and families.

comments.commentText:
Dear Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services,

I am writing to respectfully express my strong opposition to the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other eligible nonimmigrant workers under DHS Docket USCIS-2026-0364.

As an H-1B professional working legally in the United States for the past 10+ years, I respectfully request that DHS preserve this important protection and carefully consider the serious financial, professional, educational, and humanitarian consequences its elimination could have on workers and their families.

Many H-1B professionals and other nonimmigrant workers have spent years building their careers, establishing their families, and contributing their knowledge, skills, and expertise to the United States. Through their hard work, innovation, dedication, and economic contributions, they have played a meaningful role in strengthening the U.S. economy, advancing American industries, and supporting the nation's continued growth and global competitiveness. We have purchased homes and vehicles, taken on mortgages and financial obligations, paid federal and state taxes, enrolled our children in American schools, and contributed our education, technical expertise, and professional experience to the U.S. economy.

Even the existing 60-day grace period is often insufficient in today's competitive job market. Finding a suitable employer, completing multiple rounds of technical interviews, obtaining an employment offer, and coordinating an H-1B petition can take considerably longer than 60 days.

Eliminating this grace period would create an extremely difficult situation for professionals who unexpectedly lose their employment through layoffs, restructuring, or other circumstances beyond their control.

For families with children, homes, and financial commitments, the consequences would be particularly severe and very tough. It is not realistically possible to immediately sell a house, settle mortgage and vehicle obligations, arrange international relocation, pack years of household belongings, withdraw children from school, withdraw children from enrolled extra-curricular classes (music, arts, dance, etc.) and return to home country without substantial financial losses and emotional hardship.

Innocent Children (mostly U.S. citizen kids and U.S. born kids) should not have to experience sudden disruption to their education, classes, stability, and family life because a non-immigrant parent unexpectedly loses employment.

The grace period also serves a practical purpose for employers. It provides a limited opportunity for businesses to recruit experienced professionals already residing in the United States and complete the necessary immigration procedures. Eliminating this flexibility could disrupt hiring, reduce workforce mobility, and make it harder for employers to retain valuable technical expertise.

I recognize DHS's interest in maintaining clear immigration requirements and reducing administrative burdens. However, I respectfully ask the Department to evaluate whether eliminating the grace period would create disproportionate hardship compared with the administrative benefits of the proposed change.

I request that DHS consider the following alternatives:

Retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period for eligible nonimmigrant workers and their dependents.

Evaluate extending the grace period to 90 or 180 days, particularly for non-immigrant workers experiencing involuntary layoffs.

Consider the time reasonably required to complete employment searches, hiring interviews, employer-sponsored immigration filings, and family relocation arrangements.

Assess the economic and humanitarian impacts on homeowners, taxpayers, spouses, and school-aged children before finalizing any regulatory changes.

H-1B professionals are engineers, scientists, researchers, healthcare professionals, technology specialists, and other skilled workers who contribute to American businesses, economy, innovation, research patents, and communities.

We respect U.S. immigration laws and understand the importance of maintaining lawful immigration status. We are simply requesting a reasonable transition period when unexpected employment changes occur.

Losing a job should not immediately become an immigration emergency that threatens an entire family's financial stability, housing, and innocent children's education.

I respectfully urge DHS and USCIS to preserve the 60-day grace period and consider providing greater flexibility for lawfully employed and tax-paying nonimmigrant professionals and their families.

Thank you for considering my public comment and the real-world circumstances of families who would be severely affected by this proposed regulation. Thanks for your understanding.

Sincerely,

A Concerned H-1B Professional, Parent of two young kids, Homeowner, and U.S. Taxpayer

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose removing 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I submit this as an H-1B holder, including in response to DHS’s request for comment on reliance interests (Section IV.D).

Immediate loss of status with no time to respond.
DHS states that workers and dependents “would be considered to be immediately failing to maintain their nonimmigrant status the day after” employment ends. A layoff, often without notice, would put a family out of status overnight, exposing them to deportability (INA 237(a)(1)(C)(i)), possible unlawful presence consequences (INA 212(a)(9)(B)), and adjustment bars (INA 245(c)(2)). DHS itself anticipates Notices to Appear. No one can sell a home, end a lease, relocate a family, and settle finances in one day.

DHS’s reliance analysis is conclusory and contradicts its own findings.
DHS acknowledges that families have “purchased houses, paid taxes, and invested in the local community,” then dismisses reliance as “misplaced” because the grace period was discretionary. But it has been codified in regulation since January 2017. People bought homes, signed leases, enrolled children in school, and made investments relying on a published rule, not on guesses about enforcement discretion. Footnote 32 admits affected people must “immediately cease any activity related to the local community,” yet treats this as common to departures. An agency must weigh serious reliance interests (FCC v. Fox; State Farm). Admitting a loss and dismissing it is not that.

Concrete harms.
Home and property: day-one departure means distressed sales, lease penalties (which DHS acknowledges), and unmanaged property.
Investments and finances: retirement accounts, loans, and other commitments can’t be unwound in a day. Forced liquidation causes losses and tax penalties.
Children and family: about 208,000 dependents per year (DHS’s estimate) lose status the same day. Children can’t be withdrawn from school, transfer records, and relocate overnight.

Reentry: DHS says workers may later “apply for admission,” but that requires a new employer, an approved petition, visa processing abroad, and admission, with no guaranteed timeline. DHS also acknowledges that failure to maintain status is a negative factor in future discretionary adjudications.
Settling affairs: DHS recognizes “opportunity costs of time to get their legal and personal affairs in order.” This rule removes that time.
The cost-benefit analysis understates the harm.

DHS’s lost-income estimate covers about 3,795 people per year, though it identifies about 65,752 workers annually experiencing cessation of employment. It does not estimate costs for dependents, citing data limitations. Table 1 lists no qualitative costs to beneficiaries (“None”) despite costs described in the preamble. DHS concedes its data proxy undercounts. A rule affecting hundreds of thousands of people cannot rest on an analysis that excludes most of them.
Portability and the compelling-circumstances EAD.

INA 214(n) lets H-1B workers start new employment upon filing, but extension and change of status generally require being in status when filing. Without the grace period, portability is largely theoretical for laid-off workers. The rule also narrows the window for compelling circumstances EADs, one of the few safeguards for involuntary job loss. DHS does not explain how these fit together.
Administrative burden is insufficient justification.

Reducing adjudicator workload does not justify immediate loss of status for tens of thousands of workers and hundreds of thousands of dependents. DHS dismissed less harmful alternatives without meaningful analysis.

Requested action.
Withdraw the proposal and keep 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). In the alternative: (a) retain a grace period, even if shortened or for fewer classifications; (b) adopt a transition period exempting workers already in the U.S.; (c) clarify how portability and the compelling-circumstances EAD would operate.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes removing the rule, citing immediate out-of-status harms and ignored reliance interests.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ashish Agarwal
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule eliminating the 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers whose employment ends.

I have lived and worked in the United States lawfully for over a decade on an H-1B visa. I spent more than 10 years at one employer, paid taxes throughout, bought a home, and am raising two young children here with my wife. I also hold an approved immigrant petition with a 2017 priority date, which means I have been waiting in the green card line for nearly a decade through no delay of my own.

Earlier this year, my position was eliminated in a company-wide reduction in force. That is exactly the situation the grace period exists for. A senior-level job search does not conclude in days. Interviews for roles at my level run through multiple rounds over several weeks, and a new employer's petition then has to be prepared and filed. The 60 days did not give me comfort; they gave me just enough time to do this in an orderly and lawful way, without my family losing status because of an employer's business decision I did not control.

Ending the grace period would not reduce the government's workload, and the proposal effectively admits this. Officers would still have to establish when employment ended. The difference is that a gap of even one day would then destroy status, which means more denied cases, more appeals, and more people pushed into immigration court. The proposal also states the rule would cost employers nothing, which is not credible: U.S. employers filed thousands of petitions for workers in a grace period in 2025 alone, because hiring someone already here, already vetted, and already contributing is good for them too.

The human cost falls on families, not just workers. My children are in school here. A mortgage, a home, and a family's entire life cannot be unwound overnight because a layoff happened on a Tuesday. Workers who lose status the day after a layoff are not people who broke the rules; they are people the system invited here, who followed every rule, and who are being punished for their employer's decision.

I respectfully ask DHS to withdraw this proposed rule. At a minimum, the grace period should be retained for workers with approved immigrant petitions and long lawful residence, who have the deepest roots here and the fewest realistic alternatives.
comments.reason: Opposes the proposed rule, explaining how the grace period was necessary during a sudden layoff.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose this proposed rule. DHS should withdraw it and keep the 60-day grace period.

In 2019 I was laid off. I needed 30 days to start a new role, and the grace period gave me that time. Everything I have built since depends on it.

DHS invited comment on reliance interests. Here are mine: I now have a two-year-old. Leaving within a day of a layoff would mean one day to deal with a house, cars, daycare, our finances, and every professional and personal commitment I have outside work. The alternative would be removal proceedings in immigration court, which DHS's own analysis anticipates. DHS puts the cost of attending that hearing at $204.43 to $300.53 per person, and its Table 1 lists the rule's qualitative cost to affected workers as "None."

The harm reaches whole families. Dependent spouses and children lose status when the worker does, and a working spouse's authorization depends on that status. One layoff can end both of a family's incomes overnight.

DHS's own data shows the scale. From FY 2021 to FY 2025, an average of 65,752 covered workers a year lost or left jobs, peaking at 80,034 in FY 2023. About 18,000 a year had a new employer file for them within the grace period. Each of those filings came from a U.S. employer hiring someone already here, yet Table 1 lists the quantified cost to employers as "None."

This rule is cruel, and DHS has not shown any benefit in return. It lists the rule's monetized benefits as "Not Estimated" and says it cannot estimate how much time grace-period review adds to a case. Its 1.9 million figure counts extensions, changes of status, and other filings that officers must review for maintenance of status regardless of any grace period. That review won't go away: officers will still have to establish when a job ended to decide whether status was maintained. With no margin, a one-day gap or an unclear final paystub will decide cases, which means more requests for evidence, denials, and appeals. DHS also concedes the rule would add immigration court referrals and work for DOJ and ICE.

If discretionary review is the burden, DHS could apply the grace period by default and limit discretionary review to cases with signs of fraud, unauthorized work, or other violations. None of the alternatives in Section IV.E considers that.

DHS says the grace period is inconsistent with the statute, but INA 214(a) authorizes DHS to set the time and conditions of admission, and the grace period is one of those conditions. Congress gave H-1B workers portability so they can start with a new employer as soon as it files. With no grace period, a laid-off worker could use it without leaving the country only if a new employer filed by the day the old job ended, which a sudden layoff rarely allows.

DHS's claim that reliance is misplaced because the grace period is discretionary fails too: in Department of Homeland Security v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), the Supreme Court held that a policy's discretionary nature does not automatically defeat reliance interests. If this rule is finalized, a single layoff makes a worker and their dependents deportable the next day, puts them at risk of unlawful presence that can trigger 3- or 10-year bars on returning, and can bar them from adjusting to permanent residence. DHS's own preamble lists every one of these consequences.
comments.reason: Opposes the rule and urges DHS to withdraw it, detailing severe personal and family impacts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I came to the United States in 2006 and have been living and working here on different visas for most of the past 20 years.

When my visa ended, I returned to India for my daughter's birth and came back to the U.S. a few years later on a different assignment. This also affected my green card process, putting me back in the queue. At that point, my plan was always to eventually return to India, so I never imagined that I would still be in this situation almost 20 years later.

Things changed as my daughter grew up here. She has lived in the U.S. since she was two years old and is now in high school. She has gone through almost her entire schooling here. Moving her to India now would be a very difficult transition, especially with the differences in the education system.

We had thought about returning earlier, but COVID disrupted those plans. After that, she was going through middle school, and we didn't want to interrupt her education. Before we knew it, she was starting high school.

I was laid off once, and the 60-day grace period helped me stay in the country and look for another job. I know firsthand how important those 60 days can be. Losing a job is already stressful, especially when your visa status depends on your employer. Without that grace period, people like me would have to make a decision about leaving the country almost immediately, even when we have children attending school.

And leaving the U.S. doesn't necessarily solve the problem. Even if I find another employer willing to hire me after returning to India, getting a visa stamping appointment can be another major roadblock. The uncertainty makes it difficult for both the employee and the employer.

I understand that these are temporary visas and that we are expected to follow the immigration rules. I have always understood that. But after living here legally for so many years, the reality is that our families, and especially our children, have built their lives here.

I am not asking for a green card or special treatment through this rule. I am only asking that people who lose their jobs through no fault of their own be given a reasonable amount of time to find another employer or make arrangements to leave.

The 60-day grace period is not a permanent solution. It is just a small window of time that makes a huge difference when someone suddenly loses their job.

I am absolutely willing to return to India, especially as my parents are aging and I want to be there for them. But I also don't want to disrupt my daughter's education in the process. Even moving from one coast to another within the U.S. had a huge impact on her life. I can only imagine how much harder it would be for her to move to a different country and adjust to an entirely different education system.

I request DHS to keep the existing 60-day grace period and consider the impact its removal would have on families like mine, particularly children who have spent most of their lives in the United States.
comments.reason: Shares personal experience of how the grace period helped during a layoff and opposes removal.

comments.commentText:
​1. H-1B Professionals Fill Critical STEM Shortages and Boost Domestic Productivity
​High-skilled foreign workers fill persistent talent deficits in critical fields such as artificial intelligence, semiconductor manufacturing, biotechnology, and advanced engineering. According to economic studies, H-1B workers complement rather than replace native-born workers, helping American firms expand, launch new product lines, and increase overall domestic productivity.
​2. Eliminating the Grace Period Causes Severe Brain Drain to Global Competitors
​Top-tier foreign researchers, engineers, and founders choose the United States because of its dynamic and stable career ecosystem. Stripping away basic workplace transitions forces elite talent to migrate to countries with foreign-talent-friendly policies (such as Canada, the UK, Germany, and Australia), directly handing American technology and intellectual property leadership to foreign rivals.
​3. H-1B Workers Generate Net Domestic Jobs for American Citizens
​Research from the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) consistently demonstrates that high-skilled foreign workers drive entrepreneurship and corporate growth. For every H-1B professional employed, domestic companies build broader teams, indirectly creating multiple secondary jobs in management, operations, sales, and local services for American workers.
​4. Sudden Layoffs Threaten Tax Revenue and Local Economies
​H-1B holders contribute billions of dollars annually in federal, state, and local taxes, alongside Medicare and Social Security contributions. They buy homes, pay rent, purchase cars, and support local small businesses. Eradicating the 60-day grace period converts productive tax-paying residents into immediate forced departures, inflicting sudden financial losses on local housing markets and municipal economies.
​5. Job Mobility Drives Free-Market Innovation and Patent Creation
​High-skilled workers are disproportionately responsible for U.S. patents, technological breakthroughs, and scientific papers. The 60-day grace period allows laid-off talent to reallocate their skills to higher-value ventures and growing startups. Eliminating this buffer starves burgeoning U.S. companies of available, specialized talent during economic realignments.
​6. Zero-Day Status Increases Administrative Friction and Backlogs for USCIS
​Without the 60-day grace period, thousands of suddenly laid-off professionals will be forced to file defensive, emergency Change of Status applications (such as Form I-539 to B-1/B-2 visitor status) merely to maintain lawful presence while winding down their personal affairs. This influx of unnecessary administrative paperwork will severely congest USCIS processing queues, adding costly agency overhead without providing any economic benefit.
​7. Protecting Workers Prevents Employer Exploitation and Preserves Wage Standards
​The grace period provides high-skilled workers with vital job mobility. If termination results in immediate deportation, workers lose all bargaining power, exposing them to potential wage suppression, unsafe working conditions, and retaliation. Maintaining a grace period protects fair market wage standards across entire industries, benefiting both foreign and U.S.-born workers alike.
