comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This comment is submitted anonymously. I oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers, and I write to point out an inconsistency inside DHS's own framework that the proposal never explains: the agency gives specialty-occupation workers employment continuity when they voluntarily change jobs, then denies the mirror-image buffer to workers who are laid off through no fault of their own.

Today's system is built around continuity. Under AC21 §105 portability, an H-1B worker with a new employer petition filed on their behalf may begin working for that new employer upon filing — they do not wait for approval. Under 8 CFR 214.2(h)(13)(i)(A), a worker with a timely filed extension petition may continue working for up to 240 days while USCIS adjudicates. The animating principle is obvious: a specialty-occupation worker who remains eligible and authorized should not be thrown into unlawful status by paperwork timing, and American employers should not lose authorized talent to administrative lag.

The 60-day grace period is the same principle applied to the involuntary case: when employment ends, the worker gets a short window to transfer to a new employer, apply for a change of status, or depart orderly. The proposal keeps the continuity machinery for the worker who chooses to move — portability, 240 days — and deletes the only continuity protection for the worker who had no choice. It is, on its face, a harsher rule for the blameless layoff than for the voluntary switch, and the NPRM offers no reason for the asymmetry.

The functional result is worse than an inconvenience: it effectively deletes the cap-exempt transfer path for laid-off workers. A new employer cannot file an H-1B transfer petition for someone who has fallen out of status on day zero; the 60 days existed precisely because transfers take time — finding the new employer, preparing the LCA, assembling the petition. Without it, a laid-off specialty-occupation worker is expected to either exit the country immediately or attempt a change-of-status from outside lawful standing. Employers willing to hire displaced U.S.-trained talent lose access to them, while the departing worker's U.S. citizen teammates absorb the knowledge gap.

DHS also retains a materially identical buffer for other categories — the same proposal leaves grace periods for dependent and student classifications untouched — and the Department's own long-standing policy recognizes that an orderly exit requires time. There is no asserted rationale for why an H-1B worker, whose classification requires a college degree and a specialty-occupation offer, deserves less runway than classifications with weaker ties to the U.S. labor market.

A regulation that treats continuity as a benefit of the voluntary case and a privilege of the involuntary case is not a coherent program; it is a penalty aimed at people who lost their jobs. DHS should retain the 60-day grace period and withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: Opposes eliminating the grace period, arguing it creates an unfair inconsistency for laid-off workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am a machine-learning engineer working in the United States on an H-1B visa, and I am writing to oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period.

The grace period has nothing to do with weakening enforcement. It exists because reality is messy: even careful, law-abiding workers can lose a job overnight through a restructuring, an acquisition, or a grant that does not renew. Sixty days is already a scramble — barely enough time to find a new sponsoring employer, file a petition, and keep one's life intact.

What concerns me most is not even my own situation. It is what happens to the expertise this country paid to attract. My colleagues and I work in fields — artificial intelligence, semiconductors, advanced computing — where the United States competes directly with strategic rivals. Governments and companies in those rival countries actively recruit American-trained talent, and they are patient: they can wait for a layoff.

Under the current rule, a laid-off engineer has 60 days to transfer to another U.S. employer, and most do — the talent stays here. Under the proposed rule, that same engineer becomes unlawfully present the day the job ends and must leave almost immediately. The talent does not vanish. It relocates — often to the very countries competing with the United States. DHS is a national-security agency, and this rule would, day after day, convert American investment in skilled immigration into a recruitment pipeline for its competitors.

This is not a theoretical risk. I have watched brilliant researchers — people who earned PhDs at American universities and built their careers inside American labs — take positions abroad after immigration setbacks. Each departure is a quiet transfer of knowledge the United States cannot get back.

No American worker gains a job from this change. The position does not reopen; the work is reassigned or automated. What the country loses is the person: the taxpayer, the consumer, the mentor, the colleague.

Please withdraw this proposal. The 60-day grace period is a small, practical measure that keeps lawful, vetted, high-skill workers contributing to the United States instead of being driven into the arms of its competitors.
comments.reason: Opposes eliminating the grace period because it harms skilled workers and drives talent to competitors.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
**Public Comment on DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period**

I support the Department of Homeland Security’s proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for certain nonimmigrant workers following the cessation of employment. I believe this proposal can help strengthen immigration enforcement, protect American workers, and reinforce the principle that temporary employment-based visa programs must serve legitimate workforce needs and operate under strict compliance requirements.

**Protect American Workers and Ensure Fair Competition**

The H-1B program should address genuine shortages of specialized skills, not become a mechanism for suppressing wages, displacing qualified American workers, or creating an unfair competitive advantage for employers that rely on temporary foreign labor. Immigration policies should prioritize a fair labor market in which American workers have meaningful opportunities to compete for jobs and advance their careers.

**Strengthen Accountability and Prevent Visa Fraud**

The government should rigorously investigate fraudulent petitions, false employment representations, sham job offers, unauthorized employment, and other abuses of the H-1B program. Employers that knowingly violate immigration or labor laws should face meaningful penalties, including financial sanctions, petition denials, and temporary or permanent debarment where authorized by law.

Eliminating the discretionary grace period should be accompanied by stronger verification of whether qualifying employment actually exists, whether employers comply with petition requirements, and whether workers maintain lawful immigration status. USCIS should coordinate with the Department of Labor and other relevant agencies to identify recurring patterns of abuse and conduct targeted audits of employers with credible indicators of noncompliance.

**Maintain the Integrity of Temporary Visa Programs**

An employment-based visa is granted for a specific authorized purpose; it should not become an indefinite pathway to remain in the United States without satisfying the applicable immigration requirements. Removing the automatic availability of an extended grace period would reinforce the connection between authorized status and its underlying purpose.

I encourage DHS to implement this proposal consistently, provide clear guidance to employers and workers, and ensure that any exceptions permitted by law are narrowly defined, objectively justified, and not used to circumvent the program’s requirements.

**Recommended Additional Safeguards**

I respectfully urge DHS to consider the following complementary measures:

1. Strengthen employer audits and verify that H-1B positions, wages, work locations, and employment arrangements are consistent with approved petitions.
2. Impose meaningful consequences on employers and other parties that knowingly engage in fraud, collusion, or systematic violations.
3. Improve transparency and enforcement data concerning H-1B violations, investigations, penalties, and repeat offenders.
4. Protect American workers against unlawful displacement, wage suppression, and discriminatory hiring practices.
5. Ensure that temporary visa programs remain subject to clear eligibility requirements and effective oversight, with no preferential treatment for employers that fail to comply with the law.

**Conclusion**

I support the proposed rule as a measure to strengthen the integrity of the U.S. immigration system. Protecting American workers, preventing visa fraud, enforcing immigration laws, and ensuring fair competition should remain central priorities of federal policy.

I urge DHS to finalize this proposal, subject to applicable law, and pair it with robust employer accountability, targeted fraud investigations, and transparent enforcement. The objective should be a lawful, fair, and accountable employment-based immigration system that protects the interests of American workers and the American public while ensuring that legitimate immigration pathways are not undermined by abuse.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: Supports eliminating the grace period to protect American workers and prevent program abuse.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I support eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period and undertaking broader reforms to reinforce the temporary, employment-based purpose of the H-1B program. Immigration policies should have clear eligibility requirements, meaningful limits, and effective safeguards against fraud and misuse.

My concerns extend beyond the grace period to provisions that permit qualifying H-1B workers to obtain extensions beyond the usual six-year limit while pursuing permanent residence. Although these extensions may be lawful, I believe policymakers should reconsider their scope and duration. In my view, the H-1B program should generally remain limited to six years, with any exceptions narrowly defined and carefully reviewed. An approved immigrant petition should not reduce the scrutiny applied to continuing eligibility.

I also believe the system should fairly recognize the different requirements of employment-based immigration pathways. Applicants pursuing classifications such as EB-1, EB-2 National Interest Waiver, and O-1 must provide substantial evidence relevant to their respective standards, including extraordinary ability or the national importance of their proposed work. Policymakers should examine whether opportunities to maintain status and employment are appropriately balanced across these pathways.

Another concern is the potential use of fabricated professional credentials, purchased authorship, manipulated citations, or misleading research claims to obtain immigration benefits. Where credible evidence identifies such conduct, authorities should investigate and impose appropriate consequences on applicants, employers, and intermediaries responsible. Stronger verification would protect both the integrity of the system and applicants whose achievements are authentic.

I also support closer oversight of hiring arrangements involving H-4 spouses, particularly when a spouse or personal associate influences recruitment or employment decisions. Such relationships should not permit sham positions, preferential arrangements that circumvent applicable requirements, or unlawful exclusion of qualified U.S. workers. Employers should be accountable for legitimate jobs, accurate representations, and compliance with applicable employment and immigration laws.

For these reasons, I support ending the discretionary grace period alongside a separate review of long-term H-1B extensions and dependent employment policies. These reforms should be clearly defined, supported by evidence, and focused on protecting U.S. workers, preventing abuse, and maintaining public confidence in the immigration system.
comments.reason: Supports eliminating the grace period and undertaking broader reforms to the H-1B program.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly support the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) for H-1B and other covered nonimmigrant workers.
The current 60-day period after employment ends gives foreign workers a significant advantage that U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents do not receive. When an H-1B worker loses a job, they currently have up to two months to remain in the United States, search for a new sponsor, and file a new petition. American workers who lose a job receive no such protected window. Removing this grace period restores a closer link between the visa status and the specific employment that justified it, as the statute intends.
In practice, the grace period has made it easier for certain employers—particularly in information technology and financial services—to maintain continuous pipelines of foreign workers. In my experience and observation at companies including Bank of America and across IT roles, there is a clear pattern in which managers preferentially hire workers from the same national or ethnic networks, often bringing in relatives, acquaintances, or individuals from the same communities abroad. These practices reduce opportunities for qualified American citizens and permanent residents who are ready and able to perform the same work. The jobs involved are frequently not highly specialized; many could be filled by U.S. workers already living here. The ability of foreign workers to remain for 60 days after termination makes it easier for these internal networks to keep positions occupied by the same groups rather than opening them fairly to the broader labor market.
Ending the grace period would reduce this incentive. Without the 60-day buffer, employers would face greater pressure to hire available U.S. workers rather than cycling foreign workers through successive H-1B positions. It would also discourage the use of the visa as a vehicle for bringing family members and building closed employment networks that systematically disadvantage American applicants.
The H-1B program was created to fill genuine specialty-occupation shortages, not to create a parallel labor market that prioritizes foreign networks over U.S. citizens. Eliminating the discretionary grace period is a necessary step toward restoring fairness for American workers. I urge DHS to finalize the rule as proposed without delay or weakening amendments.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
comments.reason: Supports eliminating the grace period to restore parity and reduce preferential foreign hiring.

comments.commentText:
I am writing to express concerns regarding the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers, and to offer a constructive regulatory alternative that balances agency efficiency with the needs of the workforce.
1. Balancing Administrative Goals with Real-World Impacts
The 60-day grace period was originally established to provide a practical and compassionate transition window for highly skilled professionals who have integrated into U.S. communities. Many affected nonimmigrants have resided in the U.S. for multiple years, purchased homes, signed long-term leases, and enrolled children in local school systems.
While the agency's goal of streamlining status tracking and reducing internal oversight burdens is understandable, the proposed rule appears to underestimate the severe logistical and financial challenges of an immediate departure. Requiring an individual to wind down their personal affairs, vacate a residence, and arrange international travel for a family within 24 hours of sudden employment termination is structurally impractical.
2. Proposed Alternative: Utilizing Existing Infrastructure for Transition Status
To satisfy the agency’s objective for clear, real-time status tracking without causing severe personal disruption, DHS could utilize its existing digital infrastructure to offer a transitional bridge.
It is proposed that upon the termination of sponsored employment, eligible nonimmigrants be permitted to submit an online notification to transition into a modified Visa Waiver Program (VWP) category without a requirement to depart the United States first.
• Mechanism: This online submission would act as an automatically approved, time-limited status update. It would grant the individual a non-extendable 90-day period solely dedicated to managing an orderly, self-funded departure and settling local financial obligations.
• Implementation: This solution minimizes administrative processing for agency staff. It could be efficiently implemented through a minor adaptation to the existing electronic travel authorization or USCIS online portal systems.
This approach ensures that DHS retains immediate data tracking and oversight of the individual's status, while preserving a humane and logical timeframe for professionals to conclude their affairs. I respectfully request that DHS consider this balanced alternative.
comments.reason: Expresses concern with eliminating the grace period and proposes a transitional bridge alternative.

As H-1B visa holders, we play a significant role in the U.S. economy by paying taxes, supporting local businesses, creating economic value, and contributing our skills and expertise. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ravi Ramanathan
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security:

I oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers who lose their jobs. I am a US citizen, and I have worked with H-1B employees in my organization, and I know firsthand that some bring expertise that cannot be replaced by posting a job opening or putting someone through a training course.

My concern is practical. If my company went out of business, these employees would not suddenly become less capable or less valuable. They would still be the same people whose judgment I trust and whose work I have seen firsthand. If I started another company, I would do everything within my capacity to hire them again, while meeting all applicable legal requirements.

But starting a company takes time. Securing funding, establishing operations, defining positions, and arranging employment cannot always happen immediately. Eliminating the grace period could force these employees to leave before I or another employer could put a lawful hiring arrangement in place.

The result would be a loss of expertise, not because that expertise was no longer needed, but because the opportunity to retain it disappeared.

One example is someone who understands how to manage complex enterprise data in Salesforce Data Cloud and make it useful for AI agents. That may sound like a software skill, but the difficult part is not knowing which buttons to click. It is understanding what the data means, how different systems describe the same customer, which information is reliable, and which relationships an AI agent needs to interpret correctly.

A company might have customer information spread across Salesforce, financial systems, support applications, and older databases. Two records might look like duplicates but represent different legal entities. Another pair might look unrelated but belong to the same customer. A field that appears outdated might still be essential to understanding a contract or a service obligation.

An experienced employee knows how to investigate those situations. They know what questions to ask, whom to involve, and when an apparently simple solution could create a serious problem.

That judgment matters when preparing information for AI agents. An agent can produce a confident answer without understanding that the underlying records were matched incorrectly or that an important business exception was overlooked. Someone must understand the information well enough to recognize those risks before they become operational problems.

This is not knowledge that comes from a certification alone. It develops through years of implementation work, difficult decisions, mistakes, corrections, and conversations with people across the business.

I am not saying that American workers cannot learn these skills. They absolutely can, and employers should invest in their development. I am saying that learning takes time. There is a difference between someone who understands the basic concepts and someone who has repeatedly applied them to complicated, real-world situations.

An experienced specialist also helps other employees become more effective. They explain decisions, review designs, mentor colleagues, and prevent a team from repeating mistakes. Losing that person can affect several people’s work, not just leave one position unfilled.

When I say that these skills could be lost forever, I do not mean that an employee would forget what they know or could never legally return. I mean that their availability to a particular American employer or team could be lost permanently.

Someone who has to leave may accept a job elsewhere, relocate their family, and build a new life. By the time an American employer is ready to hire them, returning may no longer make sense. The professional relationship and the opportunity to build something together may be gone.

I recognize the importance of immigration enforcement, fair wages, and protecting American workers. Employers should follow the rules and should never use immigration status to exploit employees. Preserving a limited transition period is consistent with those principles. It gives qualified workers and legitimate employers time to pursue a lawful next step.

A company can fail because it loses financing, a major customer, or its place in a changing market. None of those events proves that its employees have nothing more to contribute. Policy should recognize that distinction.

The 60-day grace period does not guarantee another job, and it does not independently authorize someone to work. It provides a short window to explore lawful options after an employment relationship ends. From an employer’s perspective, that window is already tight.

Removing the grace period could take that chance away before either of us has a realistic opportunity to act.

Please preserve the grace period. 

Thank you
Ravi Ramanathan
comments.reason: Opposes eliminating the grace period because starting a company or rehiring skilled workers takes time.

comments.commentText:
I oppose eliminating the 60 day grace period because it treats a layoff, which is often completely outside a worker's control, as an immediate status violation. These beneficiaries have been vetted and have built lives here around lawful employment, including leases, taxes, children's schools, and in many cases a spouse whose own work authorization depends on the principal's status, and the proposal would force families to uproot or separate with essentially no time to wind things down. Finding new qualifying employment, or even arrange departure is going to be impossible. It will not help the broader job market either. Forcing a skilled worker who has just been laid off to restart a job search from abroad, instead of transferring to another U.S. employer that already wants to hire them, does not create a job for anyone else. It just creates a vacancy that lasts longer, pushes employers, toward return transportation costs and lost productivity, and gives companies a reason to locate specialized work elsewhere, typically to countries with a stable availability of labor. Keeping a short and discretionary 60 days is a modest and practical buffer that lets the labor market actually reabsorb people who are already here lawfully, rather than turning every layoff into an unnecessary disruption for workers, families, and employers alike.
comments.reason: Treats layoffs as immediate status violations and forces families to uproot without time to wind things down.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tara Lin
comments.commentText: Please restore the grace period.
comments.reason: Asks to please restore the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write as an engineer employed in the United States on H-1B status. I respectfully ask the Department to withdraw the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), or, at a minimum, to retain a shorter bridging period and clarify the proposal's interaction with existing H-1B portability protections.

The grace period is the only orderly mechanism available to a non-immigrant worker navigating a gap between lawful employment. Since 2017, up to 60 days of discretionary grace after employment ends has given workers time to secure new employer sponsorship, apply for a change or extension of status, or arrange departure. Under this proposal, a worker would be considered to have failed to maintain status beginning the day after employment ends. For a family with small children, school enrollment, a lease, and community ties, that cliff does not produce compliance - it produces disruption that penalizes workers for events outside their control, such as a layoff.

Consider what the Department asks of a worker like me, who has lived lawfully and paid taxes here for a decade. A professional earning a competitive salary pays six figures in taxes every year - federal income tax, state income tax, Social Security and Medicare, property tax on the home the Department itself acknowledges workers have purchased. Over ten years, that is more than a million dollars contributed to federal, state, and local treasuries. The proposal would take that same worker and, the day after a layoff, reclassify him as someone who has failed to maintain status - unlawful overnight, with no grace period even to arrange an orderly departure: no time to break a lease without penalty, sell or ship a household, withdraw children from school, or book travel. The rule converts a decade of lawful, tax-paying residence into a same-day status violation with no room to leave legally. That outcome does not serve program integrity; it treats the most compliant participants in the system - long-term, tax-paying legal immigrants - worse than anyone else, who is at least given time to wind down their affairs.

The proposal's reliance-interest analysis is incomplete. The Department acknowledges that affected workers have purchased homes, paid taxes, and invested in their communities, yet concludes that administrative burden outweighs those interests. But the alternative is not costless: every worker forced into immediate departure represents lost tax revenue, abandoned leases, and employer investment in recruitment and onboarding that the Department's own data shows it evaluated in over 1.9 million petitions since 2017. The grace period does not cost the government the worker's status - it costs only the administrative evaluation the Department already performs, and it returns a more orderly immigration system in exchange.

I also note that the proposed rule does not address its interaction with H-1B portability under INA 214(n). A worker who changes employers through a timely filed petition may rely on portability, yet the proposal would simultaneously treat that worker as out of status from the day after the prior employment ends. The Department should clarify that a timely filed, non-frivolous change-of-employer petition preserves lawful status during its pendency, so the rule does not inadvertently swallow a protection Congress created.

For workers like me, the grace period is not a loophole. It is the bridge that makes orderly employer changes - the very labor-market mobility the H-1B program is designed to enable - possible without punishing families. I urge the Department to retain it.
comments.reason: Ask the Department to withdraw the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Many H-1B workers have consistently fulfilled their tax obligations and made significant contributions to the U.S. economy. Many have also made substantial financial commitments, including purchasing homes, investing in real estate, and taking out long-term mortgages from U.S. banks.

If the existing grace period is eliminated, H-1B workers who unexpectedly lose their jobs could be forced to leave the country at very short notice, leaving behind their homes, financial commitments, and other obligations. Such a policy would not only create severe financial and personal hardships for these individuals and their families but could also have broader economic implications for the United States.

A more balanced approach would be to retain the existing grace period for H-1B workers who lose their employment due to legitimate circumstances beyond their control, such as layoffs, restructuring, or business closures, where the employee is not at fault. This would provide reasonable protection to law-abiding workers while safeguarding the broader interests of the U.S. economy.
comments.reason: Retain the grace period for layoffs beyond worker control to protect workers and the economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS to retain the up to 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). The grace period has worked as intended since January 2017. It gives H-1B workers, and their families, a short and orderly window after a job ends, to prepare to leave or to find a new sponsoring employer.
The proposal would make these workers and their dependents fall out of status the day after employment ends. DHS has not shown that the grace period causes any real problem. Its stated reasons, regulatory alignment and administrative burden, are thin, and its own data undercut them. Meanwhile the costs to workers, families, and U.S employers is grave.

The impact to worker families especially U.S citizen children would be disastrous. How can families be reasonably expected to find a new home and school for the children in another country within one day?! 60-days is a short, reasonable timeframe so the family can make arrangements to depart from the U.S or find a new employer. Personally, this rule hits close to home for me. My children who are American citizens, will be shocked to learn that they will not even be allowed a chance to say good bye to their friends before they are uprooted. This is a very draconian way of treating legal, law-abiding immigrants.

I have further comments in the attached Word document. Kindly review them as well.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to retain the grace period and highlights disastrous impacts on U.S. citizen children.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To Whom It May Concern at the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:

I am writing to express my strong, unequivocal opposition to the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I respectfully demand that DHS completely withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the full 60-day grace period without any reduction or limitation.

As a high-skilled H-1B nonimmigrant worker, a homeowner in Texas, and a parent, I have built my family’s life in the United States while relying on the stability and safety net established under the existing regulations. Reducing or eliminating this window creates immediate, severe humanitarian, financial, and logistical disruptions that DHS has failed to justify:

Disruption to Children and Education: For families with school-aged children enrolled in local U.S. school districts, an involuntary job loss caused by corporate downsizing or economic constraints should not result in children being uprooted overnight. The full 60 days is the absolute minimum time required to navigate transitions without causing severe psychological distress and academic harm to school-aged children.

Real Estate and Asset Liquidation Realities: Owning real estate in the United States requires substantial time to manage, lease, or liquidate. Fulfilling mortgage obligations, working with property management companies, or selling a home in Texas cannot physically be accomplished in 30 days or less. Shortening or removing the 60-day window subjects lawful homeowners to forced asset sales, devastating financial loss, and severe risk of mortgage default.

Protection of Core Reliance Interests: High-skilled visa holders pay local taxes, support local economies, and contribute significantly to U.S. innovation. We made long-term financial commitments—such as purchasing homes and enrolling our children in school—based on the explicit legal framework established in 2017. Removing or reducing the 60-day rule unfairly penalizes lawful, compliant professionals for broader economic downturns completely beyond our control.

Final Position:
Any reduction below the full 60-day window is insufficient to address the logistical, educational, and financial realities facing nonimmigrant families. I urge DHS to listen to public feedback and maintain the 60-day grace period rule in its entirety.

Respectfully submitted,
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed rule and demands DHS completely withdraw the proposal.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Tharun Parvath

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Xavier Jimenez
comments.commentText:
I submit this comment in strong opposition to the proposed removal of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). I am a law student with ties to immigrant communities and I urge the Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) to withdraw the proposal due to the lack of true justification for removing the rule, outside of continuing the current administration's unethical and immoral war on immigrants. 
	DHS’s central argument is that the grace period “disconnects” status from employment and is “not mandated by statute.” But a regulation that is not statutorily required is not thereby inconsistent with the statute. The proposal cites no court decision or statutory text that makes the grace period unlawful. It also acknowledges that the grace period was a considered exercise of the Secretary’s authority under INA § 214(a), adopted through notice-and-comment rulemaking in 2016 and operating for nearly ten years. This is far from DHS’s claim that the grace period has not been in existence for a long time.
Further, DHS cites over 1.9 million filings in which officers “potentially” had to consider the grace period. But those are filings officers would have adjudicated anyway, and DHS concedes it cannot estimate how much time the grace period analysis actually adds. Its own data show only about 3,795 workers a year were sponsored by a new employer within the grace period. A burden that cannot be quantified does not justify displacing a rule that workers and employers have relied on for a decade. DHS also rejected the obvious alternative of clearer evidentiary requirements, without showing that it would fail.
	DHS moreover acknowledges that workers and their dependents would be treated as out of status the day after employment ends. That means abrupt uprooting for people who have leases, children in school, and mortgages, often after being laid off from their jobs, which they did not choose. The proposal’s own estimate shows affected workers could lose about $21,877 in income from a two-month gap. Calling these harms “incidental” to the rule, as the Family Assessment does, understates them. The consequences of this can follow a family, including citizen family members, for years. 
Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm and FCC v. Fox, an agency changing course must seriously consider reliance interests. DHS lists such interests (employers’ hiring plans, workers’ homes and careers, community ties) and then declares them “misplaced” because grace period eligibility is discretionary. Yet DHS itself says discretion to deny was exercised only in cases involving violations, fraud, or similar concerns. The grace period has operated as a strong rule for ordinary workers. DHS’s own internal logic within its proposal does not 
Employers lose access to workers already vetted and trained, forced to wait through consular processing instead of hiring promptly. Employers who terminate H-1B and O-1 workers must also fund return transportation, a cost DHS acknowledges. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has already urged DHS to consider how the grace period reduces disruption for companies and workers alike. The rule’s stated benefits, meanwhile, are entirely qualitative and are unsupported by proper scientific data. 
	DHS relies primary on revoked I-129 petitions as a proxy for grace period use and admits this misses many cases. It states it cannot estimate how many dependents or workers would be forced to depart. A rule that affects roughly 65,000 workers a year and over 200,000 dependents should rest on better scientific evidence, rather than inadequate statistics and the detestation of immigrant communities that the current administration has. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this immoral proposal.
comments.reason: Submits comment in strong opposition to the proposed removal of the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Bobby  Fitzpatrick
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule because DHS has not adequately explained how its categorical elimination of the discretionary grace period interacts with the H-1B portability framework Congress enacted in INA § 214(n), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(n).

Section 214(n) expressly authorizes qualifying H-1B nonimmigrants to accept new employment upon the filing of a qualifying petition by a prospective employer, without waiting for the petition to be adjudicated. Congress thereby established a statutory mechanism intended to facilitate transitions between H-1B employers, subject to the conditions specified by Congress.

DHS acknowledges the existence of this portability framework in the NPRM. It also acknowledges that the 2016 rule establishing the discretionary grace period was intended, in part, to enhance job portability, stability, and flexibility for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers following cessation of employment. Nevertheless, DHS now proposes to eliminate the grace period based on its view that the period is inconsistent with the statutory purpose of employment-based nonimmigrant classifications.

The Department has not adequately explained why a limited transition period following employment cessation is necessarily incompatible with Congress’s separate decision to authorize qualifying H-1B workers to begin new employment upon filing a qualifying petition. The fact that H-1B classification is employment-based does not, without further analysis, resolve how the Department should administer the statutory portability mechanism when an employee’s former employment has ended and a new employer is preparing or filing a petition.

I do not contend that § 214(n) independently guarantees every H-1B worker a 60-day grace period. Rather, the issue is that DHS must interpret and administer its regulatory authority consistently with the statutory framework Congress enacted and must provide a reasoned explanation when a regulatory change materially affects the practical operation of that framework.

The Department should specifically address the following questions:

1. How does DHS expect a worker whose employment has ceased to exercise the portability mechanism in § 214(n) when a prospective employer needs time to complete the petition-filing process?
2. What legal significance does DHS assign to the distinction between the cessation of the former employment, the filing of a new petition, and the adjudication of that petition?
3. How does the Department reconcile its stated objective of requiring departure immediately after employment cessation with Congress’s decision to authorize qualifying H-1B workers to commence new employment upon filing?
4. Why does the Department conclude that eliminating the grace period is consistent with the practical operation and statutory purpose of § 214(n), rather than merely consistent with a generalized preference for a closer relationship between status and employment?

These questions are material because a rule may be within an agency’s general regulatory authority yet still require a reasoned explanation of how the agency’s chosen approach interacts with a specific statutory mechanism. A generalized appeal to the employment-based nature of H-1B status does not answer the distinct statutory question presented by portability.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act, DHS must examine the relevant legal framework and articulate a rational connection between the facts found and the policy adopted. I request that DHS provide a substantive analysis of § 214(n), explain the expected consequences of eliminating the grace period for the statutory portability process, and revise or withdraw the proposal if it cannot adequately reconcile the proposed action with that framework.

DHS should not finalize this rule without addressing the specific statutory interaction raised here.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed rule due to failure to explain interaction with H-1B portability.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Kristie Walters
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule because DHS has not adequately analyzed the consequences of eliminating the grace period for the statutory eligibility requirements governing H-1B portability under INA § 214(n)(2), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(n)(2).

Section 214(n) conditions portability, among other requirements, on the filing of a nonfrivolous petition for new employment before the expiration of the period of stay authorized for the H-1B nonimmigrant. The statute therefore makes the timing and legal treatment of the worker’s authorized stay directly relevant to the availability of portability.

The existing regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(l)(2) provides that, during an applicable discretionary grace period, a covered nonimmigrant is not considered to have failed to maintain status on the basis of cessation of employment or activity, subject to the regulation’s limits and DHS’s discretion. The proposed rule would remove that regulatory treatment.

DHS must explain how it expects this change to interact with § 214(n)’s authorized-stay requirement. In particular, the Department should distinguish between the expiration of the period of stay authorized for an individual, a determination that the individual has failed to maintain nonimmigrant status, the individual’s eligibility to accept new employment under § 214(n), and the separate question of whether the individual may remain in the United States while a new petition is pending.

These concepts are related, but they are not necessarily interchangeable. The proposed rule’s assertion that workers should depart following cessation of employment does not, by itself, resolve the statutory questions concerning the filing deadline and eligibility conditions for portability.

DHS should identify the legal interpretation it intends to apply to a qualifying H-1B worker whose former employment has ended but whose prospective employer is preparing a new petition. It should explain whether the elimination of the grace period changes the Department’s interpretation of the period of stay authorized for purposes of § 214(n), and, if so, identify the legal basis for that interpretation. If DHS does not intend to change its interpretation of § 214(n), it should explain how the proposed rule will operate alongside that interpretation in realistic employment-transition scenarios.

The Department should also address whether its analysis distinguishes between a petition filed before the relevant authorized-stay deadline and a petition filed after that deadline. The statutory conditions cannot be treated as a general assurance that portability remains available regardless of timing, but neither should the Department leave employers and workers without a clear explanation of how its proposed regulatory change affects the application of those conditions.

This is not a claim that § 214(n) automatically preserves portability for every worker after employment cessation. It is a request for the Department to explain a material interaction between the proposed rule and an express statutory eligibility requirement.

The Administrative Procedure Act requires an agency to consider important aspects of the problem and provide a reasoned explanation for its action. Where a rule changes the regulatory treatment of employment cessation in a way that may affect the timing or availability of a separate statutory mechanism, DHS should explain that interaction rather than assume that the two frameworks operate independently.

I request that DHS provide a specific legal analysis of § 214(n)(2), clarify the intended treatment of the authorized-stay requirement following elimination of the grace period, and revise the proposal if the Department cannot demonstrate that the resulting framework is legally coherent and sufficiently clear for affected workers, employers, and adjudicators.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed rule because DHS inadequately analyzed statutory eligibility impacts.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Leanne Whalen
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule because DHS has not adequately explained why its generalized interpretation of employment-based nonimmigrant status justifies eliminating a regulatory mechanism that the Department itself previously adopted to facilitate employment transitions, particularly in light of Congress’s express enactment of H-1B portability.

Congress enacted INA § 214(n) to authorize qualifying H-1B workers to accept new employment upon the filing of a qualifying petition. That statutory design recognizes that the H-1B program is not limited to a system in which a worker can move between employers only after every administrative step has been completed. Subject to the statutory requirements, Congress specifically authorized a form of employment portability while a new petition is pending.

In its 2016 final rule, DHS separately established a discretionary grace period to enhance job portability, stability, and flexibility for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers following cessation of employment. In the current NPRM, DHS acknowledges that historical purpose but now concludes that the grace period is inconsistent with the purpose of the relevant nonimmigrant classifications.

The Department should not treat the general principle that H-1B employment is employer-specific as a complete answer to the distinct policy and statutory question raised by § 214(n). Employer-specific eligibility and statutory portability can coexist: a worker may be required to qualify for new employment under the applicable petition requirements while Congress nevertheless permits that worker to begin the new employment upon filing a qualifying petition.

The critical question is therefore not whether H-1B status is connected to employment. It is whether DHS has adequately explained why eliminating the transition period is necessary to preserve that connection, and how the Department’s chosen approach accounts for Congress’s separate decision to permit qualifying employment transitions without waiting for petition adjudication.

DHS should address the following issues in its final rule:

* Whether the Department considers Congress’s enactment of § 214(n) relevant to its interpretation of the permissible regulatory treatment of employment cessation.
* Why the statutory authorization to begin new employment upon filing does not support maintaining a limited transition period while a qualifying petition is prepared and submitted.
* Whether DHS has assessed the practical consequences of eliminating the grace period for workers who are eligible for portability but cannot ensure that a prospective employer will file a petition immediately upon cessation of their prior employment.
* Why the Department believes its statutory-alignment rationale justifies a categorical repeal rather than a clearly defined transition framework that preserves the statutory requirements for new employment.

The Department may have authority to revise its prior regulation, and § 214(n) does not expressly require a 60-day grace period. But neither proposition relieves DHS of its obligation to consider the relevant statutory framework and explain its policy choice. An agency may change its policy, but it must acknowledge the change and provide a reasoned explanation that addresses important aspects of the issue before it.

The Department’s own history is relevant. DHS previously determined through notice-and-comment rulemaking that a limited grace period would promote employment portability, stability, and flexibility. The current NPRM recognizes that history but does not adequately demonstrate why the Department’s present interpretation of the employment-based classifications resolves the separate statutory concerns raised by § 214(n).

I request that DHS expressly address Congress’s portability framework in its final explanation, identify the legal and factual basis for its conclusion that eliminating the grace period is consistent with that framework, and withdraw or materially revise the proposal if it cannot provide a reasoned explanation.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposed rule regarding employment transitions and H-1B portability.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write to oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary up-to-60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers. Most of the debate about this rule has focused on large employers, but I want to describe how it would look from a small business, because I live there.

I am an engineer on an H-1B visa at a company with about 30 employees. We do not have an immigration department. We do not have lawyers on retainer. When a large technology company needs to file an H-1B petition for a new hire, it is a routine line item. When a company our size does it, it means weeks of collecting evidence, paying outside counsel by the hour, and a founder signing forms they barely understand. We do it anyway, because we need the talent and the talent needs the job.

Here is what the proposed rule would do to that fragile arrangement. Suppose my employer hits a rough quarter and has to lay me off — a decision I do not control. Today, the 60-day grace period gives me a window to find another employer willing to file a change-of-employer petition, and gives a small company time to actually file it. Under the proposal, I would fall out of status the same day my employment ends. No small employer can assemble and file a petition overnight; only the largest corporations, with standing immigration counsel, could move that fast. The practical effect is that small and mid-size companies would simply stop hiring H-1B workers, and the workers they already employ would live one restructuring away from having to leave the country.

That outcome does not protect American workers. It hands the largest employers a near-monopoly on high-skilled immigration labor, raises their bargaining advantage over the workers they hire, and starves the small firms that drive a disproportionate share of U.S. innovation. A worker at a 30-person company contributes the same taxes, the same research, and the same economic activity as one at a 30,000-person company — the grace period should not become a privilege only the giants can afford.

Please keep the discretionary grace period. It is the one piece of this system that keeps the door open for small employers.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposed rule, explaining how it uniquely harms small business hiring.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period. It is a necessary time frame for a worker to seek another job and ensure that Visa requirements are being met. Visa holders contribute greatly to the US economy and pay taxes, and thus should be granted a reasonable period of time to find other employment before losing Visa status.
comments.reason: The commenter explicitly opposes eliminating the 60-day grace period, citing the need for time to find employment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
In this proposed rule, DHS proposes to eliminate the 60-day grace period afforded to certain nonimmigrant classifications following the end of their employment. Consequently, workers under E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B, H-1B1, V-1, O-1, and TN visas would be required to immediately depart the United States after their employment ends, unless they have another legal basis to stay.
DHS claims this reduces administrative burden by eliminating determinations on whether to shorten or eliminate the grace period in specific situations, but I do not believe that interest outweighs others. I believe that it is important to consider the administrative burden, reliance interests, and the real-life impact on communities the proposed rule would have. This will increase the workload on ICE and DOJ. DHS proposed the grace period rule 10 years ago, claiming this was needed to provide skilled workers more flexibility and mobility. I believe nonimmigrant workers have relied on this, made plans, and integrated into communities believing they would have 60 days to make arrangements. DHS acknowledges this would result in lost income, particularly for workers who intend to return to the United States, as they would be required to depart the country immediately, conduct their job search, and re-enter the country. Currently, a worker would have 60 days to conduct a job search and begin new employment while maintaining legal status. The workers under these visas are, by design, highly skilled workers or professionals from countries with a close economic relationship to the United States. I believe that shifting deportation efforts to expel these workers immediately following their termination of employment only serves to disrupt families and hardworking community members. I am concerned with how this rule could play out once enacted – if someone were terminated without notice as a result of layoffs or restructuring, rather than the natural ending of a contract term or voluntary resignation, they would have to immediately restructure their lives to be able to leave the country immediately or be subject to potential deportation – this comes at a huge social and financial cost. I believe the current grace period protects both the interests of nonimmigrant workers and their employers, and that the justification given by DHS for eliminating the grace period is inadequate.

comments.commentText: Hello, removing the 60 day grace period makes thing uncertain for employee and employer. More over, he has to sell, giveaway, loan or leave the things that he bought and it also hurts the organization for example if he bought a car on a loan or lease it abandoing it makes his credit score less and chances of able to loan again difficult and for the organizations the debt is not filled thus there is no intention of doing business with immigrants thus destructing the demand. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Swathi Meher
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the existing 60-day grace period for H-1B, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, and TN nonimmigrant workers following the loss of employment.

The 60-day grace period is an essential safeguard for individuals who have legally worked, paid taxes, contributed to the U.S. economy, and established their lives and families in this country. Losing a job due to layoffs, company restructuring, or economic conditions is often beyond an employee’s control. Eliminating this protection would place hardworking individuals and their families in an extremely vulnerable position, leaving them with little or no opportunity to secure new employment, transfer their immigration status, or make necessary arrangements.
Many of these workers have spent years contributing their skills and expertise to American businesses. They have purchased homes, raised children, supported local communities, and followed U.S. immigration laws. It is unreasonable and unfair to expose them to immediate immigration consequences simply because their employment ends unexpectedly.

The existing grace period also benefits American employers by allowing them a reasonable opportunity to recruit and retain experienced international professionals. Removing it would create unnecessary uncertainty, discourage skilled workers from building their careers in the United States, and ultimately weaken the country’s ability to attract and retain global talent.

The fact that the grace period is discretionary does not diminish its importance. Administrative convenience or resource considerations should not outweigh the serious consequences this change could have for legally employed workers, their dependents, and the businesses that rely on their contributions.

I strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider and withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety. Preserving the 60-day grace period is a matter of fairness, economic stability, and respect for individuals who have complied with immigration laws and contributed meaningfully to American society.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule, stating the grace period is an essential safeguard for workers and employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I disagree with the proposal. To put any family in such a situation is inhumane. A grace period should be provided for existing workers as they were invited to work in the country and have paid taxes as much, if not more as any other resident. To invite them, give a job, and give them hope to establish a living here, and if layoffs happen at no fault of them, to not give them grace period to figure out their next steps is not the right thing to do.
comments.reason: The commenter disagrees with the proposal, calling it inhumane to deny laid-off workers time to figure out next steps.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sarah M
comments.commentText:
As a U.S. citizen and recruiter, I strongly oppose removing the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders who lose their jobs. This period provides a critical window for skilled professionals to find new employment, transfer their H-1B sponsorship, and continue contributing to the U.S. economy.

Removing this protection would create unnecessary hardship for legal workers and their families while potentially pushing highly skilled talent to other countries. From my experience in recruiting, companies already have access to a vast global talent pool, and policies that make it harder for skilled workers to remain in the U.S. could further incentivize businesses to move jobs and operations overseas.

If our goal is to protect American jobs, we should focus on upskilling the domestic workforce, encouraging investment in the U.S., and ensuring fair competition based on skills and merit—not making it more difficult for legal workers to navigate an unexpected job loss.

I urge policymakers to retain the 60-day H-1B grace period. A strong economy is built by keeping jobs, talent, and investment in America while giving workers a reasonable opportunity to recover from employment disruptions. Let's focus on making our workforce more competitive and keeping opportunities in the United States.
comments.reason: The recruiter urges policymakers to retain the 60-day grace period to prevent unnecessary hardship and talent loss.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sophia Levy
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule because DHS has not adequately reconciled its proposed immediate failure-to-maintain-status framework with the specific eligibility language Congress enacted in INA § 214(n)(2)(B), 8 U.S.C. § 1184(n)(2)(B).

Section 214(n) permits qualifying H-1B nonimmigrants to accept new employment upon the filing of a qualifying petition, provided the statutory eligibility requirements are satisfied. One of those requirements is that the new-employment petition be filed before the expiration of the individual’s “period of stay authorized by the Secretary.”

The NPRM states that, following elimination of the grace period, affected nonimmigrants would generally be considered to have failed to maintain nonimmigrant status beginning the day after their qualifying employment or activity ceases, unless they are otherwise authorized to remain in the United States. This proposed treatment raises a material statutory question that DHS must answer before finalizing the rule.

The expiration of an individual’s authorized admission period, a determination that the individual has failed to maintain nonimmigrant status, and the availability of a period of stay authorized by the Secretary are legally significant concepts. DHS should not assume that they are interchangeable without explaining the relevant statutory and regulatory basis.

The distinction is particularly important under § 214(n). If DHS intends to treat cessation of employment as immediately ending the period of stay authorized for purposes of § 214(n)(2)(B), it should identify the legal authority for that interpretation and explain how it follows from the statutory text. If, instead, the individual’s previously authorized admission period remains relevant to the statutory filing deadline despite a determination that the individual has failed to maintain status, DHS should explain how the proposed rule will operate in that circumstance.

These are not merely semantic questions. The Department’s interpretation determines whether an otherwise qualifying H-1B worker can satisfy the statutory filing condition for portability after employment ceases. A regulatory change that eliminates the existing treatment of employment cessation could materially affect that determination, yet the NPRM does not adequately explain the precise legal relationship between its proposed status rule and the statutory filing condition.

DHS should expressly answer the following questions:

1. Does the Department interpret the proposed immediate failure-to-maintain-status rule as automatically ending the “period of stay authorized” for purposes of § 214(n)(2)(B)?
2. If so, what statutory text or binding legal authority supports treating employment cessation as equivalent to expiration of the authorized-stay period?
3. If not, how will DHS determine whether a new petition was filed before the statutory deadline in cases where employment has ceased but the previously authorized admission period has not expired?
4. Will adjudicators apply a uniform interpretation of this requirement following the repeal, and what guidance will govern cases in which employment cessation, petition filing, and the expiration of the admission period occur on different dates?

I do not contend that an unexpired admission record necessarily establishes eligibility for portability, or that § 214(n) independently guarantees a 60-day grace period. The issue is whether DHS has adequately explained how its proposed regulatory change interacts with the specific statutory eligibility condition Congress enacted.

Because DHS invokes statutory alignment as a central justification for this rule, it must provide a coherent explanation of how its interpretation fits the statutory framework. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, an agency must address important aspects of the problem and articulate a rational connection between the evidence and its decision.

I request that DHS provide a specific legal analysis of § 214(n)(2)(B), clarify the legal effect of employment cessation on the authorized-stay requirement, and revise or withdraw the proposal if it cannot reconcile its approach with the statutory text.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule because DHS has not reconciled it with statutory eligibility language.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Lucy Jones
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule because DHS has not adequately explained how its proposed requirement that affected workers depart following cessation of employment is consistent with the practical operation of the employment authorization Congress expressly provided under INA § 214(n)(1).

Section 214(n)(1) provides that a qualifying H-1B nonimmigrant is authorized to accept new employment upon the filing of a qualifying petition. It further provides that employment authorization continues until the new petition is adjudicated, unless the petition is denied. Congress thus established a statutory mechanism that permits qualifying workers to begin new employment without waiting for adjudication, subject to the conditions Congress specified.

The NPRM proposes eliminating the discretionary grace period and states that affected workers generally would be expected to depart following cessation of the employment or activity underlying their nonimmigrant classification, unless otherwise authorized to remain. DHS also suggests that departure generally would not preclude a future application for admission following approval of a new immigration benefit request.

That response does not adequately address the distinct statutory question raised by § 214(n). The ability to apply for admission from abroad is not necessarily equivalent to the ability to exercise the in-country employment authorization Congress provided through portability. A worker who must depart may face additional consular procedures, travel expenses, scheduling delays, and uncertainty concerning the timing of return. Those consequences may affect the practical value of a statutory mechanism intended to permit qualifying employment to begin upon filing rather than after adjudication.

DHS should not assume that the availability of a future application for admission resolves these concerns. The Department must explain how it expects the proposed departure policy to interact with § 214(n)(1)’s express authorization to accept new employment upon filing and its provision continuing employment authorization while the qualifying petition remains pending.

In particular, DHS should explain whether a qualifying worker who timely files a new petition may exercise the statutory employment authorization while physically outside the United States, whether the worker must obtain a new admission before performing the employment in the United States, and how the Department expects these circumstances to affect the practical operation of portability. The Department should distinguish the statutory authorization to accept new employment from the separate legal requirements governing physical presence, admission, and authorized stay.

The issue is not whether § 214(n) guarantees every worker a right to remain in the United States following employment cessation. It does not expressly provide a 60-day grace period. Rather, the issue is whether DHS has adequately analyzed the consequences of its proposed departure requirement for the statutory employment authorization Congress created.

If the Department concludes that mandatory departure has no material effect on the practical operation of § 214(n), it should identify the legal and factual basis for that conclusion. If it expects departure to delay or impede the exercise of portability, it should explain why that effect is consistent with its statutory interpretation and why it is justified by the objectives of the proposed rule.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act, DHS must consider important aspects of the problem and provide a reasoned explanation for its policy choice. A generalized assertion that workers may later apply for admission does not answer the specific question of how the proposed rule interacts with Congress’s authorization to begin qualifying new employment upon filing.

I request that DHS provide a substantive analysis of § 214(n)(1), distinguish in-country portability from subsequent consular processing, and explain how its proposed departure policy can be reconciled with the statute’s employment authorization provision. If the Department cannot adequately address this issue, it should withdraw or materially revise the proposal.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule regarding inconsistencies with statutory employment authorization portability.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Andrea Ryan
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposed rule because DHS has not adequately connected its own estimates of the affected population to a classification-specific analysis of the statutory portability mechanism Congress enacted for H-1B workers.

The NPRM’s economic analysis identifies a substantial concentration of affected beneficiaries in the H-1B classification. DHS reports that 99.2 percent of the beneficiaries in a particular fiscal-year dataset involving revoked petitions and subsequent filings within the grace period were H-1B nonimmigrants. The Department also estimates that new petitioners filed thousands of petitions for beneficiaries during the existing grace period.

These estimates are relevant to the Department’s decision. They indicate that the practical effects of the proposal cannot be understood solely as a generalized issue affecting multiple employment-based nonimmigrant classifications. H-1B workers are subject to a distinct statutory portability mechanism under INA § 214(n), and the Department’s own data indicate that H-1B workers constitute a particularly important portion of the population represented in the relevant records.

Yet the Department must explain how its proposed repeal interacts with the statutory eligibility conditions and employment authorization provided by § 214(n). An estimate of the number of affected petitions does not, by itself, establish that eliminating the grace period is consistent with the statutory portability framework or that the anticipated administrative benefits justify the practical effects on qualifying employment transitions.

DHS should identify which portions of its analysis are specific to H-1B workers and which rely on aggregated data covering multiple classifications. It should explain whether it evaluated the timing between employment cessation and the filing of a qualifying H-1B portability petition, the proportion of affected cases in which a new petition was filed within the existing grace period, and the extent to which elimination would prevent or delay qualifying employment transitions.

The Department should also explain how it distinguished cases in which the new petition was filed before expiration of the relevant authorized-stay period from cases in which other statutory eligibility conditions may be at issue. These distinctions are central to § 214(n) and cannot be resolved solely by counting petition withdrawals or subsequent filings.

If DHS believes that its aggregate analysis adequately captures the effects on H-1B workers, it should explain why. If the Department lacks sufficient data to evaluate the consequences for H-1B portability, it should acknowledge that limitation and explain how it affects the reliability of its conclusions. The Department should not rely on a numerical estimate of affected cases as a substitute for analyzing the statutory mechanism that governs a substantial portion of those cases.

I do not contend that a high proportion of affected H-1B workers proves that the proposed rule is unlawful. Nor do I contend that § 214(n) independently requires a 60-day grace period. The issue is that DHS’s own evidence makes a classification-specific analysis of H-1B portability material to a reasoned final decision.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act, DHS must address important aspects of the problem and provide a rational explanation for the scope of its regulatory action. I request that the Department provide a distinct analysis of the effects on § 214(n), identify the evidence supporting its conclusions, and reconsider the proposal if the available evidence does not support its current treatment of H-1B portability.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule due to insufficient analysis of its interaction with H-1B statutory portability.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period. This proposal would impose an unnecessarily harsh burden on law-abiding workers and their families who have built their lives in the United States while following immigration rules.

Losing a job is already a serious financial and emotional shock. A layoff can happen without warning because of restructuring or business conditions entirely outside an employee’s control. It should not also leave an entire family without a reasonable opportunity to find another qualifying job or prepare to leave responsibly.

These families have homes, mortgages, leases, children in school and college, and ongoing medical and financial commitments. They cannot unwind years of responsibilities overnight. Selling a home, arranging international travel, transferring education, and settling obligations require time. Children should not face sudden disruption to their education because a parent unexpectedly loses employment.

Even finding a new employer requires interviews, background checks, hiring approvals, and immigration paperwork. Those steps cannot realistically happen immediately.

A limited transition period supports compliance by giving people time to pursue available lawful options or arrange an orderly departure. Removing that time would create avoidable hardship for families and could prevent American employers from retaining experienced professionals.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing grace period. Sixty days is already a short window to find a new job or wrap up an established life. Families who have followed the rules deserve that basic measure of fairness and humanity.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to withdraw the proposal, arguing it imposes harsh burdens on law-abiding workers and families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The 60-day grace period provides a critical safety net for skilled professionals and their families who may unexpectedly lose their jobs due to layoffs, corporate restructuring, or economic downturns. Losing a job is already a significant financial and emotional hardship. Requiring individuals to leave the United States immediately would create unnecessary uncertainty and severe disruption for families who have built their lives here.

Many affected workers have spent years contributing to the U.S. economy, paying taxes, developing specialized skills, and supporting American businesses. Their spouses and children who are American citizens will also be affected, specially the children who are American citizen and enrolled in American schools. Eliminating this grace period could force families to abandon everything they built over the years without any notice period, interrupt their American born children’s education, and lose financial stability through no fault of their own.

I urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period. It provides a reasonable balance between immigration compliance and the practical realities for a professional to wrap up everything to go backt. If changes are necessary, DHS should consider targeted safeguards and reasonable transition periods rather than eliminating this essential protection.

I urge DHS to consider the significant humanitarian, economic, and family consequences of this proposal and preserve the 60-day grace period for eligible workers and their dependents.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to retain the grace period to protect families from sudden disruption and severe uncertainty.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Misty Steele
comments.commentText: As a professional software developer with over a decade of experience I can assure you that fraud is both rampant and obvious among foreign workers. They routinely claim education and experience that seems impossible given their complete lack of skill and knowledge. This policy change will help clean up this process by clearing out the frauds and getting them back home where they belong.
