comments.title: Comment Submitted by JANARDHAN REDDY MABBU
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed rule "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period" (Docket USCIS-2026-0364).

The 60-day grace period is one of the few protections that gives H-1B and other employment-based workers any real ability to stand up for themselves at work. Without it, losing a job would mean immediately falling out of status and having to leave the country. That reality would hand employers enormous leverage over their foreign workers and make exploitation far easier.

My biggest concern is what this does to workplace complaints. Today, an H-1B worker who experiences wage violations, unsafe conditions, discrimination, or sexual harassment can at least report it knowing that if they are fired in retaliation, they have some time to find a new employer. If this rule takes effect, reporting a manager to HR could cost a worker not just their job but their legal right to stay in the country. Most people in that position will simply stay silent. Victims of sexual harassment in particular will feel they have no choice but to endure it, because speaking up could mean uprooting their entire family within days.

This also harms U.S. workers. When foreign workers are afraid to report violations, those violations continue unchecked, and the same managers and practices affect everyone in that workplace. Strong labor protections only work when every worker feels safe enough to use them.

The impact on families is serious too. Many H-1B workers have children who were born here or have spent most of their lives in American schools. A sudden termination with no grace period could force a family to pull their children out of school in the middle of the year and leave the country with almost no notice. Sixty days is already a short window to find a new job, sell or end a lease, and plan for a child's education. Taking it away entirely is unreasonable.

DHS says the grace period creates an administrative burden. I would ask the agency to weigh that burden against the real human cost: workers trapped in abusive jobs, harassment that goes unreported, and children whose lives are upended overnight. A modest review burden on USCIS does not justify removing a protection that tens of thousands of workers rely on every year.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule and keep the 60-day grace period in place. At a minimum, DHS should preserve the grace period for workers who are terminated after reporting workplace violations, harassment, or discrimination, so that no one has to choose between their safety and their immigration status.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the rule because removing the grace period increases worker vulnerability and fear of reporting violations.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period (USCIS-2026-0364). For H-1B workers, the grace period is what makes it possible to report harassment or abuse without risking deportation. If a worker is fired after going to HR about sexual harassment, the grace period gives them time to find a new employer. Without it, a retaliatory firing means they must leave the country almost immediately. Faced with that choice, most victims will stay quiet. A rule that discourages people from reporting sexual harassment is bad policy, and I urge DHS to withdraw it.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the rule because eliminating the grace period discourages workers from reporting harassment.

comments.reason: The commenter opposes eliminating the grace period because it helps U.S. companies hire experienced local talent efficiently.

Lastly I want to say is life of an individual on a work visa is extremely tough, every day we work hard to maintain our current positions, by upskilling ourselves, going an extra mile to be noticed and even personal sacrifices. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Srinath Kashi Ranganath
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the proposed rule titled "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period" published by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).   
JPG

The current 60-day grace period provides a critical buffer for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers (such as H-1B, L-1, O-1, and TN visa holders) who experience unexpected job loss or lay-offs. This brief transition window allows talented professionals to secure new employment, change nonimmigrant status, or make orderly arrangements to depart the United States with their families.

Eliminating this grace period will have several negative consequences:
Economic & Innovation Loss: The U.S. risks losing skilled talent, tech workers, and specialized experts to other countries with more flexible immigration policies.
Administrative Burden: Immediate departure or status-change requirements create immense administrative strain on both foreign workers and employers seeking to hire them on short notice.
Unintended Hardship: Unexpected termination already places workers in a vulnerable position. Eliminating any grace period creates severe instability for individuals and their families who need reasonable time to pack, end leases, and settle affairs.
I urge USCIS to withdraw this proposed regulation and maintain the discretionary 60-day grace period to ensure fairness, economic competitiveness, and administrative efficiency.

Thank you for your time and consideration.
comments.reason: Expresses strong opposition, citing economic loss and administrative burden for skilled workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Jesse Newman
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my opinion about the DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 proposed by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the petition to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period. 

I believe that eliminating this grace period will increase the overall administrative burden of the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services as well as other agencies (as mentioned in section 3-C). The people that have hired the workers, the workers themselves, and the agencies who are responsible for them will need to file additional paperwork should these workers wish to return to the United States for additional employment. The proposed ruling would immediately criminalize the presence of a person and their family within the United States because of a business decision of their employer. This reduces the freedom of the employer to make employment decisions, because of the potential impact.

By their own admission, the proposed ruling may "impact aliens, employers, family members and potentially communities as a whole.” (As listed in section IV-D). This ruling also affects new employers seeking skilled labor, which the proposed ruling acknowledges. I do not believe that DHS has adequately considered the potential negative impacts of eliminating the grace period. The proposed ruling does not adequately capture the costs of changing the ruling, and does not detail the financial impact of the reduction of “administrative burden”. It seems that the burden would shift to other agencies, not get eliminated.

To create adequate travel plans, involving schools, housing, remaining family members, community members, and others, takes time. To shift from an employee to a criminal in a 24-hour period, based on the actions of their employer, is untenable. It is cruel and dehumanizing. The financial burdens of the proposed ruling are not calculated, and the human cost is mentioned but not accounted for. This change would hurt people and their families, during an already difficult period in their lives. The proposed ruling would not just be costly, but it would be cruel, and have a negative impact on Americans and their interwoven communities. Thank you for considering my opinion.
comments.reason: Believes eliminating the grace period increases administrative burdens and unfairly penalizes families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Kumar Kim
comments.commentText:
Public Comment in Support of the 60-Day Grace Period for H-1B Workers Following Employment Termination

I strongly support maintaining and strengthening the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders whose employment is terminated.

Losing a job is already a stressful experience, and for H-1B workers, it also creates significant immigration-related uncertainty. Finding a new employer, securing a job offer, completing the required immigration paperwork, and filing a new petition can take considerable time. The 60-day grace period provides a reasonable and necessary opportunity to navigate these steps while maintaining compliance with U.S. immigration laws.

H-1B workers contribute significantly to the U.S. economy through their skills, experience, innovation, and specialized knowledge. Many have established their lives in the United States, with spouses, children, housing commitments, and other financial responsibilities. An unexpected job loss should not force these individuals and their families into rushed decisions or an immediate departure from the country.

Maintaining the 60-day grace period would:

1. Provide a fair transition period: Allow workers sufficient time to seek new employment and pursue a lawful change of employer or immigration status.
2. Protect families from unnecessary hardship: Reduce the risk of sudden disruption to children’s education, family stability, housing, and financial obligations.
3. Benefit U.S. employers: Give companies a reasonable opportunity to recruit experienced professionals who are already authorized to work in specialized occupations, subject to the applicable immigration requirements.
4. Support the U.S. economy: Help retain skilled talent, preserve valuable industry knowledge, and reduce unnecessary loss of experienced professionals.
5. Promote compliance and fairness: Provide a practical window for workers to complete required immigration procedures rather than forcing decisions under extreme time pressure.

I respectfully urge the Department to retain the 60-day grace period and ensure that any proposed changes do not unnecessarily shorten this important transition window. Where appropriate, the Department should also consider reasonable flexibility for workers who are actively pursuing new employment and completing the necessary immigration procedures.

A fair and predictable grace period benefits workers, families, employers, and the United States as a whole. Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: Strongly supports maintaining the grace period to provide a fair transition for workers and protect families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I strongly oppose the proposed rule to remove the 60 day grace period. It is like if a person got hurt falling down you just shoot him to die, this seems inhumane. The workers on H1-b visa are not criminals to be treated like that, they are law abiding residents who have contributed towards the economy. H1-b professional contribute equally like any other non visa individual then i think they should be also treated fairly if not equally.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I support eliminating the H-1B 60-day grace period. Introduced in 2017, this provision was not part of the original H-1B framework, and the U.S. economy operated for decades without it.

H-1B sponsorship is tied to employment with a sponsoring employer. When that employment ends due to a layoff, the sponsorship should end with it. There is no need to provide an additional 60-day period for foreign workers to remain in the United States seeking employment with another employer.

U.S. immigration policy should prioritize American workers, encourage domestic talent development, and reduce dependence on foreign labor. Eliminating this grace period would reinforce employer accountability and ensure that employment based immigration remains aligned with its intended purpose.
comments.reason: Supports eliminating the grace period so sponsorship ends immediately with employment.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
The proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period should be withdrawn because it erodes the United States' most durable competitive advantage: its ability to attract the best talent from a global pool of 8 billion people. Major competitors, including China and India, draw primarily on their domestic populations. The United States draws on the world.
History shows what that advantage is worth. In the 1930s and 1940s, Albert Einstein, Enrico Fermi, John von Neumann, Hans Bethe, and many other leading scientists came to the United States because it offered stability and security that their home countries did not. Their work helped establish decades of American scientific and technological leadership. The lesson is that the world's most capable people go where they can build a secure life, and the country that offers that security gains a lasting advantage.
The same dynamic drives the AI industry today. An Institute for Progress analysis of the 2025 Forbes AI 50 found that 60 percent of the U.S.-based companies on the list were founded or co-founded by immigrants. Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology found that over 70 percent of immigrant founders of top U.S. AI startups first came to the country on student visas. That pipeline depends on graduates being able to transition into stable work authorization and build careers here with a clear understanding of the rules.
Eliminating the grace period undermines that stability. Under this proposal, a layoff, often caused by restructuring rather than performance, would leave a worker and their family out of status immediately, with no time to secure another sponsor. Competing countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, and Germany offer more predictable paths. The most mobile and sought-after candidates will weigh that risk, and more of them will choose elsewhere.
The cost falls on American companies as well. Laid-off H-1B professionals are already in the country, already vetted, and able to move to a new employer through portability. Removing the grace period makes this pool effectively unreachable, raising the cost and uncertainty of hiring onshore and pushing work offshore. DHS's own figure of 1.9 million grace-period determinations since FY2018 shows how central this provision is to normal workforce transitions.
Retaining the grace period costs the government little. Eliminating it weakens U.S. competitiveness for talent at a time when that competition is intensifying. DHS should withdraw this proposal and retain the grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
comments.reason: Argues removing the grace period erodes U.S. competitive advantage and harms global talent retention.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers, including those in H-1B, L-1, O-1, and TN status.

The 60-day grace period, established in 2017, is a critical mechanism that brings much-needed operational reality and flexibility to the U.S. immigration and employment landscape. Eliminating this grace period will severely harm U.S. employers, disrupt critical supply chains of technical and specialized talent, and impose unreasonable hardships on legal workers and their families.

Specifically, the proposed rule fails to account for several practical realities:

Hiring Timelines and Administrative Processing: The modern high-skilled hiring process—including technical interviews, reference checks, offer approvals, and prevailing wage determinations—inherently takes several weeks. Furthermore, Department of Labor Labor Condition Applications (LCAs) and USCIS petition processing take time. Expecting an employer to file a petition on the exact day of employment termination is an operational impossibility that will effectively eliminate job portability.

Economic Competitiveness and Talent Retention: American businesses rely heavily on global talent to drive innovation in technology, healthcare, engineering, and science. Forcing workers to leave the country immediately upon job separation will push top-tier talent toward competitor nations with more reliable and stable immigration frameworks, to the detriment of the U.S. economy.

Increased Strain on USCIS: Rather than easing administrative burdens, removing the grace period will force thousands of terminated workers to flood USCIS with emergency applications (such as B-2 tourist status changes) purely to secure time to manage their affairs. This will worsen existing processing backlogs.

Severe Personal and Financial Hardship: Requiring individuals to instantly liquidate assets, break residential leases, pull children out of school, and arrange international relocation overnight disregards basic human welfare and the reality of living in a modern society.

For these reasons, I urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule and preserve the 60-day grace period, which protects U.S. labor market flexibility and ensures fair, orderly transitions for skilled workers.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposal, stating it disrupts talent supply chains and harms legal workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: Eliminating the 60-day job-search cushion will drive away the essential pool of workforce in high-tech, healthcare, and educational sectors and force them to go to other economies that are rival of the US. In the long run, it does not help the US nor the working class.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: Eliminating the 60-day grace period does not decrease administrative burden and increases the probability that wages will be driven down by organizations taking advantage of highly skilled workers who have been placed in a desperate position due to this policy. When there are restructuring plans or layoffs at major organizations some of these highly skilled visa holders may be let go of their jobs, at no fault of their own. Their status and that of their family would be subject to sudden change. Children would lose the continuity of education and other employment markets would also suffer from a sudden reduction. A grace period was established in 2016 to minimize the effects that sudden changes might have on industry in transition periods between these skilled workers. A grace period protects the workers from wage discrimination in that they don’t have to accept the first opportunity that appears, and the employer knows that the offer must be fair to be competitive. If immigrants must accept a low salary to stay legally, they will, and salary averages would then plummet. The objective of having temporary skilled workers in the U.S. is to boost the economy and knowledge base, but if DHS issues this rule it will only be spending more public funding and adding the administrative burden of pushing these invaluable contributors to society beyond our borders, only to welcome them back through an additional administrative process once another opportunity is secured. It seems that it would be less burdensome and more beneficial to the economy to allow them to stay for 60 days consuming products and services with zero additional administrative process. The immigrant in these cases has not acted incorrectly or against the spirit of the visa program. The proposed rule does not state a case that substantively demonstrates the reduction of administrative burden, or the effects that these changes will have or have had on the job market for Americans.
comments.reason: Argues eliminating the grace period risks lowering wages and creates unnecessary administrative burdens.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers. The existing provision is a reasonable and necessary safeguard that supports lawful immigration compliance, job mobility, American businesses, and family stability.

1. Employment transitions cannot happen overnight.

Even after securing a new job, an H-1B worker must rely on the employer to prepare and file an immigration petition. The Department of Labor allows up to seven working days just to review a Labor Condition Application (LCA), before other filing steps are completed.

Consider a worker laid off on Friday who receives a new job offer the following week. Even if the worker and employer act immediately, completing the necessary immigration procedures takes time. Requiring such a worker to leave the country serves no clear economic or administrative purpose.

2. Eliminating the grace period would hurt American employers.

American companies invest significant time and resources in recruiting skilled professionals. Removing the grace period would make it harder for businesses to hire qualified workers already present in the United States, potentially forcing unnecessary departures and subsequent international hiring procedures.

The existing grace period supports labor-market flexibility without granting unrestricted employment authorization.

3. Job loss should not immediately threaten an entire family's stability.

Layoffs frequently occur for reasons unrelated to employee performance. An unexpected termination should not force a family to immediately disrupt children's education, housing, a spouse's employment, and years of established community ties.

Many employment-based immigrants have lived legally in the United States for over a decade while waiting in green-card backlogs. Sixty days is already a limited window to find employment, pursue another lawful status, or arrange an orderly departure.

4. The existing regulation already contains safeguards.

The 60-day grace period is discretionary, not an unconditional entitlement. DHS already has authority to shorten or deny it based on individual circumstances. Concerns about misuse should be addressed through existing enforcement mechanisms rather than eliminating the protection for everyone.

5. The proposal should account for its broader consequences.

When DHS introduced this provision in 2016 (81 FR 82398), it recognized the importance of employment flexibility and stability for workers and U.S. employers. Any reversal should demonstrate why those original policy objectives no longer justify the protection.

Eliminating the grace period may also create additional administrative work through departures, consular processing, and subsequent petitions rather than meaningfully reducing the government's overall burden.

I respectfully urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

Sixty days is not an unreasonable privilege. It is a modest transition period that allows law-abiding workers and American employers to navigate a complex immigration process responsibly.

Immigration enforcement and basic fairness are not mutually exclusive. A sound immigration system should distinguish between deliberate violations and an unexpected loss of employment, while providing a reasonable opportunity to maintain lawful status.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposal because employment transitions require time and prevent family instability.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based nonimmigrant workers, because the rule punishes the wrong person: it inflicts the maximum penalty on the worker for a decision made entirely by the employer.

Consider the basic facts of a layoff. The employee does not resign, does not underperform, and commits no status violation. The employer — for a restructuring, a budget cut, a pivot — decides to end the job. Yet under this proposal, the person who made no choice at all bears the entire consequence: immediate loss of lawful status, with no time to do anything about it. In every other area of American law, penalties follow wrongdoing. Here, the worker's only "offense" is being laid off, and the sentence is the loss of their immigration status.

Even where the law does penalize without fault, it gives notice and a wind-down. The WARN Act requires employers to give 60 days' notice before mass layoffs — the same length as the grace period this rule would erase — precisely because an abrupt termination is recognized as a serious harm. Severance exists for the same reason. This proposal moves in the opposite direction: not merely withdrawing a cushion, but converting a sudden termination into a legal cliff, with the harshest possible outcome landing on the least responsible party.

That asymmetry has a predictable effect on behavior. It hands leverage to bad actors: an employer that knows a worker loses status the day the job ends gains coercive power — over wages, over hours, over tolerance of abuse — because quitting or being fired means immediate deportability, not just unemployment. And it rewards layoffs of the compliant: a worker who does everything right, pays taxes, follows every rule, is treated more harshly than someone whose status issues arise from their own actions.

The 60-day grace period is not leniency. It is proportionality — the principle that the consequence should match the conduct. The worker did nothing wrong; 60 days to transfer a petition, find a new sponsor, or make arrangements is the minimum a fair system owes them. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposal.
comments.reason: Opposes the rule as it unfairly penalizes workers for employer-driven layoffs without giving time.

Eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers who lose their jobs would be an unfair and deeply harmful policy. Many H-1B families have children enrolled in American schools, mortgages to pay, and deep roots in their communities. They have contributed to the U.S. economy, paid taxes, and made Social Security contributions for years. They have planned their lives around their careers, their children’s education, and their long-term commitment to American society. The 60-day grace period is not a free pass or a guarantee of permanent status. It is a reasonable window to find another employer, manage a difficult transition, and make informed decisions about the family’s future. Eliminating it would punish workers for circumstances often beyond their control and could force children to abruptly leave their schools and communities.

America benefits from fairness, stability, and respect for the people who contribute to its economy. The 60-day grace period should be preserved, not eliminated. Immigration policy should provide a reasonable opportunity to recover from unexpected job loss rather than turn an already difficult situation into an immediate family crisis.

I am writing to express my opposition to the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers. 

The current 60-day grace period is a vital safety net that keeps the U.S. immigration system fair and practical. When professional projects end or companies restructure, skilled workers need a reasonable amount of time to handle their personal affairs, interview with new employers, and allow corporate legal teams to process the extensive paperwork required for visa transfers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am submitting this comment as an H-1B visa holder with an approved Form I-140 (Immigrant Petition for Alien Worker) and a long-term contributor to the U.S. economy to express serious concerns regarding the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period. While the grace period is widely understood as a critical bridge for securing new employment or filing a change of status, its practical necessity extends far beyond immediate job-seeking activities.

The abrupt removal of this transition window overlooks the complex logistical, financial, and personal realities that highly skilled workers establish during their tenure in the United States, particularly those who have built a multi-year footprint on the path to permanent residency.

1. Impact on Workers with Approved I-140 Petitions and Long-Term Stakes

A significant portion of the H-1B workforce has lived in the United States for years, navigating the multi-year backlogs of the employment-based green card system with approved Form I-140 petitions. These individuals have built their professional and personal lives under the good-faith expectation that their long-term contributions would be accommodated. Eliminating the grace period disproportionately harms workers who are deeply integrated into the U.S. economy and awaiting permanent residency, turning an unexpected employment separation into an immediate emergency eviction from the country.

2. Conflict with Statutory Portability and Market Realities

Congress intentionally designed statutory mechanisms (such as AC21 portability provisions) to allow skilled workers to transition between employers. Stripping away the grace period creates an irreconcilable conflict with these provisions, rendering legal job mobility a theoretical right rather than a practical reality. Furthermore, the rule underestimates the operational friction placed on U.S. employers, who require a brief window to conduct interviews, process compliance, and file transfer petitions for specialized talent.

3. Real Estate and Financial Obligations Require Orderly Liquidation

H-1B workers and their families invest significantly in the U.S. housing and financial markets. Many maintain long-term residential mortgages, property leases, vehicle financing, and other contractual commitments. Unwinding these obligations—such as selling a home, breaking residential leases responsibly, and closing financial accounts—requires a predictable and reasonable timeframe. Forcing an immediate departure without this buffer creates severe financial distress and inflicts unintended systemic friction on local housing and credit markets.

4. Family Stability and Minor Children

Many visa holders have built families in the United States, including children enrolled in local schools and educational programs. Uprooting a family involves far more than booking a flight. It requires transferring academic records, notifying educational institutions, and managing household logistics. A narrow or nonexistent timeline fails to account for the best interests of minor children who are integrated into American communities.

5. Administrative and Practical Feasibility of Departure

An orderly departure requires comprehensive international relocation logistics, including the shipment of household goods, disposition of assets, and international pet relocation. These processes inherently require weeks of active coordination. A 60-day grace period provides the bare minimum operational runway necessary to exit the country in an organized, lawful manner should employment termination occur.

Conclusion

While the Department of Homeland Security maintains authority over immigration administration, regulatory changes should account for the reliance interests of long-term taxpaying residents and those anchored by approved I-140 petitions. Retaining the 60-day grace period ensures a humane, orderly, and administratively sound process that balances enforcement goals with basic operational reality.

Thank you for the opportunity to submit these comments for consideration.

Sincerely,

A Concerned H-1B Professional and Family Member
comments.reason: The commenter argues that removing the grace period causes immediate hardship for long-term workers awaiting green cards.

comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers following termination of employment.

The existing grace period is a reasonable and practical safeguard. It recognizes that job loss can occur unexpectedly and for reasons entirely outside an employee’s control, including layoffs, corporate restructuring, mergers, project cancellations, and economic downturns.

Eliminating this period would create significant uncertainty without addressing the underlying goals of the H-1B program.

An H-1B professional who unexpectedly loses a job cannot realistically secure new employment and complete the immigration process immediately. Professional hiring frequently involves multiple interviews, internal approvals, background checks, negotiations, and preparation of an H-1B petition by the new employer. Even when a company wants to hire the worker immediately, many of these steps are outside the employee’s control.

The 60-day grace period provides a limited and reasonable amount of time to navigate this process.

Eliminating it could also harm U.S. employers. H-1B workers who lose their jobs may possess highly specialized skills and years of experience in areas such as engineering, technology, medicine, research, and other professional fields. The grace period gives another American employer an opportunity to hire that worker. Without it, skilled professionals may have to leave the country before U.S. companies can complete their hiring processes.

There is also a significant human impact.

Many H-1B professionals have lived legally in the United States for years. They may have spouses, children attending American schools, homes, leases, financial obligations, and deep connections to their communities. Some are also waiting through lengthy employment-based permanent-residence processes.

An unexpected layoff is already financially and emotionally disruptive. Immigration policy should not unnecessarily turn an ordinary employment event into an immediate immigration crisis for an entire family.

The grace period also reduces the imbalance of power between workers and employers. If losing a job immediately threatens a worker’s immigration status, employees may feel unable to leave unhealthy working conditions or report inappropriate employer conduct. A reasonable transition period gives workers some independence while still requiring them to obtain qualifying employment promptly.

Importantly, the current grace period is only 60 days. It is not an indefinite extension of H-1B status or an unrestricted employment authorization. It is a short transition period intended to accommodate the realities of the labor market.

If DHS identifies specific misuse of the grace period, it should address that misuse directly through enforcement and appropriate eligibility requirements. Eliminating the protection for every H-1B worker because of potential abuse by a small number of individuals would be disproportionate.

The United States competes globally for highly skilled talent. Other countries actively seek engineers, scientists, researchers, physicians, entrepreneurs, and other professionals. Immigration policies that create unnecessary uncertainty after routine layoffs can make the United States a less attractive destination for these workers.

The existing 60-day grace period strikes a reasonable balance. It protects the integrity of the immigration system while recognizing that employment relationships sometimes end unexpectedly.

I respectfully urge DHS to retain the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and other eligible nonimmigrant workers.

Workers who follow U.S. immigration laws should have a reasonable opportunity to find another qualifying employer after an unexpected job loss. Maintaining this limited transition period benefits workers, families, American employers, and the broader U.S. economy.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes eliminating the safeguard that helps workers handle unexpected job loss.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge DHS to retain the 60-day grace period available to H-1B workers after an unexpected loss of employment.

Eliminating this protection would create a system in which a routine employment event—a layoff—could immediately become an immigration emergency. That is neither necessary nor beneficial to the United States.

H-1B workers are subject to the same economic realities as other employees. Companies reduce staff, eliminate divisions, lose funding, cancel projects, merge with other businesses, and change strategic direction. None of these events necessarily reflects anything about an individual worker’s performance or compliance with immigration law.

The immigration system should recognize this reality.

Sixty days is already a relatively short period in the professional hiring market. Finding specialized employment often requires several rounds of interviews, technical assessments, compensation approvals, background checks, and internal reviews. An H-1B worker must additionally find an employer willing and able to complete the required immigration process.

Removing the grace period would not make those hiring processes faster. It would simply make workers and their families bear the consequences of circumstances they cannot control.

There is also an important worker-protection issue. H-1B status is closely connected to employment. If termination immediately creates an immigration crisis, workers become even more dependent on individual employers.

Employees should not feel compelled to tolerate unreasonable working conditions because losing a job could immediately threaten their ability to remain in the country. A limited transition period provides an important safeguard while preserving the fundamental employer-sponsored structure of the H-1B program.

American businesses also benefit from this flexibility. When one company lays off a skilled professional, another U.S. company may need exactly that person’s expertise. Allowing a reasonable period for the worker to transition between employers helps keep valuable skills and experience within the American economy.

Without such a period, the United States risks forcing skilled workers to leave while American companies are simultaneously attempting to recruit people with those same qualifications.

Families would also face unnecessary hardship. Many H-1B workers have spouses and children who have lived in the United States for years. Children may be enrolled in school, spouses may have careers, and families may have homes and significant financial obligations. They should not be forced into immediate upheaval because an employer announces a layoff.

The 60-day grace period does not provide permanent immigration status, nor does it guarantee that a worker can remain indefinitely. It simply provides a short window to find another qualifying position, change status where legally permitted, or make arrangements to depart the United States.

That is a reasonable and balanced policy.

If DHS is concerned about misuse, targeted enforcement against actual violations would be more appropriate than eliminating the grace period for everyone.

I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing 60-day grace period. Immigration enforcement and basic fairness are not competing objectives. The United States can maintain strong immigration rules while giving lawful, highly skilled workers a reasonable amount of time to respond to an unexpected job loss.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to retain the grace period, arguing sudden loss of status creates an immigration emergency.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ketan Supanekar
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposed rule to eliminate the 60-day grace period for high-skilled non-immigrant workers following job separation. Although DHS frames the proposal as administrative streamlining, it risks significant economic harm by encouraging offshoring, reducing U.S. tax revenue, weakening local economies, and pushing highly skilled talent toward international competitors.
Hurts Local Businesses: High-skilled workers are consumers who support American communities through spending on housing, restaurants, retail, childcare, transportation, healthcare, and other services. Forcing families to leave following a temporary, market-driven layoff removes consumers from local economies and can reduce revenue for small businesses that employ American workers. DHS should consider these downstream economic effects.

Encourages Offshoring: DHS reports that 328,758 beneficiaries experienced employment cessation or a change of employer from FY2021–FY2025, averaging approximately 65,752 per year. During that period, 18,975 workers successfully obtained a new employer petition within the existing 60-day grace period. This demonstrates the grace period's practical role in facilitating continued employment in the United States.

A displaced high-skilled worker is not necessarily replaced by an American worker. Research by Wharton’s Britta Glennon found that restrictions on high-skilled workers increased employment at foreign affiliates, with approximately 0.42 foreign jobs created for every unfilled H-1B position, rising to approximately 0.93 for highly internationalized firms. The effects included both R&D and non-R&D employment. Eliminating the grace period therefore risks moving specialized engineering, research, and technical work overseas rather than transferring those jobs to American workers. When the work moves overseas, American workers do not benefit.

Reduces U.S. Economic Activity: DHS reports a $131,000 median annual wage for H-1B workers in the relevant transition population. These workers contribute through federal income and payroll taxes, applicable state and local taxes, and consumer spending. If workers and their jobs move abroad, the United States risks losing both economic activity and associated tax revenue.

Loses Global Talent: Many workers affected by this proposal have already studied at U.S. universities, worked for American companies, paid taxes, purchased homes, and built families and communities here. If they relocate to competing economies, America risks losing future innovation, research, entrepreneurship, and economic growth.

A policy intended to protect American workers should not inadvertently cause American jobs, investment, economic activity, and talent to leave the country. I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the 60-day grace period while pursuing targeted enforcement against actual violations.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule due to potential economic harm, offshoring risks, and impacts on local businesses.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Docket: USCIS-2026-0364
Re: Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period, 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2)

Dear USCIS and DHS Officials,

I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing discretionary grace period of up to 60 days following cessation of employment. I am an H-1B professional who has worked lawfully in the United States for over ten years. Eliminating it could harm workers, families, and American employers.

**My Experience**

I moved to the United States in 2016 with my wife and our six-month-old daughter after ten years of professional experience in my home country. I now work in specialized engineering for a major U.S. automotive manufacturer. My employer began my employment-based green card process in 2019, and I have an approved Form I-140 with a 2019 priority date. Because of the immigrant visa backlog, I still depend on H-1B status while awaiting permanent residency.

We have purchased a home, established community ties, and raised our children here. Both attend U.S. schools. Our younger child, born in 2017, is a U.S. citizen. Following an unexpected layoff, losing the grace period could leave us little practical time to pursue lawful alternatives. We could face the painful choice of relocating our U.S.-citizen child from the only country he has known or separating our family. Our children's schooling, friendships, and our housing obligations cannot be resolved overnight.

**Why a Transition Period Matters**

Even 60 days is a difficult window for specialized technical recruitment. Finding a suitable position can require technical interviews, several levels of employer approval, and preparation of a new H-1B petition. While eligible H-1B workers may begin employment once a qualifying petition is properly filed, finding a willing employer and completing that filing require time. Layoffs and restructuring are often beyond the worker's control. Eliminating the grace period could prevent a lawful transition even where a U.S. employer needs the worker's skills.

**DHS's Rationale and Reliance Interests**

I recognize DHS's goals of linking nonimmigrant status to qualifying employment and reducing administrative burden. However, the current grace period is limited and discretionary; it does not provide unrestricted work authorization or indefinite residence.

In Section IV.D of the proposed rule, DHS acknowledges that workers and their families may have built careers, purchased homes, and invested in their communities. I respectfully ask DHS to give particular consideration to people who have maintained lawful employment for many years and already have approved immigrant petitions, but cannot complete the green card process because visa numbers remain unavailable. These are significant reliance interests.

**Potential Long-Term Effects on the United States**

A worker's sudden departure may disrupt engineering projects and impose recruitment, onboarding, and productivity costs on U.S. employers. A transition period helps companies retain expertise already in the country. Over time, uncertainty about the consequences of an involuntary layoff may also influence whether skilled professionals choose to build careers in the United States.

DHS's regulatory impact analysis recognizes possible wage losses for affected workers and temporary productivity losses for some employers. I request that DHS assess whether the administrative benefits of elimination outweigh these potential employment and workforce costs, including in advanced manufacturing, engineering, and research.

**Requested Alternatives**

In light of Section IV.E, which discusses alternatives, I respectfully request that DHS:

1. Retain the existing discretionary grace period of up to 60 days.
2. If it eliminates the general grace period, retain a limited transition period for H-1B workers with approved I-140 petitions who are awaiting immigrant visa availability, using objective and clearly defined eligibility criteria.
3. Consider a reasonable transition period after involuntary layoffs or restructuring, allowing time to pursue a new qualifying petition, another lawful option, or orderly departure.
4. Evaluate effects on dependent families, U.S.-citizen children, and employers, and explain whether a narrow exception is feasible.

I am not asking to work without authorization or to remain indefinitely without lawful status. I am asking for a reasonable opportunity to respond lawfully to an unexpected job loss after more than a decade of contributing to American industry and building a family life here.

Thank you for considering my experience and these proposed alternatives.

• Economic Instability and Market Uncertainty: Sudden, unexpected workforce reductions introduce immense operational risks for American businesses. The resulting market uncertainty undermines long-term business planning, stalls project timelines, and inflicts broader damage on the U.S. economy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am an H-1B worker from India who has lived and worked in the United States for 10 years as a software engineer. I have an approved I-140 and am now waiting in the green card backlog with a priority date of 2026.

For workers born in India, the grace period is not a convenience. It is the only protection we have. Because of the per-country limits on employment-based green cards, Indian nationals with approved immigrant petitions often wait many years, sometimes decades, for permanent residence. Workers from most other countries move to a green card within a few years and are no longer tied to a single employer. We are not. For the whole of our long wait, our lawful presence, and that of our spouses and children, depends on keeping one specific job without a single day’s gap.

Layoffs are almost never the worker’s fault. Restructurings, budget cuts and company closures happen to good employees, often with no warning. Without the grace period, a worker laid off on a Friday is effectively out of status that day, before they could realistically find a new employer, have a petition filed, or arrange an orderly departure. That outcome punishes people for decisions they had no part in. It also means a family with children in school, a lease, a mortgage, and years of tax-paying contributions would have to uproot their lives with no time at all.

DHS says the grace period is inconsistent with the purpose of these classifications. But the grace period does not let anyone work without authorization. It is a short, one-time window, available at most once per validity period and never past the end of the authorized stay. Its purpose is to let a worker either find new qualifying employment or leave in an orderly way, and both of those outcomes are consistent with the statute. DHS reached the same conclusion when it adopted this provision, and nothing in the proposal shows that workers have abused it.

DHS also cites administrative burden. Removing the grace period is likely to increase that burden. Without it, more workers will file emergency change-of-status requests, more employers will file petitions in a rush, and DHS itself acknowledges that some affected people could receive Notices to Appear, which adds cases to an immigration court system that is already overloaded.

The grace period also benefits U.S. employers. It lets companies hire experienced, already-vetted workers who were laid off elsewhere, instead of losing that talent to other countries. Eliminating it would make the United States a less reliable place for skilled workers to build careers, and it would push many of us to take our skills to countries that offer more stability.

Over the past ten years I have seen colleagues laid off with no notice. The grace period gave them time to find new employers and keep their families here. Without it, a single layoff would force me to leave the country with my family immediately, after a decade of building a life and paying taxes here.

Workers like me have planned our lives around this rule for nearly ten years. I urge DHS to withdraw the proposal and keep the grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). If DHS does go ahead, it should at least keep a grace period for workers with approved I-140 petitions who are stuck in per-country backlogs, and for workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.
comments.reason: The commenter details why the grace period is an essential protection for workers facing unexpected layoffs.

This flexibility helps both workers and U.S. employers by allowing companies to retain access to skilled talent without forcing workers to leave after a brief gap in employment. H-1B workers can remain in status only for a short period if they find another legal basis to stay and any new job must still meet all immigration requirements. The grace period does not remove those rules, it simply gives workers reasonable time to comply with them.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by SriCMConsulting
comments.commentText:
Regarding: Proposed Rule – Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364)
I am writing to express my strong support for the Department of Homeland Security's proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B, L-1, O-1, E, and TN nonimmigrant visa holders. Returning to the standard where a nonimmigrant worker's lawful status ends immediately upon the termination of their qualifying employment is a common-sense measure that strengthens the integrity of the U.S. immigration system and protects the domestic labor market.
First, this proposal correctly aligns the practical reality of nonimmigrant programs with their statutory intent. Temporary work visas are fundamentally designed to fill specific, immediate labor shortages for designated employers. They are not intended to serve as a floating or open-ended authorization to remain in the United States without active, qualifying employment. When a visa holder's employment ends, the underlying justification for their legal presence under that specific visa classification also concludes.
Second, eliminating the 60-day grace period is a pro-worker measure for the domestic labor force. The current buffer period allows a large pool of foreign professionals to remain in the country and compete directly with domestic job seekers during periods of economic instability or localized layoffs. Removing this discretionary period ensures that available positions are prioritized for the domestic workforce, preventing artificial wage suppression and ensuring fair labor competition.
Finally, the current policy imposes an unnecessary administrative burden on U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. Tracking individual grace periods, managing speculative status changes, and overseeing individuals who remain in the country after their authorized activity has ended drains critical agency resources. Streamlining this process will lower administrative costs, reduce backlogs, and allow the agency to focus on efficiently processing valid, employer-sponsored applications.
For these reasons, I urge the Department of Homeland Security to finalize this proposed rule without delay. Restoring accountability and clear boundaries to our employment-based visa programs is essential for a fair and well-regulated immigration system.

Sincerely,
Nagendra Venugopalrao

To Whom It May Concern:
I am writing to submit my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for high-skilled non-immigrant workers, including those on H-1B, L-1, E, O, and TN visas. As a senior Data engineer with over 15 years of experience building critical enterprise data architecture and software systems in the United States, and family man residing in Redmond, Washington, I believe this proposed change introduces severe operational risks, unfair labor dynamics, and profound humanitarian hardships.
The elimination of the 60-day grace period will negatively impact skilled professionals, their families, and the U.S. economy in several critical ways:
1. Disregard for the Logistical Realities of Established Households
For professionals who have spent years building a life, a career, and a family in the United States, an abrupt, zero-tolerance transition period is unworkable. My wife,our child, and I—like countless other immigrant families—are deeply integrated into our local community. We maintain a household, lease  enroll our child in local schools, and contribute regularly to the regional economy. Stripping away the 60-day runway creates an impossible crisis in the event of an unexpected corporate layoff or restructuring, forcing families to instantly uproot decades of professional and personal investment overnight.
2. Unbalanced Labor Dynamics and Chilling Effects on Workers
The 60-day grace period serves as an essential safety valve that allows skilled professionals reasonable time to secure alternative employment or wind down their affairs when an employer-employee relationship ends. Without this buffer:
 Workers facing sudden termination would face immediate unlawful presence, robbing them of the capacity to properly negotiate or transition.
 This dynamic creates a dangerous chilling effect. Employees subjected to toxic work environments, contract breaches, or labor infractions will be paralyzed from speaking out or reporting violations out of fear of immediate deportation.
 This inadvertently empowers unscrupulous employers with absolute leverage, undermining fair labor standards.

Conclusion
The existing 60-day grace period balances the operational needs of immigration enforcement with basic human dignity, economic stability, and fair labor practices. Eliminating it does not streamline immigration; it destabilizes high-skilled workers, harms U.S. competitiveness, and inflicts unmanageable hardship on families.

It’s not just a matter of leaving a country; it’s about being forced to leave behind an entire life. That kind of treatment is deeply inhumane.
comments.reason: Asking people who built their lives here to leave overnight is inhumane and unfair.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Nikhitha Reddy Busireddy
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule because it could negatively affect the rights, safety, and dignity of immigrant workers in the United States.

Immigrant workers deserve the same opportunity as every other worker to speak up against workplace injustice, discrimination, harassment, exploitation, unfair treatment, or violations of their employment rights. However, when a worker's immigration status is tied to their employment, the fear of losing their job and being forced to leave the country can make it extremely difficult to report misconduct or challenge an employer's actions.

If this rule makes it harder for workers to remain in the United States when they lose their jobs or face employment-related difficulties, it could leave vulnerable workers with an unfair choice: remain silent about workplace violations or risk losing their livelihood, immigration stability, and the life they have built for themselves and their families.

No worker should be forced to tolerate injustice simply because they are an immigrant.** Workers must have a reasonable opportunity to report violations, seek legal advice, pursue complaints, and find alternative employment without facing disproportionate immigration consequences for standing up for their rights.

Immigrants contribute significantly to the American economy, businesses, innovation, and communities. They should not be placed in a position where employers can potentially exploit their immigration vulnerability or where fear of having to leave the country discourages them from reporting wrongdoing.

I urge USCIS to reconsider this proposed rule and carefully evaluate its impact on worker protections, workplace accountability, and the ability of immigrant workers to seek justice. Any policy changes should include meaningful safeguards that allow affected workers reasonable time to address employment issues, report violations, and transition to alternative employment where legally permitted.

Fairness, accountability, and protection from workplace exploitation should not depend on immigration status.** A policy that discourages workers from speaking up against injustice is not fair to workers, their families, or the broader American workforce.

I respectfully urge USCIS not to implement this rule without adequate protections for immigrant workers and a thorough assessment of its potential consequences.
comments.reason: Rule threatens immigrant worker safety and deters reporting of workplace injustices.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I oppose the elimination of the 60-day grace period because it would disrupt work that cannot simply be paused — including healthcare and federally funded research where H-1B professionals are deeply embedded.

I work in medical research, and our lab runs on NIH-funded projects that take years to complete. Several of our postdoctoral researchers are on H-1B status. When a grant is not renewed or a university restructures, these researchers can lose employment through no fault of their own. The 60-day grace period is what lets them transfer to another lab or employer so their research continues. Without it, a scientist in the middle of a clinical study would fall out of status on day one and be forced to leave the country immediately — taking years of institutional knowledge with them and abandoning research that American taxpayers already funded.

The same logic applies to physicians in underserved areas. Programs that place international medical graduates in communities that struggle to attract doctors would be undermined by this rule: a hospital closure or restructuring would instantly strip those communities of their physicians.

DHS frames the grace period as generosity, but it is practical engineering. It keeps specialized work — cancer research, patient care, semiconductor fabrication, critical infrastructure — from breaking overnight when employment ends. Eliminating it does not create a single additional job for an American worker; it creates abandoned research projects, understaffed clinics, and wasted federal investment.

A rule that cannot distinguish between a status violator and a researcher whose grant ended is not enforcement — it is sabotage of the country's own research enterprise. Please keep the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: Eliminating the grace period disrupts critical healthcare and federally funded research.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText: I respectfully oppose the purpose of eliminating the 60-day grace period. We need more skilled people irrespective of status as Ai is evolving. We need this skilled people to contribute to IT sector and contribute to American Economy
