comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This comment is submitted anonymously. I write in opposition to two related DHS proposals: removing deference to prior USCIS eligibility determinations (8 CFR 214.1(c)(5)) and eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers. Both take settled, previously approved status and make it precarious — and on the agency's own numbers, neither buys any program integrity.

Start with deference. DHS's difference-in-differences analysis estimates that removing deference raises the RFE rate by 2.9 percentage points — roughly 6,044 additional Requests for Evidence a year, each adding an average of 64 days — while finding "no corresponding change" in denial rates. That is the whole case in one sentence: more delay, more cost, zero change in who is approved. The $22.17 the preamble assigns to each RFE response, built on a ten-minute-response assumption, is not a serious price for the attorney and HR time a de novo specialty-occupation re-litigation actually consumes.

The human cost lands first on patients. H-1B physicians staff rural and underserved communities — critical-access hospitals, community health centers, VA facilities — because domestically trained physicians overwhelmingly practice in metro areas. When the only physician staffing a rural emergency department has an extension re-litigated on facts USCIS already approved, the 64 extra days become uncovered shifts, transferred patients, delayed care. DHS priced the agency and the petitioners. It never priced the patients.

The proposal also sweeps far beyond its own rationale. Section 214.1(c)(5) governs extensions across part 214 — L-1 transferees, O-1 workers of extraordinary ability, TN professionals, E treaty investors, P athletes and entertainers — yet the preamble's fraud narrative is built entirely on H-1B site visits. No case is made for de novo review of these other classifications' extensions; the deletion is blanket, the record is not.

And the ledger is one-sided. DHS counts the fraud it hopes to catch in a targeted, suspicion-selected site-visit sample, but never counts the meritorious extensions that will not be filed at all. DHS's own analysis says 57 percent of classifiable H-1B extension petitioners are small entities; facing recurring de novo re-litigation at real costs in the thousands, some will simply stop sponsoring, and the work — and the worker — will move abroad. Competitor countries understand this: Canada's Global Talent Stream offers two-week processing and settled status. A rule that makes the American extension the least predictable renewal in the market is a relocation incentive wearing an enforcement costume. The existing exceptions for material error, material change, and new material information already let USCIS disregard a bad prior approval; system-wide re-litigation is unnecessary.

The grace-period proposal repeats the pattern. Every H-1B petition carries the ACWIA training fee — $750 or $1,500 — which Congress directed to Department of Labor grants that train American workers, NSF STEM scholarships for American students, and USCIS fraud detection. A laid-off worker who transfers within 60 days generates a new petition and a new contribution. A worker forced to depart generates nothing. Eliminating the grace period defunds the very programs Congress built to prepare American workers, in the name of protecting them.

It also changes employer behavior for the worse. With the grace period, a layoff triggers an orderly wind-down: records updated, final wages handled, a defined window to transfer or depart. Without it, every layoff becomes an instant status violation attached to the employer's own petition — a compliance tripwire. In-house counsel will respond rationally: sponsor less, or move the role offshore. The specialty-occupation jobs do not go to American workers; they go abroad or go unfilled.

DHS should withdraw both proposals, retain 8 CFR 214.1(c)(5), and keep the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: Removes settled status, introduces precariousness, and harms rural patient care.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by A K
comments.commentText:
To the DHS & USCIS:

Picture an engineer who has lived in the United States for twelve years. She pays a mortgage on a home in a quiet suburb, drives a car she is still paying off, and has two children in the local schools, one of them born here. On a Tuesday morning, her company announces layoffs. Under the rule DHS/USCIS has proposed, she and her family would be out of status the very next day.

That evening she would have to sit her children down and explain that they may be leaving the only home they remember, that they may not say a proper goodbye to friends or teachers, and that their parents do not know where they will be living in a few weeks. No family that has followed every rule should face that conversation with no time to prepare.

I urge the Department to withdraw this proposal and keep the 60-day grace period in place.

Families like this one are not on the edges of American life; they are part of its foundation. They borrow from American banks, shop at American stores, vacation in American towns, and pay American tuition. They pay federal, state, and local taxes year after year, often for decades. They coach teams, volunteer at schools, and show up for their neighbors. It is hard to justify a policy that accepts all of that contribution and then allows a single day’s notice when circumstances change through no fault of the worker.

The human cost falls hardest on children. A child should not be pulled out of a classroom in the middle of the year because a parent’s employer restructured. Many of these children have known no other home, and some are American citizens. Sixty days is a modest amount of time to tell a child, withdraw them from school, pack a household, and plan an international move. Taking even that away is not simply strict; it is inhumane.

The practical damage is just as real. No one can sell a house, pay off a mortgage, or end a car loan or lease in a day. Forcing departures on that timeline would lead to rushed sales, defaults, and abandoned obligations, and those losses would spread to neighbors, lenders, landlords, and local housing markets.

American employers would also lose. The grace period lets companies quickly hire experienced professionals who are already here, already vetted, and ready to work. Without it, that talent leaves the country, along with the tax revenue and the innovation it brings.

If the Department is concerned about fraud or misuse, the answer is targeted enforcement against those who break the rules, not a blanket penalty on everyone. The vast majority of H-1B workers follow every requirement, and they should not pay for others' misconduct. I also want to be clear about a concern many Americans share; companies should not replace American workers with cheaper labor, and those that misuse the visa system to do so should face real penalties. But that decision is made in a company office, not by the employee. The H-1B worker who is laid off had no say in it. They are losing a job too, often along with American coworkers. Punishing the employee and their children by forcing them out overnight is not fair. The answer to corporate abuse is accountability for corporations, not the sudden removal of families who did their jobs honestly.

The 60-day grace period is not a loophole. It is a small measure of fairness and dignity for families who have built their lives here lawfully. I respectfully ask DHS and USCIS to preserve the 60-day grace period.

Respectfully,
A K
comments.reason: Immediate status loss upon layoff inflicts severe emotional and logistical costs on children.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
As an F-1 student with an H-1B petition filed for future employment, I oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period. The grace period gives workers a short, lawful window to find a new sponsor or change status after a job loss instead of falling out of status overnight through no fault of their own. Removing it would push people toward status violations or force immediate departure, and add churn for employers and USCIS.

H-1B workers also drive US growth directly. They fill critical skill gaps in technology, healthcare and engineering, pay federal and state taxes from day one, and their spending and entrepreneurship create jobs for Americans. Cutting the grace period makes the US a riskier bet for global talent, and that talent will go to competing countries instead. Keep 8 CFR 214.1(l) as is.
comments.reason: Grace period allows lawful window to find a new sponsor without falling out of status.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Hello,

While I completely welcome the fight against fraudulent H-1B and other employment-related visas, I oppose eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period, as it serves no purpose in that fight. Nor does this proposed policy serve any other purpose.

 The following points highlight why I oppose this proposed rule:

1) USCIS and DOL have already introduced or are in the process of introducing various policy changes to fight fraud. Those are welcome moves to fight fraud. When stringent rules and tighter monitoring are being established, why would USCIS hesitate to keep the 60-day discretionary period open?

2) An employee may be laid off because of economic downturns, company performance, and other factors that may have no bearing on his performance or skill set. While the fight against fraud is much needed, how reasonable is it to push that person — who has already lost a job — into deeper turmoil by immediately stripping them of legal status? They should be given time (currently set at 60 days) to seek employment, and if they are legally hired by another employer, they should be allowed to remain in the US; otherwise, they would have to leave the country anyway. The least that can be done to support laid-off people on visas is to give them the 60-day period to get hired or to plan their departure.

3) If someone who is laid off is not provided the 60-day period to wrap up, are they considered to have wilfully violated their duration of stay from the very next day? Does this close the path for them to ever reapply for US work visas? If so, why are they being made victims of circumstances?

4) Finally, it is not just about the individual. This proposed rule concerns the affected family. Kids, spouses, elderly parents, and others are greatly impacted because someone who has legally lived in the US lost their job. Is this how we wish to frame our legal immigration policies?

Death may come unannounced, but legal immigration policies should never take that route.

Thanks for your time and consideration. I certainly hope we reconsider this proposed policy bill and allow folks already in distress the 60-day time period to plan their next steps.
comments.reason: Punishing laid-off workers by immediately stripping legal status serves no valid purpose.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the elimination of the 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers who lose their employment.

Job loss is often involuntary. Layoffs, company closures, restructurings, and failed funding rounds are not choices made by the worker. The proposed rule would make a sudden termination an immediate immigration violation, which penalizes workers for decisions they did not make and cannot control.

The rule ignores the lives people build here. Nonimmigrant workers live in the United States for years. They sign leases, take on car loans and other financial obligations, enroll children in school, and form community and family ties. Many have spouses and dependents whose status is derived from theirs and who would lose status the same day. Requiring a household to leave immediately would force them to break leases, abandon contractual obligations, pull children out of school mid-year, and settle their affairs in days. Sixty days is already a modest window for that.

Immediate departure is impractical. Selling or subletting a home, shipping belongings, closing accounts, and arranging international travel for a family cannot responsibly be done overnight. Without a grace period, the likely outcomes are unpaid debts, unresolved obligations to landlords and creditors, and disorderly departures that harm the people left behind.

The grace period serves a real function. It gives workers time to find a new sponsor, file a transfer petition, change status, or depart in an orderly way. Eliminating it means a worker with a promising job offer in hand could still lose status before the paperwork is filed. That is a loss for the worker and for the U.S. employer that would have hired them.

The scale is significant. DHS’s own estimate is that, on average, about 65,752 workers covered by the grace period lost a job or changed employers each year between 2021 and 2025. This is a routine feature of the labor market, not a rare edge case.

Employers and the economy bear costs too. Employers who hire from the pool of workers between jobs lose access to that talent, and workers will be less willing to take risks on startups or growing companies if one setback ends their stay. The administrative burden DHS cites is a reason to streamline processing, not to remove a protection that has operated for nearly a decade.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: Involuntary job loss should not become an immediate immigration violation overnight.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Lorin Hochstein
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I am a naturalized American citizen who previously lived in the United States on both F-1 student and H-1B employment visas. Although I was fortunate never to experience a layoff while on an H-1B visa, I understand firsthand the uncertainty associated with having one's ability to remain in the United States depend on maintaining a particular immigration status.

I believe the existing grace period is a reasonable accommodation for foreign workers who lose their jobs. Eliminating it would impose significant hardship on workers and their families, create unnecessary obstacles for American employers, and potentially undermine the United States' ability to attract and retain talented people. I do not believe DHS has demonstrated that these costs are justified by corresponding benefits to the American public.

## Job loss should not result in immediate immigration consequences

Losing one's job is not evidence of wrongdoing. Workers may lose their employment because of layoffs, corporate restructuring, or circumstances entirely beyond their control. A foreign worker who has complied with every condition of their visa may nevertheless find themselves suddenly unemployed.

For an American citizen, losing a job is already a significant hardship. For a foreign worker whose immigration status depends on employment, the consequences can be considerably more severe. In addition to losing their income, they may face the prospect of uprooting their family, withdrawing children from school, and leaving the country where they have established their lives.

The existing grace period provides a modest amount of time to find another employer, pursue a change of immigration status, or make arrangements to depart the United States. Sixty days is hardly an excessive allowance for navigating these challenges.

## The proposed rule could harm American employers and the economy

When a foreign worker loses their job, another American employer may wish to hire that individual. The grace period allows time to arrange this transition without unnecessarily disrupting the worker's ability to remain in the country.

Eliminating the grace period could prevent American businesses from hiring qualified workers who are already living in the United States. It could also impose additional recruiting costs, delay hiring, and discourage foreign professionals from pursuing employment opportunities here.

The interests of foreign workers and American employers are not necessarily in conflict. Policies that facilitate reasonable employment transitions can benefit both.

## The proposed rule does not adequately justify eliminating the existing protection

The existing grace period is already discretionary. Under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), DHS has the authority to shorten or eliminate the grace period in individual cases when circumstances warrant.

Why is it necessary to eliminate the grace period for all affected workers, rather than exercising the authority DHS already possesses to address cases that present legitimate concerns?

In conclusion, I urge DHS to withdraw the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period and retain the existing provisions of 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
comments.reason: Grace period is a reasonable accommodation; eliminating it creates unnecessary hardships.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Pavan Kumar Yanmanagandla
comments.commentText:
I am writing to strongly urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to withdraw the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers (8 CFR 214.1(l)(2)). Removing this fundamental transition window imposes inhumane hardships on law-abiding legal immigrants, penalizes families without due consideration for basic human dignity, and severely disrupts local communities and schools.

1. Human Rights and Basic Dignity for Law-Abiding Immigrants
Legal nonimmigrant professionals contribute significantly to the U.S. economy, pay taxes, and maintain continuous compliance with federal immigration laws. Forcing a family that has consistently complied with all regulations to execute an immediate, overnight international departure due to a sudden job loss—often completely outside their control—is extraordinarily harsh and fundamentally unjust. Treating compliant, tax-paying families with such abrupt hostility disregards basic standards of human dignity, humiliating individuals and families who have acted in good faith throughout their tenure in the United States.

2. Severe Disruption to Minor Children and Educational Continuity
Denying families a reasonable window to handle relocation logistics severely harms school-age children. Forcing children to instantly abandon their schools, teachers, and peers mid-term creates profound psychological distress and academic instability. Furthermore, this sudden displacement affects their American classmates and educators, who are forced to witness close friends and top students abruptly pulled from their classrooms overnight through no fault of their own.

3. Unrealistic Relocation and Administrative Hassles
Expecting families to break residential leases, liquidate personal property, settle financial and tax accounts, transfer medical records, and arrange international travel without a transitional grace period is an administrative impossibility. Without a 60-day cushion, families face severe financial penalties and logistical chaos simply attempting to comply with immediate departure expectations.

4. Conclusion and Recommendation
The 60-day grace period is not a loophole; it is a critical, humane safeguard that ensures orderly, dignified transitions for lawful residents. Eliminating it creates unnecessary cruelty toward legal immigrants and their children. I respectfully urge USCIS to maintain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period in its entirety.
comments.reason: Removing the transition window imposes inhumane hardships and disrupts children's schooling.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period
To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:
I respectfully submit the following comments concerning the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
The proposal raises important questions about administrative efficiency, economic costs, reliance interests, and the availability of less disruptive regulatory alternatives. I request that DHS address the following issues with additional evidence and analysis before finalizing the rule.
1. Quantification of Administrative Savings (Section IV.C)
DHS identifies administrative complexity as a justification for eliminating the grace period. However, the proposal should provide a clearer quantitative assessment of the expected savings.
How many adjudication hours are attributable specifically to determining grace-period eligibility? What is the estimated annual cost of these reviews? How much of this work would otherwise be required when adjudicating subsequent petitions involving employment termination?
DHS should distinguish genuinely avoidable administrative costs from review activities that would remain necessary under the proposed rule.
2. Reliability of the Affected-Population Estimates (Section V.A.3, Table 3)
DHS relies on withdrawals of approved Form I-129 petitions as a proxy for employment cessation and potential grace-period use.
However, employer withdrawals may not coincide with actual termination dates, and not all terminated workers are necessarily represented by timely withdrawal records.
I request a sensitivity analysis evaluating how delayed withdrawals, unreported employment terminations, and workers who transition between employers before petition withdrawal could affect the estimated population and regulatory impacts.
The analysis should also distinguish actual use of the grace period from petition-filing activity that merely falls within a similar time window.
3. Economic Costs to U.S. Employers and Workers (Section V.A.3)
Eliminating the grace period may create additional costs through interrupted recruitment, international relocation, consular processing, delayed onboarding, and loss of project continuity.
These consequences may be particularly relevant to specialized occupations involving multiple interview stages and employer-sponsored immigration petitions.
DHS should evaluate potential delays and costs under multiple realistic employment-transition scenarios, including unexpected layoffs and prospective employers prepared to file new petitions.
Any administrative savings should be considered alongside incremental costs to employers, workers, and the federal government.
4. Evaluation of Less Disruptive Alternatives (Section IV.E)
DHS discusses alternatives, including a shorter grace period and more stringent evidentiary requirements, but should provide a more detailed comparison of their expected costs and operational effects.
Potential approaches include standardized employer-termination evidence, clearer eligibility criteria, streamlined verification procedures, and differentiated transitional arrangements.
I request a quantitative or otherwise evidence-based explanation of why such alternatives would not sufficiently address the identified administrative concerns.
5. Government-Wide Administrative Impacts (Section V.A.3)
DHS acknowledges possible increases in Notices to Appear and workload involving immigration enforcement and adjudication agencies.
The regulatory analysis should more clearly compare anticipated USCIS adjudication savings against any additional downstream administrative and enforcement costs across affected federal agencies.
A reduction in workload within one agency should not automatically be treated as an equivalent reduction in total federal administrative costs.
Conclusion
I respectfully request that DHS provide additional quantitative analysis, address limitations in the underlying data, evaluate relevant reliance interests, and more thoroughly compare available alternatives before making a final regulatory determination.
Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: "The proposal raises important questions about administrative efficiency, economic costs, reliance interests, and the availability of less disruptive regulatory alternatives." The commenter challenges the justifications for the rule and highlights the disruptive impact of eliminating the grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Vino Marimuthu
comments.commentText:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS)
Department of Homeland Security
RE: Public Comment on Proposed Rule Changes Affecting Nonimmigrant Grace Periods
Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364

To Whom It May Concern,
I am writing to submit my formal public comment regarding the proposed adjustments to the 60-day grace period policy for nonimmigrant workers, specifically those on H-1B and related professional visas. While I understand the administrative goals of regulatory updates, removing or significantly reducing this critical transition window will introduce immediate, severe logistical and financial hardships for long-term residents and their families.
As a professional working in the United States, I ask USCIS to consider the following profound disruptions this policy change would cause:

1. Residential and Financial Instability (Mortgages and Leases)
Many high-skilled nonimmigrant workers are deeply rooted in their local economies, having transitioned from renting to homeownership or holding long-term residential leases. Selling a home, resolving a mortgage, or breaking a lease legally and responsibly is impossible to execute within a truncated timeframe. For homeowners, a sudden policy change forces a choice between facing foreclosure and severe financial loss or risking non-compliance with immigration rules. For renters, breaking a lease abruptly leads to heavy financial penalties and damaged credit histories, undermining long-term financial stability.

2. Severe Disruptions to Children's Schooling and Family Well-Being
Nonimmigrant professionals frequently have families with school-aged children who are enrolled in local school districts and fully integrated into their communities. Abruptly uprooting children in the middle of an academic year inflicts immense academic and emotional distress. It fragments their development and cuts off vital community support systems. A rigid timeline leaves families with no viable window to coordinate a stable, orderly transition for their children's education.

3. Significant Impact on Mental Health and Personal Well-Being
The pressure of managing high-stakes professional roles while navigating complex immigration framework is already substantial. Removing the predictability of the 60-day grace period amplifies this stress exponentially. The constant anxiety regarding sudden, unmanageable timelines negatively impacts mental health, reduces workplace productivity, and places immense emotional strain on both the visa holders and their dependents.

4. Broader Economic and Community Contributions
H-1B holders and other nonimmigrant professionals are not temporary visitors; they are active taxpayers, homeowners, consumers, and dedicated community members who have spent years building lives here. Forcing an abrupt departure prevents these individuals from winding down their affairs in a lawful, organized manner, which ultimately harms local businesses, real estate markets, and neighborhood communities.

Conclusion and Proposed Alternatives
A 60-day window is the bare minimum required to handle complex legal and personal responsibilities, such as liquidating assets, settling bank accounts, and coordinating international relocation safely. I respectfully urge USCIS to maintain the current 60-day grace period framework or consider extending it to mirror the complexities of modern residential and family life.

Thank you for your time, consideration, and review of these critical concerns.
Respectfully submitted,
Vino Marimuthu
comments.reason: Removes transition window, causing severe financial and logistical hardships for workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I write to submit this comment in strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security's(DHS) Notice of Proposed Rulemaking(NPRM) seeing to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers in E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B, H1-B1, L-1, O-1 and TN classifications. 
If finalized in its current form, this rule would violate the Administrative Procedure ACT(APA), 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), as arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, and contrary to the statutory framework established by Congress under the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act (AC21) and the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).
1. Failure to account for serious reliance interests (DHS v. Regents of the University of California): Under well-established Supreme Court precedent an agency which reverses a long-standing policy is required to consider whether there are reliance interests, whether those interests are significant and to weigh those interests against any competing policy considerations (DHS v. Regents of the Univ. of Cal., 140 S. Ct. 1891, 1913 (2020) (citing Encino Motorcars, LLC v. Navarro, 579 U.S. 211, 221-22 (2016))). For nearly a decade thousands of highly skilled professionals, US employers and academic/research institutions have structured their entire projects, capital investments, residential leases and complex technical operations around the 60 day grace period which was codified in 2016. Highly skilled professionals in complex fields (e.g. semiconductor design, AI, biomedical engineering) are simply not able to carry out the complex job transitions required to move from one employer to another, to obtain a certified LCA from the DOL and to file a new non-immigrant petition in the 24-48 hours following an unexpected layoff. DHS has summarily dismissed these enormous personal, financial and contractual reliance interests without providing the "more substantial justification" required where a prior policy has given rise to serious reliance (FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009)). 

2. Frustration of Congressional intent under AC21 job portability: Congress enacted INA § 214(n) (8 U.S.C. § 1184(n)) via AC21 to provide job flexibility and market mobility to specialty occupation professionals so that they would not be left in a position of immediate jeopardy in the event of a corporate reorganization or sudden termination. The elimination of the 60 day window frustrates that very statutory mechanism. Given that the DOL prevailing wage and LCA processing takes a minimum of 7-10 business days, an immediate cessation rule renders the statutory portability mechanism effectively impossible for laid off workers unless an employer is able to initiate a petition weeks in advance of the layoff (a situation which is rarely the case in the context of a sudden downsizing). It is simply not possible for a lawful professional to be left in an unauthorized status immediately upon layoff and that directly contradicts the statutory purpose of AC21. 

3. Unsupported economic and administrative justifications: Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983) an agency action is arbitrary and capricious if it fails to consider the relevant data or if the agency's explanation is inconsistent with the evidence before it. DHS contends that the grace period creates an "administrative burden" and weakens immigration enforcement. DHS provides no empirical data to support the assertion that the current 60 day discretionary grace period has in any way created an enforcement risk or systemic abuse. On the contrary, the proposed rule will significantly increase the backlogs at USCIS by requiring thousands of workers to file defensive, time-critical Change of Status petitions (e.g. B-2 visitor applications) in order to buy time to secure an employer transfer which will in turn dramatically increase the volume of adjudications. 

4. Failure to consider less restrictive regulatory alternatives: DHS acted arbitrarily in failing to consider the availability of a number of viable, less restrictive regulatory alternatives to complete revocation such as: Reducing the grace period (e.g. to 30 or 45 days) rather than eliminating it altogether; Conditioning eligibility on the provision of expedited notification or on the existence of an existing pending I-140; or Providing transition periods for ongoing engineering and technical projects of national economic interest. The failure to consider these obvious, less disruptive alternatives renders the proposed rule legally deficient under the APA. 

Conclusion: Because the NPRM fails to take into account serious reliance interests, frustrates the statutory portability mechanism under AC21, relies upon unquantified justifications and fails to consider reasonable and less restrictive alternatives, DHS must withdraw the proposed rule and preserve 8 CFR § 214.1(l)(2) in full. 

Respectfully submitted
comments.reason: Opposes eliminating the grace period, arguing it violates the APA and ignores reliance interests.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364, RIN 1615-AD22, Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period (91 FR 57807)

I oppose this proposed rule and ask DHS to withdraw it. I am a software engineer in E-3 status and an Australian citizen. I have lived in the United States for a few years with my wife, whose status depends on mine. I have relied on the grace period once, and my experience shows what it is for.

My employer divested part of its business to another company, including my department and my entire team. I was not laid off and did not choose to leave; my job continued under the new owner. But an E-3 worker cannot start work for a new employer until a new petition is approved, and I was out of work for more than six weeks. The grace period kept my wife and me in lawful status while the petition was prepared and filed. Colleagues on my team in H-1B and TN status went through the same process.

Under the proposed rule, that transaction would have put us out of status the following day, while my job was waiting for me. DHS says the rule restores the expectation that workers depart when the employment behind their status ends. My job did not end. It paused for paperwork.

Layoffs, restructurings and closures put workers in the same position. The law already allows these workers to change employers without leaving the country, and the proposal does not change that. What it changes is who can still do so. A worker who changes jobs by choice can have the new petition filed before leaving. A worker whose job ends without warning cannot, and would be out of status the next day. The rule would fall hardest on the people with the least control over what happened to them.

The proposal's cost analysis prices attending a removal hearing and some lost income, but puts no figure on what it costs a family to leave the country at once. No family can do that overnight: booking international flights and packing alone take days. Beyond that, we would have to break a lease, sell our cars at a steep loss, and abandon a household built over several years, including belongings we brought from Australia. We would have to close our U.S. bank accounts and liquidate our brokerage investments, taking savings now invested in the United States out of the country. None of that fits in a suitcase, and none of it appears in the analysis.

The harm also begins the day the rule takes effect, before anyone loses a job. I came here lawfully, at the invitation of a U.S. employer and with the government's approval. I work in a highly skilled, well-paid field and pay substantial federal and state taxes. Without the grace period, my wife and I would live every day knowing that a decision made by someone else could force us to abandon our home at once. That is not a fair way to treat people who were asked to come and who contribute. I would seriously consider leaving the United States rather than live with that risk, and I doubt I would be alone. The analysis counts none of this: not the stress, and not the skills, investment and tax revenue lost when people leave, or decide never to come.

DHS argues that reliance on the grace period is misplaced because it was always discretionary. What we relied on is a minimum protection if something outside our control happens. The 60-day period was part of the terms on which we decided to move here, and in practice it was rarely denied. Taking it away means that a worker who loses a job through no choice of their own goes overnight from lawfully present to someone who can be placed in removal proceedings. That is not how people who followed every rule should be treated.

Finally, DHS says the grace period creates extra work: checking when a job ended, and deciding whether to shorten or deny the 60 days. Removing the grace period does not end the first task. USCIS would still need to know when a job ended to decide when the worker fell out of status. It only ends the second, and simply giving everyone the full 60 days would do the same while keeping the protection.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: Asks DHS to withdraw the proposed rule as it creates immediate out-of-status issues during restructuring.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Shreyans Jain
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers.

I have lived and worked legally in the United States for many years and have built my career and family life here. Throughout that time, I have followed U.S. immigration laws, paid substantial federal, state, and local taxes, and contributed my professional skills to the American construction and real estate industry. My work helps deliver projects that create housing, jobs, investment, and economic activity in the United States.

The 60-day grace period is not a loophole or an extended vacation. It is a practical safeguard for skilled professionals who can unexpectedly lose or leave employment and need a reasonable amount of time to secure another qualifying position and have a new employer file the appropriate petition. Sixty days is already a very short period for a professional hiring process, particularly for senior or specialized positions that require multiple interviews, negotiations, background checks, and immigration filings.

Eliminating this grace period would have consequences far beyond the individual worker. H-1B professionals have spouses, children, homes, financial obligations, and established lives in the United States. My own family has built its life here. An unexpected employment change should not immediately put an entire family’s lawful ability to remain in the country at risk before the worker has even had a reasonable opportunity to find another employer.

It would also place responsible H-1B employees in an unnecessarily vulnerable position. Workers could feel compelled to remain with an employer under unfavorable circumstances simply because losing or leaving a job could immediately jeopardize their immigration status and their family’s stability. A reasonable grace period gives workers some mobility while still requiring them to quickly obtain qualifying employment and comply with immigration law.

I understand and support the government’s responsibility to enforce immigration laws and prevent abuse of the H-1B program. However, eliminating the 60-day grace period would primarily hurt people who have followed the rules, worked hard, paid taxes, developed their careers in America, and made meaningful contributions to the U.S. economy.

The United States should continue attracting and retaining skilled professionals while maintaining appropriate immigration safeguards. Keeping the 60-day grace period strikes that balance.

I respectfully urge the government to retain the existing 60-day grace period for H-1B workers and their families.
comments.reason: Argues the grace period is a vital practical safeguard for skilled professionals facing unexpected layoffs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Prem Balaraju
comments.commentText:
I respectfully request that the Department reconsider the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period and retain the existing discretionary framework. At a minimum, the Department should fully evaluate the economic, administrative, humanitarian, and family-related consequences of the proposal.

The Department should also demonstrate why less restrictive alternatives would be insufficient to achieve its objectives. That explanation should be supported by evidence rather than assumptions about how workers, employers, and families will respond.

A comprehensive assessment should address:

• The number of workers who use the grace period to secure new employment.
• The time employers typically require to complete recruitment and immigration procedures.
• The costs associated with forced departure and international relocation.
• The effect on U.S. businesses that rely on specialized expertise.
• The consequences for spouses and children.
• The potential increase in emergency filings and administrative disputes.
• The effectiveness of targeted compliance measures.
• The feasibility of retaining or modifying the grace period rather than eliminating it.

The Department should also consider whether the proposal would make the United States less competitive in attracting and retaining global talent. Highly skilled professionals evaluate not only salary and career opportunities, but also the predictability and stability of the immigration system. A policy that makes an unexpected layoff an immediate international relocation event could discourage qualified professionals from accepting U.S. positions or encourage existing workers to pursue opportunities in countries with more flexible transition rules.

Conclusion

A sound immigration policy should uphold the integrity of the law while accounting for legitimate employment disruptions, administrative realities, and the interests of U.S. businesses and families. Preserving a limited and appropriately regulated transition period would allow these objectives to be considered together rather than forcing an unnecessarily abrupt choice between immediate departure and the possibility of securing another qualifying opportunity.

The 60-day grace period is a practical safeguard for workers who experience unexpected job loss. It does not eliminate immigration requirements or provide unrestricted employment authorization. Instead, it recognizes that employers and workers need a reasonable amount of time to respond to changing circumstances.

Eliminating the grace period could impose disproportionate consequences on law-abiding professionals, disrupt families, increase costs for employers, and weaken the United States’ ability to retain specialized talent. It could also shift administrative burdens rather than eliminate them.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to withdraw the proposal or adopt a narrower alternative that preserves a reasonable transition period for eligible workers following involuntary employment termination. Any final regulatory action should be supported by a comprehensive assessment of its legal, economic, administrative, family-related, and human consequences.

Thank you for considering these concerns.
comments.reason: Requests the Department reconsider and retain the existing discretionary framework.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Rohan Dhunke
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule, which would eliminate the 60-day grace period currently available to H-1B, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, and TN nonimmigrant workers following cessation of employment.

This rule would cause severe, immediate harm to lawfully present workers and their families through no fault of their own. A layoff or business restructuring — events entirely outside an employee's control — would instantly render workers and their dependents out of status, with no time to pursue a new employer petition, change of status, or orderly departure. The human cost is real: families who have purchased homes, paid taxes, and built lives in U.S. communities would face sudden unlawful presence and potential bars to future admission.

DHS itself acknowledges these reliance interests in the preamble yet proceeds anyway. That is arbitrary and capricious. The agency's rationale — that the grace period is "discretionary" and resource-intensive — does not justify eliminating a protection that has functioned effectively since 2017 and that serves the legitimate interests of both workers and U.S. employers who have invested in sponsoring them.

This rule would also damage U.S. competitiveness by making the nonimmigrant work visa system more punitive and unpredictable, deterring global talent from choosing the United States.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: Argues the rule causes severe harm and urges DHS to withdraw it in its entirety.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Pujitha  Padmala
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Proposed Rule — “Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period”
RIN: 1615-AD22
DHS Docket No.: USCIS-2026-0364

I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider its proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for certain employment-based nonimmigrant workers and their dependents.

As a spouse and parent in a family that depends on a worker’s continued employment and immigration status, I am concerned about the practical consequences this proposal could have on families who have established their lives in the United States. Our children are in school, and we have established a home here. These commitments make the prospect of an unexpected and potentially time-sensitive departure a serious concern.

Losing a job is already a difficult experience. Finding new qualifying employment is not always immediate. The process may involve searching for suitable positions, attending interviews, receiving an offer, completing employer hiring procedures, and addressing immigration-related requirements. Even a qualified worker who is actively pursuing employment may not be able to complete these steps within a very short period. Eliminating the existing grace period could leave families with significantly less time to navigate these circumstances and make informed decisions about their future.

The consequences would extend beyond the worker. Children could face disruption to their education, friendships, and established routines. Families could also have difficulty managing housing costs, leases, mortgages, and other financial commitments if they had to relocate unexpectedly. These are practical consequences that deserve careful consideration when evaluating changes to immigration policy.

I recognize that DHS has identified maintaining the connection between nonimmigrant status and qualifying employment, as well as reducing administrative burdens, as objectives of this proposal. However, I respectfully ask DHS to consider whether these objectives can be achieved without eliminating the transition period entirely. Retaining the existing discretionary 60-day grace period would preserve an opportunity for affected workers and their families to assess their options, pursue new qualifying employment, and make necessary arrangements. DHS could continue to exercise its existing discretion to shorten or eliminate the period when warranted.

I also encourage DHS to fully evaluate the real-world effects of this change on families, children, employers, and communities before adopting a final rule.

A reasonable transition period provides important flexibility during an unpredictable event without guaranteeing that every worker will remain in the United States. I respectfully request that DHS retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period and carefully consider the stability of affected families when making its final decision.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to reconsider eliminating the grace period to protect established families and children.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposal to remove 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2), and I urge DHS to withdraw it.

1. The rule is lawful and has worked since 2017. INA Sections 103(a) and 214(a) let DHS set the "time and conditions" of nonimmigrant stay, and DHS used that authority in the 2016 AC21 rule. The statute does not require a worker to leave the day a job ends, and DHS offers no new evidence that the 2017 choice has failed.

2. Abuse is already covered. The current rule lets USCIS shorten or eliminate the grace period case by case, for example in cases of fraud. Eliminating it for everyone also punishes the many workers who are laid off through no fault of their own.

3. The burden rationale is thin. DHS cites "over 1.9 million petitions or applications" that "potentially" required grace-period assessment, but does not say how many actually did, or how much time or money that took. Its benefits line reads "Not Estimated." Adjudicators already review employment end dates in extension and change-of-status cases, and DHS dismisses the alternatives (a shorter period or clearer evidence rules) in a few sentences. The proposal would also create new work: DHS admits USCIS "would devote resources to issue NTAs and initiate removal proceedings."

4. The harm falls on people who did nothing wrong. H-1B, L-1, O-1, E, and TN workers are often laid off in downsizings and closures. Under the proposal, status ends the day employment ends. Without the grace period:
- Workers who have already found a new job could fall out of status before the new employer can file.
- Dependents lose status through no act of their own, including children in school.
- Workers with pending I-485 applications risk years of progress toward permanent residence.
- Workers must leave within days or stay out of status.
DHS's own figures, about 3,795 people losing income and $204.43 to $300.53 per person in time and travel costs, probably understate the harm and leave out what it costs to uproot families.

5. Reliance interests are brushed aside. DHS acknowledges that workers and employers "may have made business arrangements" and that people have "purchased houses, paid taxes," then says "any reliance ... would be misplaced" because the grace period is discretionary. Under DHS v. Regents of the University of California, 591 U.S. 1 (2020), an agency changing a long-standing policy must meaningfully weigh reliance interests. A discretionary policy published as a rule in 2017 still creates them.

6. The rule hurts employers. DHS admits "a temporary loss of productivity." U.S. employers hire laid-off specialized workers, such as engineers and researchers, who can start quickly if they can lawfully stay. Without the grace period, employers lose those candidates and roles stay open longer. The grace period supports the "job portability, stability, and flexibility" that DHS cited in 2016 and that Congress endorsed in AC21.

7. It is inconsistent with other rules. F-1 students get a 60-day period after completing their program (8 CFR 214.2(f)(5)(iv)), and the WARN Act requires 60 days' notice of mass layoffs because workers need time to adjust. A laid-off worker should not be treated more harshly than a student who finishes a degree.

Requested action: DHS should withdraw the proposal and keep 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2). If it proceeds, it should at a minimum preserve the grace period for dependents and for anyone with a pending I-485, extension, or change-of-status filing; adopt a transition period for people already in the U.S.; publish data on grace-period use and adjudication burden; and fully analyze reliance interests and less drastic alternatives, as Regents requires.

Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to withdraw the proposal as harm falls on innocent workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by MC N
comments.commentText:
I understand and respect DHS’s objectives of protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of employment-based visa programs. I respectfully believe that these goals can be achieved while retaining a reasonable grace period for workers who unexpectedly lose their jobs.

1. Job loss should allow a reasonable opportunity to find another job
Many H-1B and other employment-based visa holders have spent years in the United States, complying with its laws, paying taxes, and contributing to its economic and technological development.
When they lose their jobs, often due to circumstances beyond their control, they should have a reasonable opportunity to find another qualifying position or arrange their departure. The grace period provides time to pursue lawful options; it does not automatically authorize employment or guarantee continued status.

2. Sixty days is already a limited period to find a job
Finding a suitable position involves applications, interviews, hiring decisions, and immigration procedures, all of which take time. Even 60 days can be insufficient, particularly for specialized roles.
Eliminating this period altogether would create additional hardship without clearly demonstrating how it would create more opportunities for American workers.

3. Address misuse directly rather than penalizing everyone
If some individuals or employers abuse visa programs, DHS should address those problems through appropriate screening, oversight, and targeted enforcement. People who comply with immigration laws should not be treated as though they have misused the system simply because they lose their jobs.
If the concern is that visa programs are being misused, the appropriate response is to strengthen eligibility requirements and enforcement rather than eliminate a reasonable transition period for everyone.

4. Consider the impact on families who have built their lives in the United States
Many of us have lived in the United States for more than a decade while waiting in the employment-based green card queue. During these years, we have purchased homes, taken on mortgages, invested our life savings, and built stable lives for our families.
Our children have grown up here, attended American schools for much of their lives, built friendships, participated in extracurricular activities, and pursued their dreams. For these families, the United States is not simply a temporary workplace; it is the place they call home.
Eliminating the 60-day grace period could force families to make life-altering decisions with very little time to prepare. Selling a home, settling a mortgage, disposing of other valuable assets, and arranging an international relocation cannot realistically be accomplished within such a short period without potentially substantial financial losses.
For children who have spent most of their lives here, an abrupt departure could also cause significant emotional distress and disrupt their education, friendships, activities, and future aspirations.
These concerns reflect the real circumstances faced by families who have established their lives in the United States over many years. The consequences extend beyond employment and immigration paperwork; they affect families' financial security, stability, and well-being.

I understand and respect DHS’s objectives of protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of employment-based visa programs. I respectfully believe that these goals can be achieved while retaining a reasonable grace period for workers who unexpectedly lose their jobs.

People who have complied with U.S. laws, paid taxes, and contributed to this country for many years should have a reasonable opportunity to find qualifying employment or prepare to depart if necessary.

I humbly request that DHS consider the significant human, financial, and family consequences of this proposal, particularly for long-term residents who have spent years waiting in the green card queue and whose children have grown up in the United States.

Please reconsider eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period and explore alternatives that address the agency's concerns while allowing affected workers and their families reasonable time to plan their next steps.
comments.reason: Believes visa integrity can be protected while retaining a reasonable grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by SC N
comments.commentText:
I respectfully request that DHS reconsider the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period. While I understand the importance of protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of employment-based visa programs, I believe it is equally important to consider the real-life circumstances of individuals and families who have spent many years building their lives in the United States.

Many of us have lived in the United States for over a decade, followed its laws, paid taxes, contributed to its economy, and built our lives here while waiting for our green cards. Losing a job, often due to circumstances beyond our control, does not necessarily mean someone has misused the visa system or can no longer contribute to the country. Finding another qualifying job within 60 days is already challenging, given the time required for interviews, hiring decisions, and immigration procedures.

For families like mine, the consequences extend far beyond employment. We have homes, mortgages, life savings, and children who have spent much of their lives in the United States, attending school, building friendships, participating in activities, and pursuing their dreams. Being forced to leave on short notice could result in significant financial losses, disrupt our children's lives, and cause considerable emotional hardship.

I humbly request that DHS retain the existing grace period. Providing a reasonable opportunity to find another qualifying job or prepare for departure would help families navigate an already difficult situation with dignity, while continuing to respect immigration laws and protect the interests of American workers.
comments.reason: Requests DHS retain the existing grace period to prevent major financial and emotional hardship.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers.

1. The 60-day period is already limited.

Losing a job due to layoffs, restructuring, or budget cuts is often beyond a worker's control. Finding a new employer, completing interviews, securing sponsorship, and filing an H-1B transfer petition can take several weeks or longer. Eliminating the grace period would force qualified workers to leave the country even when they are actively seeking employment and trying to comply with immigration law.

2. Established workers and families have significant financial commitments.

Many H-1B professionals have spent years contributing to the U.S. economy, paying taxes, purchasing homes, paying mortgages, financing vehicles, and saving for retirement. Abruptly eliminating the grace period could create severe financial hardship for workers and their families, who cannot immediately unwind these long-term commitments.

3. The impact could extend to American homeowners and the housing market.

If affected H-1B homeowners are forced to leave the country on short notice, some may need to sell their properties quickly and potentially below their reasonable market value. A concentration of such sales could increase supply and put downward pressure on local home prices, potentially affecting neighboring homeowners, including American citizens. The nationwide impact would depend on the scale and geographic concentration of these sales, but DHS should consider these potential indirect economic consequences.

4. The proposal could harm U.S. employers and economic competitiveness.

The United States benefits from experienced professionals who contribute specialized skills, institutional knowledge, and productivity. Eliminating the grace period could cause employers to lose qualified workers who might otherwise transition to another U.S. employer, increasing recruitment costs and disrupting ongoing projects.

Conclusion

I support immigration compliance, but eliminating the discretionary 60-day grace period would impose disproportionate consequences on workers who lose employment through no fault of their own, their families, U.S. employers, and potentially American homeowners.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw the proposal and retain the existing 60-day grace period in full. This limited protection provides a necessary opportunity for workers to seek new employment, pursue lawful immigration options, and make responsible arrangements without facing an immediate forced departure from the United States.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to withdraw the proposal, citing short notice and financial distress for families.

comments.title: REDACTIONS (PII- IEP SCHOOL ID, D.O.B, etc.): Comment Submitted by Siva Prasad Bhushetty
comments.commentText:
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 (RIN 1615-AD22), Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

To the Regulatory Coordination Division, USCIS:

Introduction
I am writing in response to the proposed rule published September 11, 2026, which would remove 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2) and require H-1B workers and their dependents to depart the United States immediately when employment ends. I respectfully urge DHS not to finalize this change. I am an H-1B worker, a taxpayer, and the parent of a young autistic child who is a U.S. citizen.

My family's situation
My son is four years old. He is a U.S. citizen and he is autistic. He receives ongoing behavioral and occupational therapy, along with other developmental supports. These are a structured, continuous program built around his needs and delivered by professionals who know him. I have attached a redacted copy of his IEP.

Children with autism depend on routine and trusted relationships. Progress is built slowly, and interruptions can cause regression that takes far longer to repair than the interruption itself. At four years old, my son is at the stage where early intervention matters most.

What the proposal would mean
Today, an H-1B worker who loses a job has a short window to find a new employer and have a petition filed. Under the proposal, the worker would be out of status the day after employment ends and expected to leave immediately. A layoff, which an employee does not control, could force my family to decide within days whether to dismantle our life here, with no time to find a new employer or transition his care.

Harm to a U.S. citizen child
My son is an American citizen. The rule targets workers, but its consequences would fall directly on children like him. If we were forced to leave abruptly, he would lose his therapists, program, doctors, and home, and be moved to a country where services for autistic children are extremely limited. The therapy he receives here cannot realistically be replaced there. Autistic children often find transitions very difficult, and a sudden move combined with the loss of every therapy he relies on could cause severe distress and set back years of progress. A U.S. citizen child should not lose access to necessary care because of an administrative change aimed at a different purpose.

A stabilizing mechanism
DHS notes that the grace period is discretionary, not required by statute, and that removing it would reduce administrative burden. I understand these goals. But the grace period has been in the regulations since January 2017 and has served a practical purpose: it lets workers who lose jobs seek new employment in lawful status instead of facing immediate departure. Employers, workers, schools, and medical providers have relied on it. The administrative burden argument carries less weight when weighed against harm to children who need uninterrupted care.

Reliance interests
DHS has invited comments on reliance interests. Families like mine chose where to live, which employers to work for, and how to arrange our children's care based on rules that included a short safety net. Many of us signed leases and built treatment plans with providers on the assumption that a job loss would not mean instant forced departure. Therapy waitlists are long, and it takes months to find the right providers and build trust with a child. Removing the grace period would undermine decisions made in good faith.

Added hardships
For most H-1B families, health insurance is tied to employment, so a job loss can also end coverage for a child's therapies. Finding a new sponsor takes time and money, and without a grace period there would be no lawful time to do it. Spouses, including the caregiver who manages a child's therapy schedule, would also have to leave, disrupting the child's whole support system. An abrupt departure also carries heavy costs for a family already paying for therapy.

Requests
I respectfully ask DHS to:
1. Retain the 60-day grace period in 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
2. If DHS proceeds, protect families with children who have documented disabilities or ongoing medical needs, through an extended or case-by-case grace period.
3. Analyze the effect on U.S. citizen children in the impact assessment.
4. Provide a reasonable transition period for existing H-1B holders.

Conclusion
The 60-day grace period is a modest but meaningful protection that allows people who lose employment to respond in an orderly way. For families raising children with autism, it can be the difference between continued care and a traumatic move to a place where our child's needs cannot be met. Thank you for your careful consideration.

Respectfully,
Siva Prasad Bhushetty
Morrisville, NC
comments.reason: Urges DHS not to finalize the change, citing severe disruptions to a U.S. citizen child's therapy.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Opposition to DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364: Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I strongly oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for employment-based nonimmigrant workers and their dependents.

- Severe impact on established families: I am an H-1B professional with H-4 dependent family members. My family has built our life in the United States through lawful employment, paying taxes, homeownership, and participation in our community. Losing employment should not require an entire family to leave the country immediately.

- Families have significant reliance interests: We have a mortgage and substantial long-term financial obligations. We made these commitments while complying with U.S. immigration laws and relying on the existing regulatory framework. Immediate departure following an unexpected layoff could create devastating financial consequences, including difficulty maintaining mortgage payments or selling a home on extremely short notice.

- Children would suffer consequences for circumstances beyond their control: My children attend high school and are preparing for college. An immediate departure could disrupt their education during some of the most important academic years of their lives. Children should not suddenly lose their school, teachers, friends, activities, and college preparation because a parent's employment unexpectedly ends.

- The 60-day period promotes lawful compliance: The grace period does not provide unrestricted employment authorization. Instead, it provides a short and reasonable period for a worker to find another sponsoring employer, pursue an eligible change of status or adjustment of status, or arrange an orderly departure. Removing it turns an unexpected job loss into an immediate immigration crisis.

- Job loss is often outside the employee's control: Layoffs can result from restructuring, economic conditions, mergers, budget reductions, or elimination of positions. A worker who has followed every immigration requirement should not immediately lose the ability to remain in the country simply because an employer eliminates a position.

- Administrative convenience does not justify severe family hardship: DHS cites administrative burden as one reason for eliminating the grace period. That burden should instead be addressed through clearer documentation requirements, standardized reporting of employment termination dates, or other administrative improvements. Eliminating an important protection for thousands of lawful workers and their families is unnecessarily harsh.

- The proposal could also hurt U.S. employers: The current grace period gives American companies an opportunity to recruit experienced workers who have unexpectedly lost employment. Requiring these workers to leave immediately can delay hiring, disrupt projects, increase relocation and immigration-related costs, and cause employers to lose access to specialized skills.

- The economic impact extends far beyond lost wages: Families like mine have mortgages, vehicles, insurance, household expenses, financial accounts, and community obligations. An immediate departure could require families to sell homes and other property under severe time pressure while simultaneously arranging international relocation.

- Even families that ultimately must depart deserve reasonable transition time: Families need time to handle housing, finances, school records, medical care, transportation, personal property, and other basic responsibilities. Requiring immediate departure after employment ends is neither practical nor humane. A limited 60-day transition period provides families an opportunity to resolve these obligations responsibly.

- DHS should retain the existing 60-day grace period: At minimum, DHS should adopt a defined grace period rather than eliminate it entirely. Strong safeguards could address fraud, unauthorized employment, criminal conduct, or national-security concerns without imposing extraordinary hardship on law-abiding workers and their dependents.

My family has followed U.S. immigration laws, contributed through employment and taxes, purchased a home, established roots in our community, and planned our children's education in the United States. We are not asking for unlimited status or employment authorization. We are asking for a reasonable amount of time to respond to an unexpected loss of employment without putting an entire family's home, finances, education, and future at immediate risk.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by V G
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period. Instead of eliminating it, I propose revising the grace-period framework in a way that better protects the interests of the American economy while maintaining appropriate immigration controls.

H-1B workers can lose their jobs suddenly for reasons completely outside their control, including layoffs, restructuring, or other business decisions. The current grace period provides these workers and their dependents with an important transition period following the cessation of employment. The existing regulation provides a discretionary grace period of up to 60 days, or until the end of the worker's authorized validity period, whichever is shorter.

In practice, even 60 days can be a challenging timeframe. An individual must search for an appropriate position, complete the employer's recruitment and interview process, receive and accept an offer, and then allow the new employer and its immigration counsel sufficient time to prepare and file the necessary H-1B petition. The economic value of the grace period is therefore not simply additional time to remain in the United States. It provides a limited opportunity for skilled workers already participating in the U.S. economy to transition to another U.S. employer rather than having their careers disrupted because of an unexpected termination.

Rather than eliminating the grace period, I respectfully propose that DHS consider a structured, tiered grace-period framework based on objective criteria.

For example, DHS could consider factors such as the individual's length of lawful employment in the United States, history of maintaining lawful immigration status, employment and tax history, education, occupational qualifications, industry they have contributed to, and other relevant factors.

An illustrative framework could be:

1 to 5 years of qualifying U.S. employment: up to 60 days
5 to 10 years of qualifying U.S. employment: up to 120 days
More than 10 years of qualifying U.S. employment: up to one year

These time periods are offered as an example for consideration rather than as definitive thresholds. DHS could determine appropriate durations and eligibility criteria based on economic and immigration data.

Such an approach could also require an affected worker to affirmatively request the grace period and demonstrate eligibility under the applicable tier, rather than treating every case identically. This could provide DHS with a structured mechanism for evaluating eligibility while preserving a meaningful transition period for workers with substantial histories of lawful employment in the United States.

This approach would recognize an important distinction: a professional who has lawfully worked in the United States for many years, consistently maintained immigration status, paid taxes, developed specialized expertise, and established a long-term employment history represents a significant accumulation of human capital within the U.S. economy. An unexpected layoff should not unnecessarily cause that experience and expertise to leave the U.S. labor market simply because the individual could not complete a new hiring and immigration process within a short period.

The United States should not lose skilled professionals solely because their employment ended unexpectedly and they were unable to secure another qualifying employer within an inflexible timeframe.

I therefore respectfully request that DHS reconsider eliminating the grace period and instead evaluate reforms that preserve the transition period while making it more structured, objective, and directly connected to the economic contributions and immigration history of the affected worker.

This would, in my view, better balance immigration oversight with the long-term economic interest of the United States.

I am writing not only as an H-1B professional, but also as a parent, homeowner, taxpayer, and long-term resident who has lived lawfully in the United States for nearly 12 years. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
This comment is submitted anonymously. I oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B nonimmigrants, for a reason the preamble never accounts for: each H-1B slot is a scarce, rationed public resource, and destroying the worker's ability to transfer within 60 days destroys the slot itself — at zero benefit to anyone.

An H-1B cap number is not fungible the way the proposal pretends. Congress authorizes 85,000 new H-1B visas per fiscal year — 65,000 regular cap plus 20,000 for U.S. advanced-degree holders. For FY 2026, roughly 344,000 registrations were filed for about 336,000 unique beneficiaries, and only about 35.3 percent were selected. Each selected registration represents a lottery slot that was won, once, against nearly three-to-one odds — a slot that cannot be re-created, re-issued, or recovered within the fiscal year.

The 60-day grace period is the mechanism that conserves that slot when employment ends. A specialty-occupation worker who is laid off — an engineer, a physician, a researcher — and who finds another sponsoring employer within 60 days does not consume a new cap number: the transfer is cap-exempt, so the original slot survives. The worker keeps contributing in a specialty occupation, the new employer keeps operating, and the agency spends nothing to make this happen. The grace period is, in resource terms, a conservation policy.

Eliminate the grace period and the math inverts. The same laid-off worker, given zero days to transfer, must depart — and the cap number that was won at three-to-one odds is destroyed. It cannot be handed to the next registrant, because selection ran months earlier; it cannot be rolled over, because the statute does not allow it. Congress's allocation of 85,000 shrinks in practice: every layoff that lands on day zero of the new rule converts a won slot into a dead one. Multiply that across thousands of temporary separations per year — reorganizations, mergers, project completions, ordinary business churn — and the proposal systematically shrinks the effective supply of H-1B workers the economy was allocated, while the 35.3 percent selection rate means the economy has no way to backfill them.

The agency's cost-benefit analysis counts the administrative savings of fewer grace-period cases while assigning zero value to the destroyed cap numbers. That is the relevant omission. A slot won at three-to-one odds against 336,000 beneficiaries is worth, at minimum, the economic contribution of the specialty-occupation worker who would have filled it — a figure the preamble never attempts to price. DHS also never explains why a cap-exempt transfer, which costs the agency nothing and consumes no new cap number, must be prohibited in service of a fraud concern the grace period does not create: the transfer petition still undergoes full adjudication, with the same evidence and the same officer review as any other.

This is not a humanitarian plea for more time. It is resource arithmetic. The grace period conserves a rationed national resource at zero cost; its elimination destroys that resource with every layoff. An agency steward of a lottery-allocated program should not burn winning tickets. DHS should retain the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes eliminating the grace period because it conserves H-1B cap slots and allows transfers.
