comments.title: Comment Submitted by Davi  Ramon
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other nonimmigrant workers. I am an H-1B software engineer working in the United States since 2021. The grace period is the only thing that keeps a sudden job loss from immediately making a lawful, tax-paying worker and their family deportable.

1. Job loss is usually beyond the worker's control. Layoffs, restructurings and project cancellations happen without warning, often to high performers. Removing the grace period punishes workers for their employer's business decisions, not for anything they did.

2. Sixty days is already short. In that time a worker must find a new role, get through interviews, receive an offer, and have the new employer file an H-1B petition. Hiring for skilled roles often takes longer than 60 days. Without any grace period, even a worker who already has an offer could be out of status in the days between jobs.

3. Families would be uprooted overnight. Spouses and children in dependent status lose status along with the worker. Children would be pulled out of school mid-year. Families would need to break leases, sell homes and cars at a loss, and arrange international moves within days, often while still paying a mortgage or lease in the United States. Spouses who work under their own authorization would lose their jobs too.

4. It would weaken the system it is meant to protect.
- Workers would become more dependent on their current employer. They could not risk any gap between jobs, which makes it harder to leave poor working conditions and easier for employers to hold down wages.
- The rule would push people into rushed decisions: hurried departures, or accepting the first offer available instead of the best fit.
- The United States would lose talent it has already invested in, to countries with more predictable immigration rules.

5. The grace period is already limited and discretionary. It is used once per validity period, capped at 60 days, and ends sooner if the I-94 expires. It gives no work authorization; it only gives people time to act lawfully. Removing it would not change who is admitted. It would only make an ordinary event like a layoff catastrophic for the worker's family.

6. Visa appointment backlogs abroad make the risk much worse. H-1B workers who travel need a visa stamp in their passport to re-enter. In India, the average wait for an H-1B interview at a US consulate is currently more than 9 months. That creates three problems:

- Workers can't travel safely. Many skip weddings, funerals, and care for sick or dying parents, because leaving the US can mean being stuck abroad for most of a year waiting to return.
- Workers abroad would be stranded. Anyone outside the US when a layoff happens, or right after starting a new job, may be unable to come back for months. Without a grace period, their status could lapse while they wait for an appointment they have no control over.
- No grace period plus a 9-month backlog leaves no safe option. Someone laid off inside the US couldn't stay long enough to find a new job, and couldn't leave and expect to return in any reasonable time. Their spouse and children would face the same choice: remain in limbo or uproot their lives entirely.

The grace period is one of the few protections that works around delays the government itself creates. Removing it while consular wait times are this long would turn routine life events into crises for families who have followed every rule.

I urge the agency to keep the 60-day grace period. If anything, extending it would better reflect how long skilled hiring actually takes.

Respectfully,
H1B worker

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing as an H-1B nonimmigrant who has lived and worked in the United States lawfully for over 8 years. I oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period, and I ask DHS to withdraw it. My comment addresses the practical impossibility of the proposal's central premise: that a person can "depart the United States immediately" the day after employment ends.

1. The proposal treats years-long residents as day visitors.

I have built a life here: a residential lease, a car, bank accounts, utilities, tax obligations, and professional commitments. If my employment ends, I cannot unwind any of this in a single day — no American could either. My lease requires 60 days' notice to terminate; breaking it early triggers thousands of dollars in penalties. Selling a car under 24-hour pressure is impossible. Closing accounts, canceling services, arranging international travel for myself and handling the logistics of an intercontinental move are weeks of work, not hours. The 60-day grace period exists precisely because employment cessation is not an event that begins and ends in a day — it is the start of a process: seeking new employment, filing for a change of status, or arranging an orderly departure. The proposal replaces that process with a single-day cliff.

2. DHS's cost analysis understates the harm.

The NPRM acknowledges that eliminating the grace period could create "real financial and logistical difficulties" and estimates roughly 3,795 nonimmigrant beneficiaries could face lost income from a forced, immediate departure. That figure captures only lost wages — not lease penalties, credit damage from broken contracts, forced asset sales at a loss, or the cost of emergency international relocation. These are not hypothetical; they are the standard financial facts of renting and living in any American city. The true cost to affected workers and their families is multiples of what the analysis reflects.

3. Eliminating the grace period creates violations rather than compliance.

The grace period does not authorize employment. It allows a person who is actively trying to remain in compliance — filing an H-1B transfer petition with a new employer, applying for a change of status, or booking travel home — the time to do so lawfully. Under the proposal, a worker who loses their job through no fault of their own becomes a status violator overnight, even while taking every lawful step available. The rule would manufacture the very noncompliance it claims to prevent, and accrue unlawful presence that can trigger three- and ten-year bars on future admission.

4. The "administrative burden" justification works against the agency's own interests.

A workforce that cannot transition in an orderly way is more likely to accrue unlawful presence, require enforcement attention, and generate removal proceedings — all of which burden the agency and the immigration courts far more than maintaining the current, rarely contested grace-period framework.

Request:

 I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal. If any change is finalized, the grace period should at minimum be preserved for workers with established U.S. residence, no change should apply retroactively to workers already in the country, and the agency should publish a revised cost analysis that accounts for the full financial consequences described above.

I came to this country legally, have followed every rule, paid taxes, and contributed to the American economy and community in good faith. The grace period is not a loophole — it is the minimum decency owed to people who did everything right. Thank you for considering this comment.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes the proposal and asks DHS to withdraw it.

comments.title: MM38 Comment Submitted by Ram Immaneni

I respectfully oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B workers.

I am an H-1B professional from India who legally lives and works in the United States. Like many H-1B workers, I work, pay taxes, support American businesses, and contribute to my local community. Losing a job is not the same as choosing to violate immigration law. An H-1B worker can lose employment because of a layoff, new company priorities, project cancellations, company restructuring, acquisition, or economic downturn, even when the worker has performed well and maintained lawful status.

The 60-day grace period is extremely important because finding another H-1B job is not instantaneous. A worker may need weeks to apply, interview, receive an offer, complete background checks, provide immigration documents, and have the new employer and immigration attorneys prepare and file the required petition. The employer also needs time for internal approvals and immigration processing. Sixty days is therefore a practical transition period, not an excessive benefit.

Most importantly, an H-1B worker is often supporting an entire family. Consider a family with an H-1B worker, an H-4 spouse, children in American schools, a mortgage or lease, car payments, health insurance, childcare expenses, and years of community ties. If the worker is unexpectedly terminated, the consequences affect everyone. The spouse may lose employment authorization, children may have to leave their schools, and the family may suddenly face the possibility of selling a home, terminating a lease, selling vehicles, arranging international travel, and leaving the country.

The grace period also benefits the U.S. economy. If an H-1B worker loses one job but finds another U.S. employer within 60 days, the worker continues earning income, paying taxes, spending money in the local economy, and contributing valuable skills to an American company. Without the grace period, a worker could be forced to leave the United States shortly after termination, even when an American employer is prepared to hire that person. This creates unnecessary disruption for the worker, family, employer and economy. The worker may ultimately return to the United States for another job, meaning the immediate departure may accomplish little beyond creating substantial financial and emotional costs.

The 60-day grace period is not permanent status, a guarantee of another job, or permission to disregard immigration law. It is a short bridge that allows a law-abiding worker to find another qualifying employer, complete the required immigration process, or make an orderly departure.

Please preserve this important protection for H-1B workers and their families.

I strongly oppose this proposed rule, which would eliminate the 60-day grace period currently available to H-1B, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, and TN nonimmigrant workers following cessation of employment.

This rule would cause severe, immediate harm to lawfully present workers and their families through no fault of their own. A layoff or business restructuring — events entirely outside an employee's control — would instantly render workers and their dependents out of status, with no time to pursue a new employer petition, change of status, or orderly departure. The human cost is real: families who have purchased homes, paid taxes, and built lives in U.S. communities would face sudden unlawful presence and potential bars to future admission.

DHS itself acknowledges these reliance interests in the preamble yet proceeds anyway. That is arbitrary and capricious. The agency's rationale — that the grace period is "discretionary" and resource-intensive — does not justify eliminating a protection that has functioned effectively since 2017 and that serves the legitimate interests of both workers and U.S. employers who have invested in sponsoring them.

This rule would also damage U.S. competitiveness by making the nonimmigrant work visa system more punitive and unpredictable, deterring global talent from choosing the United States.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule, stating it causes severe harm to lawfully present workers and families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Josephine Joseph
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security and USCIS:

I oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period and ask DHS to withdraw it. I am an H-1B worker, and my family would be directly affected.

1. The timeframe is impossible. The proposal ends status the day after employment ends. A layoff often comes with little or no notice. Within a day, a family would have to do all of the following:

Sell or exit a home. Closing a sale takes months, and a forced sale means heavy losses. Renters face lease penalties and lost deposits.
Pay off car loans and sell vehicles.
Sell, ship or dispose of a household's belongings.
Pull children out of school mid-year.
Close out final pay, health insurance, retirement accounts, taxes and bank obligations.
Interrupt medical care, including pregnancy or a family member's treatment.
No family can do this lawfully and responsibly in a day. Even 60 days is demanding.

2. It punishes people who did nothing wrong. Workers laid off through no fault of their own would fall out of status immediately. The grace period gives them time to find a new sponsor and file a change-of-employer petition. Without it, a qualified worker loses the chance to stay and work for a U.S. employer.

3. Reliance interests are substantial. The grace period has been in the regulations since 2016. Families have bought homes, signed leases, enrolled children in school and planned their lives around it. DHS asked for comment on reliance interests. Removing the rule with no transition period ignores them and is arbitrary.

4. The cost analysis is incomplete. The proposal does not account for forced-sale losses, lease penalties, relocation costs, disrupted schooling, lost spousal income or the cost to employers of losing workers they would rehire. A rule with these effects needs a full accounting before it is finalized.

5. Administrative convenience does not justify the harm. The grace period does not authorize work. It only prevents an immediate status violation while a worker finds a new employer or arranges an orderly departure. DHS has not shown that it causes a real integrity problem.

Request DHS to consider retaining the grace period. If it makes a change, it should be considerate the below :

Set a minimum of 30 days or more.
Provide a transition period for people already in the U.S.
Give extra time to dependents, especially children in school.
Complete a full cost-benefit analysis first.
comments.reason: The commenter opposes eliminating the grace period, detailing the impossible timeframe for wrapping up life affairs.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Sam  S
comments.commentText:
I write to urge DHS to protect the 60-day grace period, a critical measure that ensures fairness for compliant foreign workers and benefits American employers.

Losing employment due to a company layoff or market downturn is an unforeseen event, not a willful violation of status. Finding a replacement position and navigating the legal transfer process—from LCA certification to attorney filing—takes time. Without a reasonable transition window, workers are forced to uproot their lives overnight, even when domestic employers are ready to hire them.

Many Indian H-1B holders have built lives in the U.S. over many years while waiting in green-card backlogs with approved I-140s. Abruptly ending a grace period inflicts immediate harm on families: children must leave their schools, spouses lose their jobs, and households must immediately manage leases, mortgages, and international relocation costs.

Maintaining the 60-day grace period is a practical, common-sense rule that helps U.S. companies retain skilled talent and prevents unnecessary financial trauma for families who do everything right. Please preserve this crucial protection.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to protect the grace period as a critical measure ensuring fairness and economic benefit.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ram Sai
comments.commentText:
Subject: Opposition to DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I strongly oppose the Department of Homeland Security’s proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other affected employment-based nonimmigrant workers.

As an H-1B professional working in the United States, I believe eliminating this grace period would create unnecessary hardship for skilled workers, their families, and American employers. Losing a job can happen unexpectedly due to layoffs, restructuring, project cancellations, or business decisions that are beyond an employee’s control. Such circumstances should not automatically force a skilled worker to leave the United States immediately.

The existing 60-day grace period provides a reasonable and limited opportunity for affected workers to find another sponsoring employer, pursue an eligible change of immigration status, consult an immigration attorney, or make orderly arrangements to depart the country. It is not an unlimited benefit; it is a practical safeguard that allows workers and employers to navigate a complex immigration system responsibly.

Eliminating this protection would place workers under extreme time pressure. Securing a new position, completing interviews, receiving an offer, coordinating with an employer’s immigration counsel, and filing the necessary petition can take several weeks or longer. Even when a worker is qualified and actively seeking employment, these processes cannot always be completed immediately.

This proposal could also harm American businesses. Employers may lose access to experienced professionals who could otherwise transition to new positions within the United States. Companies would face greater recruitment uncertainty, while workers would be forced to make rushed decisions about relocation, housing, financial commitments, and family responsibilities.

Furthermore, many H-1B professionals have made substantial investments in their careers and lives in the United States. Some have spent years contributing to American businesses, paying taxes, developing specialized skills, and pursuing permanent residence through employment-based immigration. Abruptly removing the grace period would create significant uncertainty for people who have followed the rules and built their lives around the existing regulatory framework.

If DHS is concerned about administrative burden or misuse of the grace period, it should consider targeted safeguards rather than eliminating the protection for everyone. For example, DHS could retain the existing maximum 60-day period while continuing to evaluate eligibility and enforce applicable immigration requirements.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and preserve the existing 60-day grace period. At a minimum, DHS should retain a reasonable transition period that gives affected workers a fair opportunity to secure new employment, pursue another lawful immigration option, or prepare for departure without unnecessary hardship.

A balanced immigration system should protect compliance while recognizing the realities of employment transitions. Preserving the 60-day grace period supports workers, families, American employers, and the broader U.S. economy.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Docket No.: USCIS-2026-0364
RIN: 1615-AD22
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes the rule, noting the grace period provides a necessary practical safeguard.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Ragha Y
comments.commentText:
I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers H-1B. Removing this crucial provision will harm U.S. businesses, disrupt the lives of legal high-skilled workers and their families, and create unnecessary systemic inefficiencies.
### 1. Severe Harm to U.S. Employers and Market Stability
The 60-day grace period allows U.S. employers to recruit highly skilled talent already present and integrated into the domestic workforce. Forcing workers to immediately depart the United States upon termination—often due to sudden corporate restructuring or layoffs outside their control—deprives American businesses of a critical talent pool. Requiring foreign workers to depart and go through consular processing abroad adds significant delays, operational downtime, and increased costs for U.S. companies seeking to fill key roles quickly.
### 2. Undue Hardship on Lawful Nonimmigrant Workers and Families
Nonimmigrant workers on E, H, L, O, and TN visas reside in the United States legally, pay taxes, sign residential leases, buy homes, and enroll children in local schools. Expecting individuals and their families to liquidate assets, settle legal obligations, pack up their lives, and depart the country within 24 to 48 hours of employment termination is unfeasible and punitive. The grace period provides a basic, humane window to wind down personal affairs or transition to another lawful status.
### 3. Increased Agency Burden and Backlogs
DHS argues that eliminating the grace period reduces administrative burden; however, forcing immediate departure will likely have the opposite effect. Without a transition window, the rule will lead to an increase in emergency change-of-status applications, increased litigation, and a higher volume of Notices to Appear (NTAs) and removal proceedings in already overburdened immigration courts (EOIR). This shifts administrative work from standard petitions to costly enforcement proceedings.
### 4. Undermining American Competitiveness
High-skilled nonimmigrant workers drive innovation across tech, healthcare, engineering, and research sectors. Removing basic protections like job portability and transition security makes the U.S. less attractive to top global talent, driving skilled professionals to countries with more predictable and stable immigration policies.
**Conclusion:**
The 60-day grace period strikes a reasonable balance between maintaining program integrity and offering essential flexibility for employers and workers alike. I urge DHS and USCIS to withdraw this proposed rule and retain the existing 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
comments.reason: The commenter expresses strong opposition, stating removal will harm U.S. businesses and disrupt workers' lives.

Comment in opposition to the proposed changes to the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers

Docket No.USCIS-2026-0364

I am an H-1B professional writing to oppose eliminating or shortening the 60-day grace period.

I came to the United States legally, earned a master’s degree here, and have worked here in health technology ever since, building products that aim to improve healthcare for millions of Americans. I have followed every rule along the way and paid my taxes. My wife and I are raising our two five-year-old sons, both born in the U.S. This is the only home they know.

I support the government’s efforts to stop fraud and abuse in the H-1B program. But the 60-day grace period does not enable abuse. It applies only to workers who were lawfully employed and lost their jobs, and it gives them a limited window to find a new sponsor or another lawful status. Eliminating it does little to stop unlawful actors, who are by definition not relying on it, while it directly harms people like me who have followed every rule. Enforcement should target fraudulent employers and unlawful conduct, not remove protections from workers who did nothing wrong.

Layoffs are a normal part of the American economy, especially in technology and healthcare startups. When a job is lost through no fault of the worker, 60 days is the window to find a new employer, secure a transfer, or pursue another lawful path to stay. Without it, a layoff would mean an immediate scramble to leave the country, uprooting children from their school, their friends, and the only country they know, with no real chance to find a solution.

Removing this cushion doesn’t make the system more orderly. It penalizes workers for economic events they cannot control, and it discourages skilled professionals from taking jobs at startups and smaller companies, where much of the innovation in healthcare happens.

I respectfully urge DHS to preserve the 60-day grace period.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Venkatesh Vuppu
comments.commentText:
Re: USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I respectfully oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days for H-1B and other covered nonimmigrant workers following cessation of employment. I urge DHS to retain this protection for workers and their dependents.

As an H-1B professional, I understand that continued immigration eligibility depends on meeting legal requirements. However, losing a job does not necessarily reflect misconduct or an unwillingness to comply with immigration law. Layoffs, restructuring, project cancellations, and business closures can occur with little warning. A reasonable transition period helps affected workers respond lawfully and responsibly.

1. The grace period supports lawful compliance.

The existing grace period provides limited time to identify an eligible employer, prepare an appropriate immigration filing, explore another lawful status, or arrange departure. Eliminating that time would make compliance more difficult precisely when workers are dealing with an unexpected loss of income and employer support. A short, defined transition period promotes orderly decisions and departures.

2. Finding a sponsoring employer requires time.

Recruitment commonly involves several interviews, internal approvals, background checks, and coordination with immigration counsel. Even when a qualified worker receives an offer quickly, preparing the necessary petition and supporting documentation takes additional time. Workers cannot control every step of this process. Eliminating the grace period could prevent otherwise eligible workers from completing a lawful transition to an employer that needs their skills.

3. U.S. employers also benefit from a reasonable transition period.

The grace period allows employers to consider qualified workers already present in the United States. Removing it could interrupt recruitment and create additional uncertainty for businesses seeking to fill legitimate positions. DHS should assess the effects on employers, including smaller businesses, project continuity, and U.S. employees whose work depends on stable teams.

4. Dependents face consequences beyond their control.

An unexpected job loss can affect an entire household. Families may need to address children’s schooling, medical treatment, housing obligations, transportation, and international travel arrangements. These responsibilities cannot always be resolved immediately. A limited grace period gives families time to make practical arrangements while pursuing a lawful next step.

5. The current protection is limited and discretionary.

The existing framework does not provide an indefinite right to remain in the United States. It is subject to time limits and DHS discretion. DHS should explain why these limitations and existing enforcement tools are insufficient before removing the protection for every covered worker. If the agency identifies specific misuse, it should consider targeted measures rather than eliminating the transition period broadly.

6. Eliminating the grace period may create additional administrative burdens.

Workers facing an immediate loss of status may seek emergency legal assistance or submit urgent applications to address their circumstances. DHS should evaluate whether removing the grace period would shift work into other immigration processes rather than reduce the agency’s overall workload. Its analysis should account for costs to workers, families, employers, and the government.

7. Reasonable job mobility supports fair employment practices.

Workers should have a practical opportunity to leave an unsuitable employment situation and seek another lawful position. Removing the transition period could increase dependence on a single employer and make workers more reluctant to report workplace concerns or leave harmful conditions. Retaining a limited grace period supports responsible mobility without excusing violations of immigration requirements.

I request that DHS withdraw this proposal and retain the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days. If administrative concerns require changes, DHS should consider clearer documentation standards, consistent guidance, and targeted safeguards supported by evidence.

A fair immigration system can enforce eligibility requirements while allowing a reasonable period to respond to unexpected employment loss. Retaining this limited protection would support lawful compliance, family stability, and the needs of U.S. employers.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to retain the grace period to support lawful compliance and transition time.

comments.commentText:
Subject: Opposition to the Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period for H-1B Workers

I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers following an involuntary termination of employment.

As an H-1B professional working in the United States, I believe the current 60-day grace period provides an essential and reasonable safeguard for highly skilled foreign workers while maintaining the integrity of the immigration system.

1. Job loss is often unrelated to employee performance.

Layoffs frequently result from corporate restructuring, budget reductions, mergers, or broader economic conditions. Even highly qualified and productive employees can lose their jobs through no fault of their own. Eliminating the grace period would impose disproportionate consequences on individuals who have complied with immigration requirements and contributed to the U.S. economy.

2. Finding a new employer and completing an H-1B transfer takes time.

H-1B workers cannot simply accept any available job. They must find an employer willing and able to sponsor their immigration status. Recruitment, interviews, background checks, internal approvals, Labor Condition Applications, and petition preparation can take several weeks or longer.

The existing 60-day grace period is already a relatively short window. Eliminating it would make an otherwise manageable job transition unnecessarily difficult.

3. The proposal could harm American businesses and reduce labor market flexibility.

U.S. employers invest significant resources in recruiting and retaining specialized talent. Eliminating the grace period could prevent businesses from hiring qualified H-1B professionals who become available after layoffs, even when those individuals possess valuable experience and skills.

The grace period benefits not only foreign workers but also American employers seeking experienced professionals.

4. The proposal would create unnecessary hardship for law-abiding workers and their families.

Many H-1B workers have established homes, financial obligations, and family lives in the United States. Requiring them to make immediate immigration arrangements after an unexpected layoff would create substantial financial and emotional hardship.

Workers should not face the possibility of abrupt displacement simply because their employer undergoes a restructuring.

5. Maintaining the grace period supports fairness without undermining immigration enforcement.

The current grace period is limited and does not provide indefinite immigration status or unrestricted employment authorization. It offers a reasonable opportunity for workers to transition to another employer, seek an alternative lawful status, or prepare to depart the country.

I respectfully urge DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period. At a minimum, DHS should carefully evaluate the economic consequences, administrative burdens, and potential disruption to U.S. employers before implementing any change.

The United States benefits from a predictable immigration system that allows skilled professionals and businesses to navigate unexpected employment transitions responsibly.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: Opposes eliminating the grace period, citing necessary time for H-1B transfers.

If the agency identifies specific misuse, it should consider targeted measures rather than eliminating the transition period broadly.

6. Eliminating the grace period may create additional administrative burdens.

Workers facing an immediate loss of status may seek emergency legal assistance or submit urgent applications to address their circumstances. DHS should evaluate whether removing the grace period would shift work into other immigration processes rather than reduce the agency’s overall workload. Its analysis should account for costs to workers, families, employers, and the government.

7. Reasonable job mobility supports fair employment practices.

Workers should have a practical opportunity to leave an unsuitable employment situation and seek another lawful position. Removing the transition period could increase dependence on a single employer and make workers more reluctant to report workplace concerns or leave harmful conditions. Retaining a limited grace period supports responsible mobility without excusing violations of immigration requirements.

I request that DHS withdraw this proposal and retain the discretionary grace period of up to 60 days. If administrative concerns require changes, DHS should consider clearer documentation standards, consistent guidance, and targeted safeguards supported by evidence.

A fair immigration system can enforce eligibility requirements while allowing a reasonable period to respond to unexpected employment loss. Retaining this limited protection would support lawful compliance, family stability, and the needs of U.S. employers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Comment on the Proposed Elimination of the 60-Day Grace Period for O-1 Visa Holders

I am a U.S. citizen married to an O-1 visa holder. I urge the Department of Homeland Security to reconsider the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period following the termination of employment, particularly for O-1 professionals and their families.

O-1 visa holders are individuals recognized for extraordinary ability in their fields. Many are recruited to the United States because their expertise is scarce, their work is valuable, and their contributions matter. They build companies, advance research, create jobs, and contribute to American innovation and economic growth. Their families make substantial commitments to this country, establishing careers, educating children, building friendships, and creating homes. These are not temporary arrangements that can be dismantled overnight.

Employment can end unexpectedly, even for highly accomplished professionals. A company may restructure, change ownership, reduce its workforce, or face financial difficulties. A termination is not necessarily a reflection of an individual's ability, performance, or value to the United States. Yet eliminating the grace period could turn an ordinary employment event into an immediate immigration emergency, leaving families with no time to understand their options, obtain legal advice, arrange their affairs, or make a responsible decision about their future.

The consequences reach far beyond the visa holder. A spouse may be a U.S. citizen with an established career, obligations, and deep roots in this country. Children may be American citizens attending school, participating in their communities, and growing up in the only home they know. Requiring a family to confront the possibility of sudden separation or relocation because of an unpredictable employment event imposes a severe burden that is disproportionate.
The proposed change would also create a troubling incentive for O-1 holders married to U.S. citizens. These families may be eligible to pursue permanent residence through marriage, but that does not mean they have already decided to do so. Choosing permanent residence is a consequential, deeply personal decision about identity, family, and where to build a life for the long term. It should be made deliberately, based on a genuine decision to make the United States one's permanent home, not as insurance against the possibility of losing a job.

Without a grace period, families may feel compelled to file for permanent residence as soon as the new policy takes effect, even when they are not ready to make that commitment. Waiting until a job actually ends may be too late to prepare the necessary documentation, obtain legal advice, and submit an application in time. The policy could therefore force families into a premature choice: pursue permanent residence before they are ready, or risk having to leave the country with little warning if employment ends unexpectedly.

That is an unintended and deeply concerning consequence. A policy intended to regulate immigration status should not pressure people into pursuing permanent residence simply because they fear losing the opportunity to make that choice later. Nor should it effectively force U.S. citizens to choose between their spouses and the country in which they live.

The existing grace period offers a practical and proportionate safeguard. It provides a limited window to seek another qualifying opportunity where permitted, understand available immigration pathways, consult an attorney, make arrangements for dependents, and prepare for an orderly departure if remaining in the United States is not possible. It does not grant permanent status or an unrestricted right to work. It simply recognizes that real lives cannot be reorganized instantly.

I respectfully ask DHS to retain the 60-day grace period for O-1 visa holders. At a minimum, the final rule should preserve a reasonable transition period for O-1 professionals married to U.S. citizens, allowing them sufficient time after an unexpected employment termination to assess their options and, if they choose, prepare an eligible adjustment-of-status application. The opportunity to pursue permanent residence should remain a genuine choice, rather than a decision families feel forced to make preemptively out of fear.

The United States benefits from attracting and retaining extraordinary talent. Predictable immigration rules are part of that commitment. Removing a reasonable safety net would create unnecessary uncertainty for professionals who have been invited to contribute to this country and for American families whose lives are intertwined with theirs. A limited grace period is a sensible, humane, and proportionate measure that protects families while preserving the government's ability to enforce immigration law.

Thank you for considering the impact of this proposal on O-1 professionals and the American families they are part of.
comments.reason: Urges DHS to reconsider eliminating the grace period for O-1 professionals and families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by A M
comments.commentText:
I strongly support eliminating the 60-day H-1B grace period.In fact, the entire H-1B program should be terminated for a period of no less than 10 years. 

H-1B was sold as a temporary fix for genuine specialty-occupation shortages. Instead, it has become a labor-arbitrage tool that lets companies hire cheaper foreign workers, renew them indefinitely, and move them around while undercutting American workers and graduates.

Under INA § 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b), H-1B status requires continuous employment in a specialty occupation. The 2016 AC21 rule invented a 60-day non-working buffer that lets people stay without an active employer-employee relationship, directly contradicting the statute. Employers or workers may have grown accustomed to this regulatory grace period, but that does not override DHS’s clear statutory duty to protect American workers’ wages and job opportunities.

I am an information security and threat intelligence professional with a career spanning information security, network operations, and telecommunications. I support the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period at 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I was recently laid off from an IT and information security role, and my work was outsourced. I am now competing in a job market where major technology companies are downsizing and experienced American workers far outnumber open positions. This is not new to me. Throughout my career, through several difficult economies, I have faced heavy competition for the few open roles in my field.

In that time, I have never seen an employer required to show that no qualified American candidate was available before filling a position with an H-1B worker. In one case, a role went to an H-1B worker who I later learned was related to the company’s leadership. I have also watched a coworker’s visa renewal depend on agreeing to long hours and tight deadlines. That leverage harms the visa holder, and it undercuts every American on the same team by setting workload expectations no one with a free choice of employer would accept.

How this relates to the proposed rule:

The grace period works against laid-off Americans during downturns. When a company lays off staff, its H-1B workers can remain for up to 60 days to find a new sponsor, competing for the same openings as the Americans laid off alongside them. In a shrinking market, this enlarges the applicant pool for already scarce jobs. Eliminating it ties status to the employment that justified it, which is how the program should work.
The program exists to address shortages. When employers are cutting IT and security staff in large numbers, there is no shortage to fill. Once a sponsored position ends, the basis for work status ends with it, and a grace period that keeps that worker in the labor market is inconsistent with the program’s purpose.
American workers are available. Many qualified Americans are looking for IT and security work right now, and many more could be trained quickly. Employers should be expected to hire and train them before turning to visa programs.

I urge DHS to finalize the elimination of the discretionary grace period as proposed. comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the 60-day grace period under 8 C.F.R. § 214.1(l)(2).

DHS has not provided an adequate factual or legal justification for completely eliminating this longstanding rule.

First, the proposal raises serious concerns under the Administrative Procedure Act. DHS acknowledges that employers, workers, and families have developed substantial reliance interests under the existing regulation, including employment arrangements, housing, and other long-term commitments. The Supreme Court has made clear in DHS v. Regents that an agency changing immigration policy must meaningfully consider such reliance interests. The fact that the grace period is discretionary does not make those interests irrelevant.

Second, DHS relies heavily on administrative burden but does not adequately quantify it. The NPRM cites approximately 1.9 million filings that may have required consideration of the grace period, while also acknowledging limitations in USCIS data regarding actual use of the provision. DHS does not establish how many adjudication hours, dollars, or personnel would actually be saved. Nor does it adequately account for offsetting costs from additional status applications, consular processing, enforcement actions, Notices to Appear, and immigration-court proceedings.

Third, immediate departure is not an obvious requirement of the statutory scheme. Congress expressly created H-1B portability through AC21, permitting eligible workers to begin employment with a new employer upon the filing of a qualifying petition. A limited grace period facilitates that congressional policy by giving workers a reasonable opportunity to locate a new employer and use the portability mechanism Congress created.

Finally, DHS has not adequately explained why complete elimination is necessary rather than a less disruptive alternative, such as clearer evidentiary requirements, a shorter grace period, or a bright-line rule for involuntary termination. Under State Farm, an agency rescinding an existing regulation must engage in reasoned decisionmaking and meaningfully consider important alternatives.

The existing rule facilitates lawful employer transitions, promotes labor mobility, and prevents an ordinary job termination from immediately becoming an immigration enforcement matter. DHS has not demonstrated that these benefits are outweighed by the claimed administrative savings.

For these reasons, DHS should withdraw the proposed rule and retain the existing 60-day grace period.

Behind every case, there are real people, children, parents, and families trying to build a safe and stable future.

Ending this grace period could leave many people in extremely difficult situations, causing fear, emotional distress, and uncertainty about what lies ahead. Everyone deserves compassion, dignity, and a fair chance to navigate these challenging circumstances.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security not to finalize the rule as proposed. The grace period is discretionary, and I do not dispute that. However, discretion must be exercised through reasoned decision-making. The proposal should be reconsidered because it appears to impose serious and foreseeable burdens on workers and their families.

Immediate loss of status. Under the current rule, a worker who loses a job has a defined period in which to respond. Without it, a layoff could leave the worker and the worker's family out of status at once, with no opportunity to find a new employer, file a change of employer petition, change status, or plan an orderly departure.

Vulnerable circumstances. Workers facing medical treatment, pregnancy, caregiving responsibilities, or a family emergency would have almost no time to adjust.

Financial, educational, and social disruption. Workers and their families would face abrupt costs, including relocation or travel expenses and ongoing lease and loan obligations. Children of affected workers could be forced to leave school mid-year on short notice. Families and communities, including schools, congregations, and local businesses, would experience disruption when households must leave quickly.

For these reasons, I respectfully request that DHS not eliminate the 60-day grace period.
comments.reason: Requests DHS not to finalize the rule as it causes severe foreseeable burdens on workers and families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose this proposed rule, which would eliminate the 60-day grace period currently available to H-1B, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, and TN nonimmigrant workers following cessation of employment.

This rule would cause severe, immediate harm to lawfully present workers and their families through no fault of their own. A layoff or business restructuring — events entirely outside an employee's control — would instantly render workers and their dependents out of status, with no time to pursue a new employer petition, change of status, or orderly departure. The human cost is real: families who have purchased homes, paid taxes, and built lives in U.S. communities would face sudden unlawful presence and potential bars to future admission.

DHS itself acknowledges these reliance interests in the preamble yet proceeds anyway. That is arbitrary and capricious. The agency's rationale — that the grace period is "discretionary" and resource-intensive — does not justify eliminating a protection that has functioned effectively since 2017 and that serves the legitimate interests of both workers and U.S. employers who have invested in sponsoring them.

This rule would also damage U.S. competitiveness by making the nonimmigrant work visa system more punitive and unpredictable, deterring global talent from choosing the United States.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposed rule in its entirety.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the rule as it would cause severe immediate harm to lawfully present workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed regulation that would eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers. Forcing immediate departure upon job separation is an inhumane policy that creates severe, insurmountable hardships for legally present families who have built their lives in the United States.
Removing this critical cushion unfairly penalizes skilled professionals who face sudden, unexpected job separations. Requiring immediate departure heavily destabilizes families, uprooting lives and children without adequate time to arrange travel.
For families on legal immigration tracks, the consequences of a zero-day grace period are uniquely devastating:
• Uprooting U.S.-Born Children: Many impacted professionals have U.S.-born children who are American citizens. Forcing an immediate departure gives parents zero time to withdraw children from schools, secure academic records, or prepare them emotionally for an abrupt international relocation.

• Liquidating Permanent Ties: Families who have lived in the U.S. for years cannot dismantle their lives overnight. It is impossible to sell a home, terminate property leases, close bank accounts, liquidate assets, and pack up a household in a single day.

• Financial Ruin: Without a grace period, families will be forced to abandon their property, break contracts, and forfeit hard-earned assets, resulting in catastrophic financial loss.

Furthermore, the current grace period provides essential flexibility for U.S. employers to retain top-tier, international talent during industry shifts. Finding specialized technical or executive roles inherently takes longer than zero days. Eliminating this window will severely damage American competitiveness by deterring global professionals from choosing the U.S. It also grants unethical employers dangerous leverage over workers, increasing the risk of labor exploitation.
Finally, forcing immediate departure shifts an immense administrative and consular burden onto an already backlogged State Department. The claim that this policy reduces administrative strain is unfounded and ignores severe long-term economic disruptions.
I urge DHS to withdraw this harmful rule and preserve the 60-day grace period to support workforce stability and protect families from systemic cruelty
comments.reason: Strongly opposes eliminating the grace period, citing severe hardships and disruptions for families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the Department of Homeland Security's proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for certain nonimmigrant workers whose employment ends. As a data scientist working in the United States, I believe this proposal should be evaluated not only in terms of immigration administration, but also in terms of its practical consequences for American employers, local communities, taxpayers, and small businesses. Eliminating this limited transition period could create avoidable economic disruption without adequately accounting for the financial obligations and community ties that established workers leave behind.

The proposal could impose unnecessary financial risks on local landlords and small property owners. Many professional workers sign residential leases, pay security deposits, and commit to monthly rent based on the expectation of continued employment and a reasonable opportunity to manage a transition if circumstances change. If employment ends unexpectedly and a worker must leave the country almost immediately, there may be insufficient time to provide proper notice, find a replacement tenant, arrange an early lease termination, or settle outstanding balances. Landlords could face unpaid rent, unexpected vacancies, cleaning costs, and additional expenses associated with finding new tenants or recovering debts. These risks may be particularly significant for small property owners who depend on rental income to cover mortgages, insurance, property taxes, and maintenance. Retaining the grace period would give both tenants and landlords a more realistic opportunity to resolve their obligations responsibly.

The effects would extend to automobile markets and other local businesses. Workers who must depart on short notice may need to sell vehicles, furniture, and household possessions under considerable time pressure. They may have to accept lower offers, pay for storage or transportation, or abandon arrangements that would otherwise have been resolved through an orderly departure. This could create avoidable losses for individuals while affecting local used-car dealers, repair shops, moving companies, storage providers, and other service businesses. Workers and their families also contribute to local economic activity through spending on groceries, restaurants, utilities, transportation, childcare, and housing. When established residents leave unexpectedly, communities may lose customers and economic activity that would otherwise continue during a reasonable transition period.

Eliminating the grace period could also reduce government revenue and increase economic inefficiency. Employed professionals contribute through federal income taxes, Social Security and Medicare taxes where applicable, and state and local taxes. They also support businesses through their ordinary household spending. If qualified workers leave the United States because they cannot complete a job transition in time, the government may lose future tax contributions, while employers incur additional recruitment, onboarding, and training expenses. These outcomes are not inevitable in every case, but they are foreseeable consequences that deserve consideration in the agency's economic analysis. The existing grace period does not guarantee continued employment or authorize unrestricted work; it provides a limited opportunity to arrange a lawful transition.

I respectfully urge DHS to retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period. Losing a job is already a significant financial and professional disruption. Requiring an immediate departure would compound that disruption by making it harder for workers to settle debts, fulfill contractual obligations, arrange transportation, and support family members. A reasonable transition period benefits not only workers but also American employers, landlords, small businesses, and the communities in which these individuals have lived and spent their earnings. The existing framework allows flexibility without guaranteeing a new job or immigration benefit. DHS should preserve this practical safeguard and avoid imposing unnecessary costs on local communities and the broader U.S. economy.
comments.reason: Opposes the proposal due to practical consequences like economic disruption and landlord risks.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Opposition to Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I respectfully oppose DHS’s proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for H-1B and other eligible nonimmigrant workers.

Recognize the purpose of the grace period: Sudden job loss creates significant practical and emotional challenges. Workers need time for either secure new employment or sell their homes, terminate leases, sell cars and household belongings, manage children’s schooling, and cope with the mental stress of uncertainty.

Prevent fraud, not worker protections: Address immigration abuse through targeted enforcement and stricter compliance—not by penalizing law-abiding professionals who lose their jobs unexpectedly.

Recognize the AI era: As AI transforms the workforce, employers increasingly need specialized, highly skilled professionals. Securing a new position requires proven expertise, multiple interview rounds, and lengthy hiring and immigration procedures. The grace period provides time to compete for opportunities; it does not guarantee employment.

Strengthen H-1B standards: Higher wage requirements, rigorous qualification criteria, and stronger oversight are more effective ways to prevent misuse and attract genuine global talent.

Consider existing restrictions: H-1B proclamation fee for certain new petitions has already introduced a significant financial barrier to new H-1B hiring from abroad. Alongside additional H-1B entry opportunities for FY 2026 and FY 2027 and broader immigration reforms, these measures make eliminating the grace period an additional restriction without a clear, compelling justification.

Protect America’s competitiveness: Eliminating the grace period risks driving skilled professionals, their expertise, tax contributions, and future innovation to competing countries.

I urge DHS to withdraw this proposal and retain the existing discretionary 60-day grace period. Target fraud, strengthen H-1B eligibility standards, and preserve reasonable transition time for skilled professionals and their families during unexpected job loss
comments.reason: Opposes eliminating the grace period, suggesting targeted enforcement rather than penalizing workers.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to oppose the proposal to remove the 60-day grace period for H-1B nonimmigrants whose employment ends.

1. Immediate loss of status is not workable. Under the current rule, a worker whose employment ends has up to 60 days to find a new sponsor, change status, or depart. Removing that period would end lawful status the day a job ends. A worker laid off on a Friday afternoon cannot lawfully depart the same day. Arranging travel, closing a lease, ending utilities and accounts, shipping or selling belongings, and moving a family all take weeks.

2. It would create unlawful presence through no fault of the worker. Workers who did nothing wrong would begin accruing unlawful presence the next day, with consequences for future visas and admission. Layoffs are decided by the employer, and workers don't control them.

3. It would defeat the purpose of portability. H-1B workers may change employers, and employers file new petitions. That process takes time. Without a grace period, the portability the law already provides becomes unusable, because a worker would lose status before a new employer could file.

4. Harm to families. Spouses on H-4 status, and children, depend on the principal worker's status. They would lose status the same day, which affects children's schooling, spouses' work authorization and health insurance.

5. Costs to employers and the economy. Employers would lose skilled workers they might otherwise rehire when business improves, and the rule would discourage skilled workers from coming to or staying in the United States. [Add if relevant: your own industry or role.]

6. Public safety and administrative burden. Same-day status loss produces enforcement and processing problems for agencies and uncertainty for employers and landlords.

Request. I urge the agency to retain the 60-day grace period, or at a minimum to provide a period that is long enough for orderly departure or status change.
comments.reason: Opposes removing the grace period because immediate loss of status is unworkable and harms families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Manoj Dewangan
comments.commentText:
To U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services  
Re: DHS Docket No. USCIS-2026-0364 — Eliminating the Discretionary 60-Day Grace Period

I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period following the end of employment. I am an Indian citizen who has worked in the United States on H-1B status for approximately 14 years. I remain on H-1B status because of the lengthy employment-based green card backlog for Indian citizens. One of my sons is in college, and the other is in middle school. Our family has built its life here, and my experience shows why this protection matters.

In 2019, I needed the grace period twice: once after my employment with Rivi Consulting ended, and again after my employment with Mastech ended later that same year. Both times, I found another job within the grace period. Those 60 days allowed me to secure new employment and continue living and working in the United States lawfully.

Finding a new position takes time. Applications, interviews, background checks, and the new employer’s immigration paperwork cannot all happen immediately. Eliminating the grace period would make it much harder for workers who lose their jobs to complete that process, even when employers are willing to hire them.

The consequences also extend to children and families. Having to leave the United States suddenly, particularly in the middle of a school year, could severely disrupt both of my sons’ education. Admission to a school or college in India is not necessarily available immediately, and differences in admission schedules, curricula, and degree requirements can make a sudden transition especially difficult.

Families also have housing commitments. Breaking an apartment lease can result in substantial penalties at the same time that a worker has lost their income. Families who own homes face the additional challenge of arranging a sale or managing their property from abroad. These responsibilities cannot reasonably be resolved overnight.

I understand the importance of maintaining lawful immigration status. The grace period provides a limited, practical opportunity to find qualifying employment, pursue another lawful option, or prepare for departure. In my case, it served that purpose twice and allowed me to return to employment within the permitted time.

I respectfully ask DHS to retain the existing 60-day grace period and fully consider the disruption its removal would cause to children’s education, family housing, and employers’ hiring processes. Families who have lived here lawfully for many years while waiting for green cards should have a reasonable opportunity to manage an unexpected job loss without immediately uprooting their children and abandoning their commitments.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes eliminating the grace period, citing family disruption and job search challenges.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I strongly oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for individuals whose immigration status is ending. This grace period serves as an essential buffer that allows people to wind down their affairs in the United States in an orderly and humane manner, and removing it would cause unnecessary hardship for countless individuals and families.
 
First, sixty days is barely enough time to handle the complex financial and logistical matters involved in departing the country. Individuals must close bank accounts, terminate leases, sell or ship personal belongings, settle outstanding debts, file final tax documents, and arrange for the transfer of assets. Many of these processes require appointments, paperwork, and coordination with multiple institutions—tasks that simply cannot be completed overnight. Without the grace period, people would be forced to abandon their property or incur significant financial losses.
 
Second, for those with pets, the process of preparing an animal for international travel is lengthy and cannot be rushed. Many countries require a rabies titer test, which can take weeks or even months to process, along with health certificates, vaccinations, import permits, and compliance with specific airline and destination-country regulations. Eliminating the grace period would leave pet owners with an impossible choice: abandon a beloved family member or violate immigration rules. This is both cruel and unnecessary.
 
Third, the grace period provides stability and predictability that benefit not only the individuals involved but also the broader community. It allows people to depart voluntarily and lawfully rather than being pushed into overstaying, which undermines the integrity of the immigration system itself. A discretionary grace period is a reasonable, compassionate, and practical tool that serves the interests of everyone.
 
For these reasons, I urge policymakers to retain the discretionary 60-day grace period. Eliminating it would create chaos, inflict undue hardship, and ultimately make the system less orderly—not more.
comments.reason: Strongly opposes the proposal, arguing removal causes unnecessary hardship and leaves no time for logistics.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Subject: Comment in Support of Retaining the 60-Day H-1B Grace Period

I strongly support retaining the full 60-day grace period for eligible H-1B workers following an unexpected loss of employment. This period is essential for finding new employment, managing immigration requirements, and addressing the significant financial, family, and logistical responsibilities that arise when a worker loses their job.

Eligible workers may be granted a discretionary grace period of up to 60 consecutive calendar days, or until the end of their authorized validity period, whichever is shorter. This period does not automatically authorize employment, but it provides a reasonable opportunity to evaluate options and make necessary arrangements.

The real world challenges of sudden job loss include:

1. Finding new employment: Securing another H-1B employer involves applications, interviews, background checks, offer negotiations, internal approvals, and coordination with immigration attorneys. These processes take time and are not entirely within the worker's control.

2. International travel: If new employment cannot be secured, workers may need to arrange international flights for themselves and their families. Booking tickets at short notice can be expensive, and coordinating travel dates, documents, baggage, and transportation takes time.

3. Housing and lease termination: Many workers have signed long-term apartment leases or housing contracts. Leaving unexpectedly can result in lease-breakage penalties, additional rent, cleaning charges, and potential security deposit losses. Resolving these obligations may require advance notice and coordination with landlords.

4. Closing a household: Workers must organize moving services, sell or donate furniture, ship personal belongings, cancel utilities and internet services, return rented equipment, and settle household accounts. These tasks cannot reasonably be completed in a single day.

5. Children's education: Families with school-age children must coordinate school withdrawals, obtain academic records, arrange transfers, and consider the impact of relocation on their children's education and emotional well-being. These decisions require careful planning.

6. Financial commitments: Rent or mortgage payments, vehicle loans, car leases, credit card balances, medical bills, insurance premiums, childcare costs, and other recurring expenses do not stop when employment ends. Workers may also face relocation expenses, legal fees, and early termination penalties while their income is interrupted.

7. Spouses and dependent family members: Families may need to review immigration options, arrange travel documents, coordinate a spouse's employment plans, and make decisions affecting the entire household. These matters are especially difficult when children are involved.

8. Healthcare and insurance: Losing employer-sponsored benefits may require families to evaluate alternative health coverage, obtain medical records and prescriptions, and arrange continued care.

9. Banking, taxes, and administrative matters: Workers preparing to leave the United States may need to settle outstanding bills, update addresses, review tax obligations, manage financial accounts, and organize important employment and financial records.

Why the full 60 days are necessary

Expecting an H-1B worker to secure a new qualifying position, coordinate the necessary immigration process, book international flights, terminate a lease, close a household, settle financial obligations, and arrange schooling and relocation for children within a day is unrealistic. Many of these tasks depend on employers, landlords, schools, financial institutions, and other third parties. Workers cannot control their processing times or availability.

A sudden job loss should not force families to make rushed decisions that result in avoidable financial losses, disrupted education, or unnecessary hardship. The 60-day grace period provides a limited but important opportunity to pursue new employment or, if necessary, plan an orderly departure while meeting existing responsibilities.

Retaining this period also benefits U.S. employers by giving them a reasonable opportunity to recruit qualified professionals affected by layoffs rather than losing that talent solely because of an unnecessarily short transition window.

I respectfully urge the Department to retain the full 60-day grace period for eligible H-1B workers. A fair and practical policy should recognize that involuntary job loss affects entire households, not just employment status. Workers need reasonable time to comply with immigration requirements, protect their families, manage financial obligations, and make informed decisions about their future.

Thank you for considering these important concerns.
comments.reason: Strongly supports retaining the grace period for employment transitions and managing logistics.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I respectfully oppose the proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period and urge policymakers to consider the real-life impact this change could have on hardworking immigrant families.

Many of us have spent more than a decade in the United States, working honestly, paying taxes, contributing to the economy, and building a future for our families. We have followed the immigration rules, maintained our status, and done our best to contribute positively to the communities we live in. Many of us even have approved I-140 petitions, yet we remain stuck in extraordinarily long green card backlogs because of per-country visa limits, particularly in the EB-2 category. After years of waiting, permanent residency can still feel impossibly far away.

In these circumstances, the 60-day grace period is more than just a provision in an immigration regulation. It is a lifeline for families who may unexpectedly lose their jobs through no fault of their own. Finding a new job takes time, especially in an uncertain economy. Removing this flexibility could leave families facing immense emotional and financial pressure, disrupting children’s lives and putting years of effort and sacrifice at risk.

We are not asking for special privileges or to avoid the immigration process. We are asking for a fair chance to recover from an unexpected job loss without immediately having to fear losing our ability to remain with our families in the country we have called home for so many years. Many of us have invested our education, professional skills, savings, and best years into building our lives here while patiently waiting for a green card through no fault of our own.

Immigration policies should protect the integrity of the system while also recognizing the realities faced by the people who depend on it. Eliminating the grace period would place an additional burden on individuals who may already be living with years, sometimes decades, of immigration uncertainty.

Please consider the families behind these applications. We are parents raising children, professionals contributing our skills, taxpayers supporting public services, and neighbors who want nothing more than to live peacefully, work honestly, and provide a secure future for our loved ones.

A person’s future should not be put at risk overnight because of circumstances beyond their control, especially after years of following the rules and contributing to this country.

I sincerely urge the administration to retain the discretionary 60-day grace period. A little flexibility during a difficult transition can make an enormous difference to a family. Fairness, compassion, and common sense should remain essential parts of our immigration system.
comments.reason: Respectfully opposes the elimination of the grace period as a lifeline for families.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
I am writing to strongly oppose the proposed rule to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period for nonimmigrant workers (8 CFR 214.1(l)(2)).

Losing a job is already a stressful, disorienting experience. Expecting individuals to uproot their lives overnight is neither realistic nor humane. Lawful visa holders are active contributors to their workplaces and local communities. When unexpected layoffs occur, workers need a reasonable window to secure new employment, wrap up apartment leases, close bank accounts, manage their children’s schooling, and make orderly arrangements without being immediately forced into unlawful status.

If the priority is American economic strength, financial stability, and global competitiveness, preserving the existing 60-day H-1B grace period is a matter of economic pragmatism. Policy changes that abruptly eliminate this transition window risk creating unnecessary financial disruption across American households, businesses, and financial institutions.

Avoid turning productive homeowners into distressed sellers. Highly paid professionals who lose their jobs may own homes in high-value communities and contribute substantially to local tax bases. Eliminating the grace period risks forcing rushed property sales, mortgage delinquencies, and avoidable foreclosures—consequences that can hurt neighboring homeowners and local governments.

Protect American lenders from preventable losses. Mortgages, auto loans, credit cards, and other financial obligations do not disappear when a worker leaves the country. Abrupt departures can increase defaults, collection costs, and unrecovered debt, shifting the financial burden onto American banks, credit unions, and lenders.

Protect America's competitive advantage in skilled talent. As AI adoption accelerates corporate restructuring, even experienced, high-performing professionals can face sudden layoffs. Eliminating the grace period would make it harder for these workers to transition to new employers, pushing valuable technical expertise, institutional knowledge, and entrepreneurial potential toward competing economies.

Preserve an essential buffer against economic disruption. The 60-day grace period provides a defined window for workers to pursue new employment, employers to arrange transitions, and households to manage their financial commitments. Removing this buffer risks converting manageable employment disruptions into avoidable economic losses.

Support orderly workforce transitions instead of forced financial liquidation. Professionals who have contributed to American businesses, paid taxes, purchased homes, and supported local communities need a reasonable opportunity to navigate corporate restructuring. Preserving the existing window provides that opportunity without guaranteeing continued employment or permanent immigration status.

The bottom line: The existing 60-day H-1B grace period is a practical safeguard against unnecessary financial disruption. Eliminating it risks harming American homeowners, exposing lenders to avoidable losses, burdening local economies, and weakening the country's ability to retain globally competitive talent.
If the objective is to put the American economy first, preserve the 60-day grace period. It offers a defined transition window that balances immigration enforcement with economic stability, business continuity, and the protection of American financial interests.

To the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services:
I am writing to respectfully but earnestly ask the Department to withdraw its proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for high-skilled nonimmigrant workers. While I understand the agency's mandate to manage our immigration system effectively, removing this grace period altogether would create immense, unnecessary human suffering for families who have dedicated their lives and talents to building up American communities.
Imposing immediate unlawful status the very day a job ends fails to account for how deeply integrated these professionals are in our society. Furthermore, the current 60-day window is already an incredibly tight squeeze in today’s economic climate. In a modern labor market marked by complex corporate restructuring and extended, multi-stage hiring processes, securing a new job and filing a new H-1B petition routinely takes several months. Shaving this buffer down to zero days places an impossible burden on honest, law-abiding professionals.
Please consider the deeply human impacts this rule change would cause:
• The Tolling Impact on Families and Children: An unexpected job loss is stressful for anyone, but under this proposal, it becomes an instant crisis for the entire household. Spouses on H-4 visas and young children who are thriving in American schools would face immediate, traumatic upheaval. Families need a compassionate window of time to handle these transitions gracefully, rather than being forced to disrupt their children’s education overnight.
• The Reality of Housing and Practical Logistics: It is simply not possible to wind down a life in 24 hours. Breaking residential leases, closing bank accounts, settling final utility bills, and packing up a home require weeks of careful, dignified planning. Forcing families into immediate status violations over basic logistical timelines is a heartbreaking outcome for individuals who have always followed the rules.
• Protecting Workplace Dignity and AC21 Alignment: Congress enacted the H-1B portability provisions of the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-first Century Act (AC21) to ensure workers have the mobility to change employers. Eliminating the grace period effectively strips workers of this right. It inadvertently gives employers complete, asymmetrical power over a worker’s legal status, making it incredibly difficult for a professional to safely speak up about workplace issues or unfair treatment.
• Preserving America’s Global Appeal: High-skilled immigrants choose the United States because they believe in the American Dream and want to contribute to our collective prosperity. Replacing a predictable grace period with an immediate trapdoor sends a discouraging message to global talent, signaling that their contributions are easily disposable.
High-skilled immigrants are our neighbors, colleagues, and friends. They invest their hearts, futures, and tax dollars into our economy, and they deserve a system that treats them with basic human dignity and operational fairness. Rather than eliminating this vital safety net, I gently urge DHS to consider expanding the grace period to match the realities of our current economy.

Congress recognized this problem through the American Competitiveness in the Twenty-First Century Act (AC21), allowing eligible workers to extend H-1B status beyond six years and change employers under specified conditions.
