comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
Strong Opposition to the Proposed Removal of the 60-Day H-1B Grace Period
I strongly oppose the proposed removal of the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers following the termination of their employment. I respectfully urge the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to retain this important safeguard to protect workers, their families, and the contributions they make to the United States.

H-1B workers come to the United States to contribute their skills, knowledge, and experience. They work hard, pay taxes, support their families, purchase homes, and contribute to their communities. Losing a job is already a stressful and unexpected event. Eliminating the grace period would make an already difficult situation worse by leaving workers with insufficient time to find another qualifying employer and complete the necessary immigration procedures.

This change would disproportionately affect workers from countries with lengthy employment-based green card backlogs, particularly India. Many workers have waited years, sometimes decades, for permanent residency because of per-country limits and processing delays. Throughout this time, they have continued to work legally, follow immigration requirements, and contribute to the American economy. They should not face additional uncertainty because of circumstances largely outside their control.

The removal of the grace period would significantly restrict job mobility and career advancement. H-1B workers already face challenges when changing employers, including sponsorship requirements, immigration paperwork, processing timelines, and uncertainty about maintaining lawful status and work authorization. Finding a suitable position, completing interviews, receiving an offer, and coordinating the required immigration filing can take considerable time. These steps are not entirely within the worker's control.

Without a reasonable transition period, workers may feel forced to remain in unfavorable employment situations out of fear of losing their ability to stay in the country. They may avoid pursuing promotions, better opportunities, or positions that more closely match their qualifications. This would limit professional growth, weaken workers' bargaining power, and make it harder for U.S. employers to recruit and retain experienced talent.

The consequences extend beyond individual workers. Many H-1B employees have spouses and children who depend on their employment and immigration status. Families may have mortgages, childcare expenses, education costs, and other long-term financial commitments. Abruptly removing the grace period could jeopardize household stability and disrupt the lives of children and families who have established roots in the United States.

The existing 60-day grace period provides a limited but meaningful opportunity to seek new employment, coordinate with a prospective employer, explore lawful immigration options, and make necessary arrangements. It does not guarantee continued employment or permanent residency; it simply provides reasonable time to respond to an unexpected job loss.

Retaining this safeguard would also benefit American businesses by helping them recruit experienced professionals and avoid losing valuable talent solely because an employee could not complete a job transition in time. It would support workforce stability, preserve institutional knowledge, and maintain the United States' ability to attract skilled professionals.

I respectfully request that DHS:

Retain the existing 60-day H-1B grace period.

Consider the disproportionate impact on workers facing lengthy green card backlogs and prolonged immigration uncertainty.

Recognize the practical time required to secure new employment and complete employer-sponsored immigration procedures.

Consider the effects on families, financial stability, career advancement, and U.S. employers.

Preserve reasonable transition protections for workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.

People who have worked hard, complied with immigration laws, paid taxes, and contributed to American society deserve a reasonable opportunity to navigate an unexpected employment disruption. Losing a job should not automatically put years of professional effort, financial investment, family stability, and future career opportunities at risk when a limited transition period can provide meaningful relief.

I urge DHS to preserve the 60-day grace period and avoid imposing additional hardship on law-abiding workers who are already navigating a complex immigration system. Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter strongly opposes removing the grace period and urges DHS to retain this safeguard.

I am an H-1B holder working as a Data Scientist at a major U.S. bank, where I build machine learning systems used in regulated lending decisions. I oppose this rule.

The 60-day grace period is not a loophole — it is a practical safeguard that keeps skilled workers in lawful status while they transfer to another employer, change status, or arrange an orderly departure. The rule would convert a manageable life event into immediate unlawful presence.

Even DHS's own analysis acknowledges the costs: workers losing wages, families facing sudden relocation expenses, and employers absorbing disruption and lost productivity. The practical effect will be the opposite of the stated goal. Rather than deterring abuse, the rule punishes compliant, high-skilled workers for ordinary job changes and hands leverage to the least scrupulous employers — precisely those firms most willing to exploit workers who cannot afford a single day out of status. That weakens, rather than strengthens, program integrity, and makes the United States less competitive for the talent its industries need.

I respectfully urge DHS to withdraw this proposal.

comments.commentText:
Dear USCIS and Department of Homeland Security,

I am writing to respectfully oppose the proposed elimination of the discretionary 60-day grace period under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).

I am a legal immigrant who has spent more than a decade in the United States, waiting patiently in the employment-based green card backlog due to country-of-birth limitations. During these years, my family and I have worked hard, paid taxes, contributed to the American economy, and built our lives around the belief that the United States is our home.

We have invested not only financially, but emotionally and socially in this country. We have purchased homes, taken on mortgages, raised U.S.-born children who attend American schools, and established deep roots in our communities. Our children know this country as their home, and our families have built their futures here.

Yet, despite following the legal immigration process for more than a decade, our ability to remain in the country can still depend on continuous employment. The green card backlog is largely outside our control, and losing a job can suddenly place everything we have built at risk.

I understand that immigration policy involves difficult decisions and that eliminating the green card backlog is not a simple task. I am not asking USCIS to resolve those longstanding challenges through this rule.

**My request is much simpler: Please preserve at least 60 days for families to make an orderly and dignified transition when employment unexpectedly ends.**

For a family that has lived in the United States for 10, 15, or even 20 years, leaving the country is not as simple as booking a flight.

We must consider:

- Selling or renting our homes and managing outstanding mortgages and financial obligations.
- Helping our U.S.-citizen children transition from their schools, friends, and the only home many have ever known.
- Closing bank accounts, transferring assets, and meeting tax and other legal obligations.
- Arranging housing, schooling, and employment in another country after spending much of our adult lives in the United States.
- Managing the emotional and financial consequences of uprooting an entire family.

These responsibilities cannot reasonably be completed overnight.

The existing 60-day grace period is not a guarantee of permanent residence, nor does it provide unrestricted employment authorization. It is a limited and reasonable safeguard that allows families time to find qualifying employment, explore lawful alternatives, or prepare to depart responsibly.

Eliminating this protection would impose significant hardship on families who have followed the rules, contributed to the economy, and waited patiently for permanent residency through no fault of their own.

It could also create unnecessary financial and administrative consequences, including distressed home sales, disrupted schooling, unsettled financial obligations, and abrupt departures from local communities.

I respectfully request that DHS:

1. **Retain the existing 60-day grace period** under 8 CFR 214.1(l)(2).
2. **Consider additional protections for long-term legal immigrants** with approved employment-based immigrant petitions who remain in green card backlogs due to per-country limitations.
3. **Ensure that families have a reasonable opportunity to depart with dignity**, even when continued employment or immigration sponsorship is no longer possible.
4. **Evaluate the impact on U.S.-citizen children, homeowners, and long-term taxpaying residents** before removing this safeguard.

After more than a decade of contributing to this country, we are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for a reasonable amount of time to handle our responsibilities and protect our families.

**If the United States cannot offer us permanent residency because of longstanding backlogs, it should at least allow us the dignity of a graceful exit.**

Sixty days is not an unreasonable request for families who have spent years, and sometimes decades, building their lives here.

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider this proposal and preserve the existing grace period.

Thank you for considering the perspective of long-term legal immigrants and their families.

Respectfully,

A Long-Term Legal Immigrant and Parent of U.S.-Citizen Children
comments.reason: The commenter respectfully opposes the proposed elimination to preserve an orderly transition.

comments.title: Comment Submitted by Anonymous
comments.commentText:
To the Department of Homeland Security,

I respectfully urge DHS to reconsider its proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B workers following the termination of their employment.

H-1B workers are not merely temporary employees. Many have lived in the United States for years, paid taxes, purchased homes, raised children, and become integral members of their communities. Unexpected job loss can happen to anyone due to layoffs, corporate restructuring, or economic downturns. Removing the grace period could turn an already difficult situation into an immediate family and financial crisis.

1. Families need reasonable time to make life-changing decisions

Finding a new employer willing to sponsor an H-1B petition takes time. Interviews, offer negotiations, employer approvals, immigration paperwork, and legal consultations cannot be completed overnight. If a new opportunity is not available, families need time to arrange international travel, secure housing at their destination, transport belongings, and settle outstanding obligations.

Without a reasonable transition period, families could face immense pressure to make major decisions within days, with little opportunity to understand their legal options or prepare for departure.

2. Homeownership, mortgages, and financial stability

Many H-1B families have purchased homes and committed to long-term mortgages, property taxes, insurance, and other financial obligations. These commitments do not disappear when employment ends.

If families are forced to leave abruptly, they may have to sell their homes under severe time pressure, potentially accepting substantial losses. Others may struggle to manage mortgage payments from abroad, increasing the risk of delinquency or foreclosure.

Foreclosures and distressed property sales can affect comparable home values, neighboring homeowners, local property-tax revenues, and mortgage lenders. Banks and financial institutions could face additional delinquencies, servicing costs, and foreclosure proceedings. These are potential downstream consequences that DHS should carefully assess before implementing this change.

3. Children and schools would face unnecessary disruption

H-1B families often have children enrolled in American schools who have established friendships, academic progress, and community connections. Children should not bear the consequences of an abrupt employment-related immigration deadline.

Parents need time to obtain school records, arrange housing and travel, address medical needs, and prepare their children for relocation. Eliminating the grace period could force families to disrupt their children's education with little notice, causing avoidable emotional and academic hardship.

4. The broader American economy is also affected

H-1B workers contribute to the economy as employees, taxpayers, homeowners, borrowers, and consumers. Their households support banks, insurance companies, utility providers, local businesses, and community services.

An abrupt departure can disrupt these economic relationships and impose costs on employers that lose experienced workers without sufficient time for knowledge transfer or workforce planning. The potential cumulative impact on housing markets, lenders, schools, and local communities deserves careful consideration.

5. The grace period provides a practical and limited safeguard

The 60-day grace period does not guarantee a new job or authorize indefinite residence. It provides a limited opportunity for eligible workers to seek another sponsoring employer, explore lawful immigration options, consult legal counsel, or prepare to depart the country responsibly.

Retaining this period would promote orderly compliance with immigration requirements while reducing unnecessary financial and family disruption. If DHS has concerns about misuse, it should consider targeted compliance measures rather than eliminating this reasonable transition period altogether.

Request

I respectfully request that DHS withdraw the proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period or retain a meaningful transition period for affected workers and their families.

Immigration policy should account not only for employment status but also for the real-world consequences of abrupt displacement. The potential disruption to children's education, mortgage payments, home values, financial institutions, employers, and local communities warrants serious consideration.

A limited transition period can make the difference between an orderly departure or job transition and a preventable family financial crisis. I urge DHS to consider these broader consequences and preserve the 60-day grace period.

Thank you for considering my comment.
comments.reason: The commenter urges DHS to reconsider and not eliminate the grace period.
